#5544. IBM puts agentic workloads at the heart of its AI operating model

Agentic workloads present a new operating challenge for enterprises putting artificial intelligence into production. As autonomous systems take on ongoing responsibilities, organizations must support decisions and actions across their data, applications and infrastructure.

IBM Corp.’s approach draws on the experiences of clients scaling AI across their organizations. That work helped identify the requirements underpinning its AI operating model, according to Ritika Gunnar (pictured), chief performance marketing officer of IBM.

“As you’re more successful in using AI, especially as AI is taking action, you now have workloads that are continuously being utilized,” she said. “You are incented to be always on because those agents are always taking action for you.”

Gunnar spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante and John Furrier for IBM’s AI Operating Model interview series in an exclusive interview on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed enterprise integration, data governance, human oversight and evaluating AI against business outcomes in preparation for IBM TechXchange 2026. (* Disclosure below.)

IBM’s AI operating model brings together four components that enterprises may already obtain from different providers. Applying them means accounting for established applications and business processes alongside emerging AI systems, Gunnar explained.

“You need to be able to integrate with your existing systems,” she said. “People aren’t going to run away from their SAP systems that exist, from their Salesforce systems that exist. What does it mean to integrate with those and have workloads that are representative of your past and your future together?”

The components have distinct roles: Data supplies current enterprise knowledge, workloads encompass applications and workflows, automation supports oversight and optimization, and hybrid cloud accommodates distributed operations. Their effectiveness depends on how they function together across agentic workloads, according to Gunnar.

“If you have your data and that data is feeding your systems, but you’re not really taking care of automation in a way where you have complete observability of all of your workloads with that AI infused, then you’re not necessarily having an optimal way of picking the right model or picking the right agents for those kinds of workloads,” she said.

The information supporting an agent’s decision may span operational systems, edge devices and context generated by other agents. Providing governed context requires enterprises to consider both the completeness of that information and how permissions travel with it, Gunnar explained.

“Our belief is if you can take data and if you can shift left a lot of the governance — a lot of the who has the right access to the right data at the right time — it becomes important because you flow that data in real time with the context and provenance of who actually has ownership of that data,” she said. “Therefore, the agents make much better decisions.”

Enterprises also depend on knowledge employees develop through experience rather than explicitly recording it in their systems. Prompts and other context can help convey that judgment, but capturing it remains an ongoing challenge, Gunnar pointed out.

“When you think about workloads today … there is a lot of it that will be autonomous in nature,” she said. “But in most cases, if you’re talking about your essential systems, you do have humans in the loop to be able to bring some of that tacit knowledge in place where the AI has not yet matured to be able to even get there.”

Agent activity generates logs of decisions and actions, while prompts record the instructions supplied to those systems. Together, that information supports an ongoing feedback loop between enterprise data and AI workloads, Gunnar explained.

“You can actually have multiple different permutations of that agent making a decision and having another set of eval loops actually doing an evaluation of, ‘Did that agent actually make the decisions?’” she said. “Would there have been a more performant way, a more accurate way, a more cost-effective way to be able to do that?”

Performance encompasses accuracy, timeliness and cost, with the intended business result guiding how those measures are assessed. Putting AI into production therefore requires organizations to examine the work itself alongside the technology supporting it, according to Gunnar.

“Make sure that you have all of these elements and that you’re really thinking about the outcomes, and you’re willing to start with what it means to take a look at the business process transformation,” she said. “That’s really where it’s at.”

#5543. Social Security COLA, tax break could narrow spending gap for older consumers in 2027

A Bank of America Institute report finds baby boomer and traditionalist households have weaker discretionary spending growth than other generations despite large wealth gains among the richest older households. Because many retirees rely on fixed income sources and benefit less from recent wage growth, their budgets have been under pressure. A temporary federal tax deduction for those 65 and older and a 3.6% Social Security cost-of-living adjustment for 2027 could modestly improve real incomes, particularly if inflation cools as forecast.   AI Summary

The spending growth of older consumers has trailed other age groups for the past year despite sizable wealth gains at the top. But a 2027 cost-of-living adjustment for Social Security recipients and temporary tax break could modestly improve their purchasing power, according to a Bank of America Institute report released last week.

Bank of America aggregated credit and debit card data to show that baby boomer and traditionalist households have posted weaker discretionary spending growth than other Americans for roughly a year. That marks a reversal from 2022 and 2023, when older households were outpacing others. Boomers were defined as those born between 1946 and 1964, while traditionalists are those born before 1946.

The report ties part of this slowdown to how wealth is distributed within the older cohorts. Using 2025 data from the Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances, the bank found that about two-thirds of net wealth among households headed by someone older than 65 is held by the top 10% of these households. This concentration means that stock market and asset gains may do little to support spending for most older consumers.

Overall consumer spending strength in 2026 appears to be driven primarily by wage and salary growth, particularly among lower- and middle-income working households. Older households, by contrast, depend on a broader mix of income sources and are less exposed to accelerating wages.

Fed survey data shows that as households age, a smaller share of income comes from wages or self-employment and more from pensions, Social Security, and interest, dividends or rental income. Bank of America’s internal data highlight the resulting divergence within older cohorts: Households over 62 that rely only on Social Security have average income and discretionary spending close to half that of their peers who drawing from Social Security, pensions and employment combined.

Discretionary spending is also more uneven across income tiers for older generations than for all households. Retirees are the least likely group to expect their finances to improve over the next six months, according to the study, reflecting the challenges of living on largely fixed income sources.

The report points to two policy levers that could support older consumers’ budgets in the near term:

COLAs are based on the year-over-year change in the third quarter for the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W). While these increases are designed to preserve purchasing power, they can be more or less generous depending on the inflation path in the year that follows.

In 2022, for example, inflation slowed sharply after a large COLA took effect, effectively boosting real benefits and helping older generations outspend other age cohorts in 2022 and 2023.

Consensus forecasts cited in the Bank of America report anticipate that overall inflation will cool in 2027, largely as the impact of higher gasoline prices fades. If that occurs, the 3.6% COLA could outpace actual price increases next year, delivering a more meaningful real income gain for households heavily reliant on Social Security.

The survey data shows that the largest spending growth gaps between older generations and all households are concentrated in discretionary categories like electronics, lodging, restaurants, clothing, furniture and airlines. In many of these areas, older cohorts’ year-over-year spending growth lags the overall population by several percentage points.

Some of this pattern likely reflects differences in preferences and life stages. But if Social Security benefits rise faster than prices in 2027 and the tax deduction continues to support middle-income seniors, the report suggests there may be room for older households’ discretionary spending growth to narrow the gap with other age groups.

Slower discretionary spending among older Americans, combined with highly concentrated wealth, underscores the financial pressures on many households that are past their peak earning years. For housing professionals, this has several implications:

Bank of America stresses that its findings are based on anonymized, aggregated transaction and survey data and should be considered alongside broader economic indicators.

#5541. Why homebuilders and lot sellers no longer price risk the same way

As slower sales and shrinking margins test homebuilders' financial flexibility, land developers and capital providers face different economic pressures. Builder Advisor Group CEO Tony Avila sees an industry adapting to a longer period of difficult conditions, even as investment interest persists.  AI Summary

Stagflation is an economic rule-breaker. It delivers the double whammy of a market downturn and high prices, both at once. The U.S. homebuilding industry’s mounting financial pressures have similarly coalesced into a riptide that grows harder to paddle against with each passing quarter.

Builders are selling homes more slowly, sacrificing margins to maintain sales volume, and finding that many of the land deals needed to replenish their pipelines no longer deliver acceptable returns and, in an increasing number of cases, barely yield positive net margins.

Yet the land developers supplying finished lots to builders have not faced the same level of financial pressure. Tony Avila, CEO of Builder Advisor Group and Avila Real Estate Capital, says that developers borrowing from his firm generally continue to earn higher margins than the homebuilders who buy their lots, and that the scarcity of finished lots in many markets continues to give sellers room to resist price cuts.

“Today there are more homebuilders than there are vacant developed lots in most markets,” Avila said in a November 2 interview with HousingWire TBD. “That makes it a lot sellers’ market as opposed to a lot buyers’ market.”

The imbalance reflects a growing fault line in the economics of U.S. homebuilding, and the risks on either side of that chasm. Builders must underwrite land based on current home prices, construction costs, incentives, and slower absorption rates, whereas developers with sufficient financial flexibility can wait for multiple bidders willing to meet their lot-price expectations, allowing some give-and-take on terms.

The result is a difficult alignment of interests among homebuilders, land sellers, lenders and investors, each of whom earns a bigger or smaller share of the return from the same ultimate source: the price a household can afford to pay for a new home.

Avila believes the industry is preparing for an indefinitely prolonged period of constrained homebuyer purchasing power rather than counting on a near-term return to the conditions that supported record profitability earlier this decade. His perspective draws on his firms’ work with homebuilders, land developers, capital providers and prospective acquirers, as well as discussions at the October 13 Forum for Housing Executives in Lafayette Hill, Pennsylvania.

“I think that everyone is getting prepared for a different landscape, a more challenging selling environment, and an environment where we are higher-for-longer on interest rates,” Avila said.

The adjustment extends beyond pricing and sales incentives. Builders are reassessing how much land they control, how quickly they can convert their investments into cash, which customers they can serve profitably, and how much financial leverage they can carry while waiting for demand to improve.

Avila compares the current environment more closely to the high-interest-rate housing market of 1981 than to the 2007 financial crisis. Appreciating the contrast and its after-effects may give those who do so a competitive jumpstart on a playbook. The GFC followed years of excessive construction, speculative investment and aggressive bank lending for residential development assets.

Today’s pressures differ markedly. The industry faces an affordability problem exacerbated by mortgage rates, inflation, household expenses and construction costs, while conventional bank financing for acquisition, development and construction remains well below the levels Avila recalls from the previous housing boom.

By his estimate, banks had more than $200 billion committed to AD&C lending around 2006, compared with about $90 billion today. Those figures are Avila’s historical comparison rather than a standardized statistical series, but they illustrate his view that the financing structure supporting residential development has changed substantially.

Private lenders and institutional land-capital providers have filled part of the gap. However, their participation does not eliminate the cost of financing land and construction, particularly when slower absorption extends the time between an initial investment and the eventual closing of a home.

Avila says his firm is seeing strong demand for private development financing, even as builders become more selective about new commitments.

“We are being deluged with loan requests right now across the board,” he said.

Financing availability is not the same as the ability to put it to profitable use. Higher borrowing costs, slower inventory turnover, and reduced homebuilding margins can make a project economically unattractive even when a lender is willing to provide capital.

The financial pressure is evident in the industry benchmarks presented at the October Forum, which brought together executives from major public, private, and internationally owned homebuilders, as well as developers and capital providers.

According to the Forum’s survey findings, public-builder gross margins have declined from about 26% at their fourth-quarter 2022 peak to about 20%, while EBITDA margins have fallen from about 18% to 9%. Sales incentives, which accounted for roughly 2% to 3% of home prices in 2021, have risen to about 8% to 12% in the current environment.

The private-builder survey data tell a similar story. Median gross margins declined from about 20% in 2024 to 18% in 2025, while returns on equity fell from about 17% to 6% and debt-to-capital ratios rose from about 52% to 62%.

These figures describe an industry in which builders have considerably less room to absorb adverse changes in selling prices, construction costs and land acquisition economics. They also help explain why capital allocation decisions that were relatively forgiving during periods of rapid sales and rising home prices now carry greater financial risk.

The differences between homebuilders’ and land developers’ financial positions have become increasingly evident in negotiations over finished lots. As builders revise their assumptions about selling prices, incentives, and absorption rates, the prices they can justify paying for land are moving further from what some developers are prepared to accept.

For developers backed by patient capital, slower lot sales may be preferable to accepting prices that do not meet their investment objectives. That financial agility can sustain land values even as builders who purchase those lots face declining returns.

“If you’re patient capital and you’re a lot seller, you just wait,” Avila said.

The resulting disagreement over land values is constraining transactions. Avila says the gap between what sellers expect and what builders can justify has become a primary obstacle to closing deals.

The difficulty is compounded when slower sales force builders to revise their expectations about how quickly a community will generate revenue. A parcel that penciled attractively when homes were selling faster may no longer produce acceptable returns if the same investment must be carried for longer.

Avila also sees signs that builders are recognizing some of those changed economics through land impairments and the write-off of deposits on transactions they no longer intend to complete. He characterizes impairments to date as relatively modest compared with the land and work-in-process assets on builders’ balance sheets, though he expects additional charges if margins continue to contract.

That does not necessarily mean a broad land-price correction is imminent. The availability of finished lots, the number of competing builders, the strength of local buyer demand, and the patience of land sellers’ financial backers can lead to very different outcomes across markets.

The customer segments a property can serve factor into the calculation. Builders targeting move-up, second move-up, and active-adult buyers may have different underwriting opportunities than competitors focused on entry-level households, which face more severe down-payment, monthly-payment, and cost-of-living constraints.

The underlying question is how much of the industry’s deteriorating economics will eventually be reflected in land prices, how much builders will continue to absorb, and how long the current disagreement between buyers and sellers can persist.

According to Avila, the challenges have not eliminated investor interest in U.S. homebuilding. Avila’s advisory firm has identified 60 prospective strategic, financial, and hybrid acquirers of homebuilding businesses.

That number represents a pool of potential buyers, not completed or pending acquisitions. Still, it suggests that investors continue to evaluate opportunities even as homebuilding profitability has weakened and valuations have become harder to reconcile.

Avila recently returned from meetings in Japan, South Korea, and Singapore, where he says interest in U.S. for-sale housing remained strong. In his assessment, the sector continues to compare favorably with several other real estate investment categories, including segments of the office, retail, and multifamily markets.

That view reflects both his capital markets experience and his firms’ commercial activities. Builder Advisor Group advises homebuilding companies on mergers, acquisitions, and strategic transactions, while Avila Real Estate Capital provides private real estate financing and investment opportunities in a market that also includes institutional land banks, global asset managers, and other specialized capital providers.

Avila therefore has direct visibility into investor inquiries and financing demand, and a business interest in expanding private capital’s role in residential development. His observations offer a useful perspective on investment activity, although the number of interested investors does not indicate how much capital will ultimately be deployed or on what terms.

When prospective buyers and sellers disagree on the value of a homebuilding company, the difference between the number of would-be investors and their ultimate motivation to put capital to work tends to come clearer.

“If your earnings are down, that’ll obviously adversely affect your valuation,” Avila said.

For owners of private homebuilding companies, this creates difficult choices about whether to pursue a sale, seek additional capital, bring in a strategic partner, or continue operating independently while waiting for stronger financial results.

The major Japanese-backed homebuilding companies have been among the most prominent acquirers in recent years. Daiwa House, Sekisui House and Sumitomo Forestry have expanded their U.S. operations through various ownership and integration strategies, supported by long-term investment horizons that can extend well beyond the planning cycles typical of American homebuilding companies.

Avila believes those three companies are now focusing on digesting, integrating and absorbing earlier acquisitions rather than maintaining the same pace of acquisitions. He says other prospective buyers remain active, though he declined to identify the companies involved in confidential discussions.

The October Forum noted 12 announced homebuilder M&A transactions in 2026, compared with 17 in all of 2025, with Japanese-backed companies accounting for approximately five of the current year’s deals.

Those figures do not telegraph a new wave of imminent acquisitions. They do suggest that the industry’s ownership structure remains in flux as investors assess the relationship among current earnings, future growth potential, land positions and the price required to acquire an operating platform.

Another development Avila describes is homebuilders’ participation in private real estate credit.

He says that approximately 15 public and private homebuilding companies, including U.S. businesses owned by Japanese parents, have invested in AREC’s debt fund. These investments are among several ways financially stronger builders are deploying available cash, alongside share repurchases and acquisitions.

The arrangement shows how some homebuilders are financing residential development beyond their direct construction operations. It also highlights differences in financial flexibility among builders, particularly between companies generating substantial cash and those relying on outside financing to support their existing land and construction commitments.

Private credit, institutional land banking and other financing structures offer different combinations of cost, control, risk and flexibility. Their attractiveness depends on whether they improve a builder’s overall return on invested capital after accounting for the cost of obtaining and using the financing.

In some circumstances, keeping land off a builder’s balance sheet can preserve liquidity and reduce exposure to declining land values. In others, the cost of such flexibility can erode too much of the margin available from selling the completed home.

The upshot is that expanding financing alternatives does not resolve the industry’s underlying economic problem. Capital providers must earn returns, land developers must recover their investment and earn a profit, and homebuilders must deliver houses at prices customers can afford while generating sufficient earnings to sustain their businesses.

Right now, those three root business drivers have gone out of sync.

Avila’s observations on the characteristics of successful builders offer a useful way to connect the capital-market discussion to decisions within homebuilding companies.

He identifies stronger margins, lower leverage, attractive finished-lot positions, higher returns on capital and the ability to serve a broader range of buyers as key indicators of financial strength. Geographic diversification can provide additional protection, although he notes that builders operating in individual markets with favorable supply-and-demand balances and dynamics can also perform well.

The strategic adjustments he describes are already underway among the builders and borrowers his firms serve.

Some companies that historically focused on entry-level buyers are re-platforming products and land positions into higher price points and move-up segments to reach households with greater purchasing flexibility. Others are reducing their reliance on speculative construction and placing greater emphasis on build-to-order sales.

Avila says that the shift toward build-to-order has become increasingly visible among his clients and borrowers.

The appeal is straightforward. When homes take longer to sell, reducing speculative inventory can limit the capital tied up in completed or nearly completed homes without buyers, though it may also require changes to sales operations, construction scheduling and customer expectations.

At the same time, builders are reviewing overhead, direct construction costs and the pace of land acquisition and monetization. The objective is not simply to cut spending but to preserve financial capacity to continue operating and investing when demand remains uncertain. For acquisition candidates, operating capabilities may increasingly shape how investors assess earnings durability and future growth potential.

Avila says prospective homebuilding company acquirers favor operators with growing earnings, strong lot positions, strong margins, and high returns on capital and equity. The ability to control or bank land for future development can also make a target more attractive.

Those criteria reinforce the distinction between having access to capital and having a business that can earn an acceptable return on that capital. Meanwhile, builders must operate within the purchasing power of today’s customers rather than on demand that may emerge under more favorable conditions.

That is the common challenge facing the industry’s capital providers and operators. The long-term need for housing may attract investors, but the immediate economics of building and selling homes determine whether their investments generate acceptable returns.

For homebuilders, the near- and medium-term future may reward companies that can preserve financial flexibility, secure land at workable prices, adapt their product offerings and improve operating performance without relying on a rapid recovery in demand.

For land developers and capital providers, the challenge is related yet distinct. Their opportunities ultimately depend on builders’ ability to convert land and financing into homes that customers can purchase profitably.

The industry has begun adjusting to that reality, Avila suggests, although the process remains spotty across markets and companies. In his view, the next phase of homebuilding’s capital cycle may be shaped as much by the terms on which builders, land sellers and investors agree to do business as by the timing of the next increase in home sales.

#5540. Salesforce to buy customer service automation startup Cresta for reported $2.7B

Salesforce Inc. has agreed to buy Cresta Intelligence Inc., a venture-backed provider of customer service software.

The cloud giant didn’t disclose the financial terms in its late Monday announcement of the deal. The Information reported that Salesforce is paying $2.7 billion.

Cresta’s platform uses artificial intelligence to answer customer inquiries. It can also perform more advanced tasks such as scheduling doctor’s appointments. The platform personalizes its output based on each customer’s preferences, past interactions with the support team and related data.

Companies can customize Cresta by creating AI voice agents optimized for specific support request categories. For example, an electronics retailer could develop an agent focused on processing device returns. Cresta makes it possible to customize details such as the AI model that powers an agent and its regulatory compliance guardrails.

The platform can split complex support requests into smaller tasks to ease processing. A company could use one agent to interpret a ticket, another to find relevant help desk articles and a third to scan those articles for troubleshooting advice. Such agent ensembles often provide faster response times than a single multi-purpose agent. They save time by parallelizing tasks that would usually have to be carried out after one another.

Cresta ships its platform with an agent called Deputy. It’s geared toward particularly complex support tickets that require multiple employees to process. Deputy automatically collects the information needed to fulfill the user’s request and then loops in the relevant workers. From there, it manages follow-up tasks such as sending reminders about outstanding tasks.

Another agent provides human support representatives with real-time guidance during customer conversations. Cresta can, for example, point out potential upselling opportunities. It can also pull relevant information from external systems.

The company offers its core support automation features alongside various related tools. A feature called Opera enables organizations to fine-tune AI models for specific customer service use cases. Another tool, Synthetic Customers, provides AI-generated support conversations. Companies teams can use that data to test the reliability of newly created AI agents.

“By uniting our platform with Salesforce, we will realize our full vision at scale, embedding real-time conversation intelligence and agentic experiences directly into Salesforce’s first-class customer service Platform,” said Cresta Chief Executive Officer Ping Wu.

The deal is the second multibillion-dollar acquisition that Salesforce has made in the customer service market this year. It previously agreed to buy Fin Inc., formerly Intercom Inc, for $3.6 billion. Like Cresta, the company developed an AI platform capable of automatically answering support requests.

Salesforce’s largest acquisition this year is the $5.66 billion purchase of Braze Inc. it signed last month. The deal will buy it an AI marketing platform that can automatically deliver personalized promotions to customers.

Salesforce expects to close both the Braze and Cresta deals in its 2028 fiscal year, which starts next February.

#5539. Jeff Glover goes indie after 17 years with Keller Williams (EXCLUSIVE)

Jeff Glover, founder of Live Unreal Companies |

Jeff Glover takes Glover Agency independent after 17 years with Keller Williams, telling Inman the move is about keeping Glover U broker-agnostic.

Glover Agency, the Michigan team Jeff Glover founded in 2008, became fully independent on Nov. 1, ending a 17-year run with Keller Williams. The move comes roughly three months after Glover sold his three Keller Williams market centers.

The team says it has been Michigan’s top homeselling team across all brands in 11 of the past 13 years and has sold more than 10,000 homes. It operates out of four offices in Birmingham, Plymouth, Fenton and Grand Rapids.

Glover Agency will now operate only in Michigan and isn’t affiliated with any franchise or national brand.

With Glover Agency out of the franchise system, none of Glover’s Live Unreal Companies are tied to a single brand, which Glover says frees Glover U to work with agents and leaders at every brokerage in the U.S. and Canada.

In an exclusive interview with Inman, Glover said the decision had a lot to do with Glover U, the coaching and training company where he now spends most of his time. Glover U has long pitched itself as broker-agnostic, but Glover said his KW ties kept closing doors, even after the market center sale.

In August, Glover sold his ownership stakes in three Keller Williams market centers across Michigan, where he served as majority owner and operating principal. He said the sale supported Glover U’s broker-agnostic approach to serving agents across the U.S. and Canada. The three market centers combined closed nearly $1 billion in sales volume in 2025.

“Most of [the potential Glover U clients], if they don’t know me and their agents don’t know me, they’re not going to return my call,” Glover said of leaders at rival brands. “I had leaders of large companies — I mean, the largest that exist today — say, ‘Hey, Jeff, that’s great you sold your franchises, and we’re definitely open to you helping our agents, but I’m sorry, I can’t put a Keller Williams guy on our stage.'”

Joining another brand would have recreated the same problem. Going independent, Glover says, removes it.

“This move furthers the brand-agnostic approach we’ve been working toward, and now there should be little to no objection to somebody trusting me with their agents, because I don’t have a dog in the fight,” Glover said. “They don’t have to worry about me pushing their agents to go to any one company when I’m independent.”

The second driver is marketing. Glover Agency has advertised under its own name for years on TV, radio and billboards, and Glover said most Michigan consumers already assumed the team was independent.

Franchise rules on how the team could advertise, down to how large its name could appear, made it harder for individual agents to build their own brands.

“It’s very hard for them to create a brand within a brand within a brand,” Glover said. “It’s confusing to consumers. It’s confusing to other agents and other companies.”

Glover said top teams that understand marketing already know where consumer loyalty sits.

“The everyday seller and everyday buyer generally doesn’t say, ‘ We’re listing our home with Keller Williams or with Coldwell Banker,'” Glover said. “They say, ‘We’re listing our home with ‘Joe Smith’ or ‘Amy Duncan.'”

For the consumer, Glover said that the brand is “just the gravy on top.” “The brand helps, but today’s consumer resonates more with an agent’s or a team’s brand than with the company’s brand,” he said.

Day-to-day operations at Glover Agency are run by CEO Taylor Kerrigan. Glover remains involved and still lists and sells. He said he was prospecting in front of the team’s agents just before speaking with Inman on Friday.

“For our clients, nothing changes about how we serve them, other than a more personalized approach,” Kerrigan said in a statement. “What does change is that the name on the door is entirely ours.”

Glover joined Keller Williams in 2009, and the company says the team climbed as high as No. 3 nationally among all groups and No. 1 among expansion teams for homes sold. Asked what would be hardest about leaving, Glover didn’t hesitate.

“Without question, my relationship with Gary Keller,” he said, pointing to Keller’s early top 100 mastermind and a smaller circle of about a dozen agents, the Pirate Group, who got regular access to the KW co-founder. “I wouldn’t be where I am today if it weren’t for him.”

Glover said he still considers Keller a mentor and expects to keep speaking at KW events “so long as I’m welcome.”

The timing puts Glover on the opposite side of an industry trend. Consolidation has dominated brokerage headlines this year, including Compass–Anywhere and Real–REMAX, and independents face growing pressure to align with a larger platform.

Glover doesn’t think independence is right for everyone. He said it works for owners who know what agents need today, such as database growth, leverage and help building personal brands, and who have the energy to deliver it.

“For the person who somewhat wants the easy button, and maybe they’re at a point in their life where they don’t have the energy or time to pour into their company,” he said, joining a franchise or a company like Real, eXp or LPT “makes a lot of sense for that individual.”

For Glover, the bigger bet is on Glover U.

“The biggest thing is neutralizing Glover U so that it will be the No. 1 training and coaching company on the planet for real estate agents at the rate we’re growing,” he told Inman. “And I can’t do that if I’m affiliated with any one brand. So that’s a big part of it. The other part is the freedom and flexibility this gives us to help our agents grow their brands even bigger.”

#5537. Generative media inference startup fal raises $1.3B at a $16B valuation

Generative media inference startup fal today announced it has raised $1.3 billion in new funding at a valuation of $16 billion, according to Bloomberg.

The company will spend the money on computing power and on hiring beyond its current 185 employees.

Fal provides a cloud platform for running image, video and audio generation models, and developers reach all of them through a single application programming interface. Entertainment studios, advertising agencies and game developers are among the customers using those models in production, according to the company.

In-house researchers also post-train some of those models to run faster. Over the past year that work has centered on video, in partnership with the open- and closed-source developers that build the models. Some of the deals pay fal licensing fees or a share of revenue, Bloomberg reported.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Burkay Gur told the outlet the round is as large as it is because demand has surged and serving it takes more compute. “We hit a point in summer where we were not able to serve our customers and had to rate-limit them,” he said. Pretraining a model of fal’s own is not on the near-term agenda, said Gur, who did not rule it out for later.

Annualized revenue at fal passed $800 million earlier this year, a person familiar with the matter told Bloomberg. The valuation puts fal just behind rival inference provider Fireworks AI Inc., which closed $1.5 billion in funding at a $17.5 billion valuation in July. Several people familiar with the finances of inference companies told TechCrunch that gross margins across the sector remain thin because compute is expensive to buy or lease.

Gur started the company in 2021 with Chief Technology Officer Gorkem Yurtseven. His resume includes leading machine learning work at Coinbase Global Inc. and an engineering role at Oracle Corp. Yurtseven was previously a developer at Amazon.com Inc.

Bessemer Venture Partners led the Series F round, and its partner Talia Goldberg is joining the board of Features & Labels Inc., as fal is formally known. Nvidia Corp., Sound Ventures, HOF Capital and T. Rowe Price Group Inc. also participated. Fal described Nvidia as a strategic investor.

Today’s announcement also covered an April round led by Sequoia Capital. That Series E round raised $350 million at an $8 billion valuation, per Bloomberg, and fal said the two rounds come to $1.65 billion combined. Last December, the company raised $140 million at a $4.5 billion valuation.

Investors have now put more than $1.9 billion into the company.

#5536. NIMBYs cite a 155-year-old law to thwart a San Francisco project

Opponents sued San Francisco over an AB 2011 approval for 848 homes at the Marina Safeway site, invoking Section 1983 of the Civil Rights Act of 1871, a Reconstruction-era law also known as the Ku Klux Klan Act, to keep the case in federal court. The developer argues neighbors have no constitutional right to a hearing and contamination issues can be addressed before occupancy.   AI Summary

California state lawmakers have spent years tilting the rules toward new housing.

Projects that meet fixed standards can skip public hearings, and cities that say no face legal and financial risk. Still, muncipal and local neighborhood opponents never seem to run out of ways to try to scuttle projects. A Northern California federal court is embroiled in one of the latest examples.

In San Francisco, one of the most expensive housing cities in the world, opponents of an 848-unit residential structure above an existing Safeway grocery store have escalated to a new level. They invoked the Civil Rights Act of 1871, a law passed to protect Black Americans from Ku Klux Klan violence, when they sued the city in September.

Assembly Bill 2011 is increasingly at the center of these disputes. The 2022 state law lets qualifying projects on commercially zoned land skip public hearings and environmental review. Lawmakers broadened it last year, while community opposition groups keep probing its edges.

Neighbors and other opponents argue that the Safeway project doesn’t qualify for the shortcut. They claim the city shut them out of the process. Last week, the Marina Safeway developer’s lawyers asked the court to dismiss the suit. The filing called the opposition’s tactic “a deeper perversion” of a law meant to protect Black Americans from Klan violence. They argue that civil rights statutes exist to protect victims of discrimination, not to serve as “a weapon” for one of San Francisco’s “most well-resourced communities” to block new home development.

The developers’ plan would replace the Safeway at 15 Marina Blvd. and its parking lot with 848 homes. Eighty-six would be for lower-income households. The homes would rise in towers of 22 and 18 stories above a newly built grocery store at ground level. The site is zoned for 40 feet.

California AB 2011 instructs city planners to check only that the plans meet fixed rules. San Francisco declared the project eligible Aug. 13.

In response, YesAnd Foundation, Neighborhoods United SF and four residents sued Sept. 11 in federal court in San Francisco. The defendants named are the city, its planning and public health directors, and PG&E. PG&E once operated a power plant on the site.

Align Real Estate and Marina Property Owner LLC are named as real parties in interest.

The complaint says the plaintiffs “support the creation of housing generally.” It accuses city planners of “rubber-stamping” a project that doesn’t qualify.

The neighbors’ only federal claim says the permitting and approval shortcut denied them a public hearing, violating their due process rights. They filed the case under Section 1983, part of a 1871 law. It is the only claim that qualifies the case for federal court.

Their other six claims arise under California law. Holland & Knight, the developer’s firm, argues that civil rights laws have long been “powerless” to undo the effects of the housing shortage. The state’s own housing law says the crisis has caused “discrimination against low-income and minority households.”

The brief says California has finally moved to end its pattern of privileging existing homeowners over people who need housing. The neighbors, it argues, want to use civil rights law “not to protect the victims of discrimination.” It says Section 1983 targeted a Klan “campaign of violence and deception,” quoting a 1985 Supreme Court ruling.

The brief also cites a 2008 Ninth Circuit ruling that rejected a similar claim from neighbors in Spokane. That court held neighbors have no constitutional right to a hearing on someone else’s permit. The brief argues that accepting the claim would turn every ministerial approval into a potential federal lawsuit.

But the plaintiffs also turned to a more common approach in fighting projects. They argue there are environmental dangers.

The Safeway sits on the site of an old PG&E steam plant, next to a former coal-gas plant. A state toxics official told city planners in December 2025 she didn’t expect the site “to qualify for streamlined approval.” She cited 2023 petroleum readings 10 times the residential screening level.

In 2024, the regional Water Board, the lead regulator, closed the cleanup of petroleum from the steam plant. It found “no unacceptable public health risks for the current land use.” That finding rested on the store’s commercial use, and the board said it “may reconsider” if the use changes.

The neighbors say the city approved the project before anyone sampled soil beneath the store. In February, the complaint says, the developer’s consultant acknowledged “a data gap.” The consultant said Safeway would not allow drilling while the store operates.

The developer’s lawyers say AB 2011 requires cleanup only before the city issues a certificate of occupancy. The neighbors argue that full contamination assessment must come first.

The brief says state law now strongly favors housing. It cites the Housing Accountability Act, which it says requires courts to give “the fullest possible weight” to approving homes. Under that law, it argues, a city’s finding can be overturned only if no reasonable person could have reached it.

The developer’s attorneys target the lawsuit’s placement in federal court. Federal courts can’t issue the California-style court orders the neighbors want, they argue. If the federal claim fails, they contend, the case belongs in state court. Their brief notes no California court has yet interpreted AB 2011. U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín will hear the motion Feb. 4, 2027.

#5534. MSRs trade at richest levels in decades as lenders, funds pile in

Mortgage servicing rights are trading at their richest levels in decades, with pristine MSR multiples nearing 7x as more lenders choose to retain servicing and build recapture platforms.  AI Summary

Chicago-based Rate has recently changed its servicing strategy, retaining mortgage servicing rights (MSRs) instead of selling.

“We’ve been retaining all of our MSRs for the last 12 months, so we’re over $50 billion in MSR retention,” CEO Victor Ciardelli said in an exclusive interview with HousingWire. “We really believe in retaining the MSRs, staying close to the customer.”

Rate’s approach reflects a broader trend of mortgage lenders holding onto their portfolios or seeking to add MSRs as a way to recapture borrowers when rates eventually fall.

John Sullivan, managing director of MSR advisory services at Milliman, has seen that shift firsthand. Speaking during IMN’s Mortgage Servicing Rights Conference in New York on Monday, he said he’s having more conversations with clients about retaining their portfolios “unless liquidity is an issue,” and about monetizing them if they are not hedging.

Higher demand for MSRs is not limited to independent mortgage banks (IMBs). Depository institutions are also showing more interest, executives told HousingWire during the conference.

“Banks historically are not great at recapture, but we think that given some changes on the Basel capital front, we’re going to see more bank participation in this space on a go-forward basis, and I think banks will think about just customer acquisition in general, cross-selling in general,” said Larry Goldstone, president of capital markets and lending at BSI Financial Services.

Strategic investors are also willing to grow their portfolios. Rob Williams, co-founder and CEO at Grander Investment Management, a specialized asset manager focused on MSRs, said he’s tactical but sees MSRs as a “spectacular asset” that can reach double-digit returns.

“I can probably be more patient,” he said during the conference, when comparing his approach to the other buyers. “I can be more tactical.”

The buyer base views MSRs through different lenses.

Rich McRedmond, managing director at CrossCountry Mortgage, said that while banks see MSRs as part of their consumer banking strategy, real estate investment trusts (REITs) see them as a pure investment. And mortgage companies see them as a borrower recapture tool “from when they get the mortgage to when they get the next mortgage.”

Conventional, pristine MSRs are seeing 7x multiples amid high demand, a level not reached in more than two decades.

“We’ve seen some pretty extraordinary multiples of late,” Goldstone said. “This is usually an inexpensive asset, and therefore an asset that people want to be able to own. I think you could hedge MSR pretty effectively and still get low-double digits, high-single digit returns up until about the last year. That’s pretty attractive for an asset that really doesn’t have a whole lot of credit risk associated with it.”

Simon Aldrich, senior executive vice president at Freedom Mortgage, believes that at this point, “it’s very difficult to be in this market if you don’t have recapture.”

“In our model, we don’t hedge, so I’m not worried about rates going up or rates going down. Rates go up, I get the pickup at slower speeds. Rates go down, our call center kicks into gear.”

Bayview Asset Management, which acquires MSRs from the bulk and flow markets and uses five different subservicers, has also built out a full recapture strategy, including through its acquisition of Guild Mortgage. Managing director Michael Lau said Bayview has partnered with investors, including sovereign wealth funds and pension funds, that have long-duration strategies.

“MSRs are great because they’re not correlated to the equity or the bond market, and gives them something alternative that also, because we hedge out all the interest rate risk for them, delivers a very consistent return on their money, net of our fees,” Lau said.

Some companies have taken advantage of current pricing to sell MSRs for different reasons, including to pay back debt or raise funds.

In the third quarter, Rocket Companies sold $23 billion of unpaid principal balance (UPB) for $379 million in cash proceeds, retaining the subservicing and recapture services on nearly 70% of the MSRs sold. Analysts told HousingWire the company usually sells production in the wholesale channel due to lower recapture possibility.

Pennymac Financial Services entered into an agreement to sell $29 billion in UPB of low-coupon conventional MSRs, with $490 million of proceeds expected to pay down debt. The transaction is expected to close in the fourth quarter.

Meanwhile United Wholesale Mortgage (UWM) sold about $60 billion — at a roughly 6x multiple — to JPMorgan Chase, sources told HousingWire. The companies declined to comment. This is part of a plan to bring up to $80 billion of MSRs to market in the fourth quarter, with the expectation of being paid more than $1.8 billion in an attempt to reduce leverage.

Newrez President Baron Silverstein said his company is taking a disciplined approach. Across the Newrez portfolio, 60% of loans were originated before or during the COVID-19 pandemic.

“In today’s market, given where we are from a rate perspective, there’s pressure in a competitive environment where MSRs get created — where that gain on sale is from an all-in gain-on-sale perspective on loans that we originate or buy. And when we think about that, we get very selective and stay very disciplined about how we put that capital to work,” Silverstein said.

“When you think about hedging in a market like this, that also requires a lot of capital, and it’s very challenging in these markets today, regardless of the interest rate environment. This has been the case for the last year to year and a half.”

Looking ahead, servicing executives believe that multiples can stay higher as elevated mortgage rates reduce prepayment risks, which supports MSR cash flows. Some of them said multiples could move lower if there’s a liquidity issue due to large bulk sales hitting the market.

Regulation could also play a role. “If Basel III goes through and the banks decide to get back into the space, I think the high-six multiples could be relatively inexpensive,” Goldstone said. “You could see multiples in the 7x-8x category.”

#5533. Block shares rise after third-quarter beat and a third straight guidance raise

Shares of Block Inc. rose more than 7% in late trading today after the payments and financial services company beat third-quarter expectations and raised its full-year guidance for the third straight time.

For the quarter that ended on Sept. 30, Block reported adjusted earnings of $1.13 per share, up from 54 cents in the same quarter of the previous year, on revenue of $6.72 billion, up nearly 10% year-over-year. Analysts were expecting $1.03 per share on revenue of $6.58 billion.

Gross profit grew 22%, to $3.24 billion, and finished ahead of the company’s own guidance. Adjusted operating income almost doubled, to a record $923 million, and the adjusted operating margin rose to 29% of gross profit. Product development spending fell 11% from a year earlier, reflecting the workforce cut Block made in February.

Operating income on an unadjusted basis rose a more modest 5%, to $428 million, held back by $435 million in contingencies, restructuring and other charges. Net income attributable to common stockholders came to $566 million, compared with $462 million a year earlier.

Cash App gross profit grew 27% to $2.07 billion. Monthly transacting actives reached 60 million in September, and Block named Neighborhoods as a key driver after the loyalty network auto-enrolled more than 30,000 Square seller locations in August. Consumer lending originations rose 40% to $19 billion, led by Cash App Borrow and Afterpay Post-Purchase. Transaction, loan and consumer receivable losses climbed 66% as that lending grew.

Square gross payment volume grew 14%, to $76.4 billion, the fastest rate since the first quarter of 2023, with U.S. growth accelerating to 10.4%. Square’s gross profit kept pace at $1.16 billion. Block’s bitcoin business shrank again, as gross profit there halved to $52 million after the company cut fees on certain bitcoin transactions in Cash App.

Business highlights in the quarter included the July alpha release of Buzz, an open-source workspace for people and AI agents that has since had more than two dozen updates. General availability of Cash App Tags tap-to-pay hardware followed in August. In September, Block said it would open Cash App Score, its in-house credit score, to outside lenders through Nova Credit Inc.

Much of Chief Executive Jack Dorsey’s shareholder letter dealt with AI. Block, he wrote, has “meaningfully crossed the chasm” in turning itself into a company that “streams intelligence as people need it.”

Pilots of Buzz with prospective customers began in October, and Block expects to book its first machine intelligence revenue in the fourth quarter. Builderlab, the ecosystem Block created to sell Buzz and related tools to other companies, will be formally introduced at a San Francisco event on Nov. 10.

Fourth-quarter guidance calls for gross profit to grow 15%, to $3.32 billion. Adjusted earnings are forecast at $1.15 per share, a cent below the $1.16 analysts had expected. For the full year, Block now projects gross profit of $12.63 billion, up from the $12.51 billion it forecast in August, and adjusted earnings of $4.15 per share, up from $4.02. The consensus estimate was $4.06.

A preliminary outlook for 2027 calls for gross profit to grow at least 15%, to $14.52 billion. Adjusted operating income is expected to rise 30% next year, to $4.58 billion, well above the $3.51 billion target Block set at its investor day in November 2025.

#5531. CrowdStrike to acquire cybersecurity startups Fiddler AI, Dreadnode for reported $495M

CrowdStrike Holdings Inc. today disclosed plans to buy Fiddler AI Inc. and Dreadnode Inc., two startups that specialize in securing artificial intelligence agents.

The company announced the deals alongside an update to its Falcon Guardian product.

The Wall Street Journal reported that CrowdStrike will spend $495 million on the acquisitions. Fiddler is believed to account for about four-fifths of that sum. The Palo Alto, California-based startup sells a platform that developers use to test their AI agents for risks before launching them. The software spots issues such as malicious AI-generated code and training data leaks.

Fiddler can try different model and configuration combinations to find the one that minimizes an agent’s risk level. If the agent still generates prompts that breach cybersecurity rules, developers can use the platform to study the reasoning workflow that produced them. Fiddler says that its software makes it easier to identify the specific processing step that went wrong and fix it.

Once an agent is in production, Fiddler uses a series of custom models called Centor to block threats. It filters malicious prompts and blocks harmful output. According to the company, Centor adds less than 80 milliseconds of latency to the requests it reviews.

“As AI security and observability converge, enterprises need to understand their agents’ actions, intervene when they go off course, and explain why,” said Fiddler co-founder and Chief Executive Officer Krishna Gade.

Dreadnode, the other startup that CrowdStrike is acquiring, takes a different approach to securing AI agents. Whereas Fiddler analyzes agents’ prompt processing workflows to identify erroneous steps, Dreadnode launches simulated cyberattacks to reveal vulnerabilities. The company says that its platform uses more than 100 breach tactics to identify weak points.

Dreadnode also looks for vulnerabilities in the MCP servers that an AI agent uses to carry out its work. The platform ranks the issues that it finds by severity, which enables administrators to fix the most urgent ones first.

CrowdStrike plans to integrate Dreadnode’s technology into its Falcon Guardian product. The latter tool can map out the AI agents in a company’s technology environment and ensure that they meet cybersecurity standards. According to CrowdStrike, Falcon Guardian will use vulnerability data from Dreadnode to generate cybersecurity improvement recommendations.

The product is also receiving a second new feature that CrowdStrike revealed in conjunction with the two acquisitions. The AI Kill Switch, as it’s called, enables administrators to manually shut down an AI agent that is exhibiting risky behavior. The feature can also be used to remove the agent’s network access and prevent it from relaunching.

“CrowdStrike introduces a decisive new way to rapidly disrupt dangerous AI activity when risk emerges,” Michael Devins, a director of product marketing at CrowdStrike, explained in a blog post. “This is the first step toward broader enforcement to coordinate containment across the endpoints, identities, cloud environments, SaaS applications, and browsers where agents operate.”

#5530. Finance of America grows origination volume but reports $110M loss in Q3

Finance of America reported a $110M net loss in Q3 2026, driven mainly by $125M in noncash fair value adjustments. Funded volume rose 24% year over year to $748M, while adjusted net income was $6M and adjusted EBITDA was $17M.   AI Summary

Finance of America (FOA) reported a net loss of $110 million in the third quarter of 2026, as noncash fair value adjustments weighed on results despite growth in the company’s home equity lending business.

The Plano, Texas-based company on Tuesday reported $748 million in funded volume for the quarter ending Sept. 30, up 24% from $603 million during the same period last year. Year-to-date funded volume reached $2.07 billion, a 17% increase from the first nine months of 2025.

FOA recorded a basic loss of $5.24 per share, compared with a loss of 98 cents per share in the third quarter of 2025. The quarterly net loss was primarily driven by $125 million in noncash fair value adjustments.

On an adjusted basis, FOA reported net income of $6 million, or 28 cents per share, compared with $33 million, or $1.33 per share, a year earlier. Adjusted EBITDA totaled $17 million, down from $55 million in the third quarter of 2025.

“The third quarter of 2026 demonstrated the continued strength of our platform, with funded origination volume growing 24% year over year. While higher interest rates drove near-term pressure on earnings, we believe this impact is temporary,” CEO Graham Fleming said in a statement. “We have already taken steps to improve margins.”

During the company’s earnings call, Fleming said the company remains focused on production growth, operational efficiency and cash generation, and explained that margins compressed after the Federal Reserve shifted from cutting to raising interest rates.

“We have already made the necessary changes to product pricing, and we expect margins to return to historical levels in the first half of 2027,” Fleming told investors.

“Finance of America has grown volumes on average by 20% each year since 2023. The third quarter was a challenging rate environment, with the 10-year Treasury yields increasing over 75 basis points during the quarter, a reaction to the Fed’s pivot to raising rates and elevated inflation,” he added.

FOA’s retirement solutions segment, which originates home equity-based financing products, including reverse mortgages, recorded $748 million in funded volume during the quarter, up 24% year over year.

“Our retirement solutions revenue margin was impacted in the third quarter, decreasing to 9%, compared with 11.3% in the third quarter of 2025, and a historical average since the start of 2024 of 10.7%,” Fleming said during the call. “We believe these impacts are temporary and do not change the underlying fundamentals of our business.”

Revenue for the segment totaled $67 million, down 1% from the prior-year period and a decrease from Q2 2026‘s $74 million. Pretax income fell to $3 million, down from $10 million a year earlier, while adjusted net income declined to $9 million, down from $20 million.

The company attributed the decline in profitability primarily to pressure on origination margins as benchmark interest rates increased during the quarter. It said it implemented product and pricing adjustments to address the impact and expects margins to return to historical levels.

For the first nine months of 2026, the retirement solutions segment generated $2.07 billion in funded volume, up 17% year over year. Revenue increased 14% to $208 million.

“Since 2023, our submission volumes have increased by 21% annually, while our funded volume has grown by 20% annually. This is across our product suite, as HECM volume is up 14% year over year, HomeSafe first liens are up 15%, and HomeSafe seconds are up 63%,” FOA President Kristen Sieffert said during the call.

FOA’s portfolio management segment, which generates revenue through net interest income and fair value changes on portfolio assets, reported a pretax loss of $138 million, compared with an $11 million loss in the third quarter of 2025.

The company attributed the loss primarily to negative non-cash fair value adjustments on retained interests in securitizations. Portfolio management reported adjusted net income of $11 million, down from $30 million a year earlier.

Assets under management in the segment increased 23% year over year to $37.4 billion. The growth reflected new originations and the acquisition of Onity Mortgage Corp.‘s HECM servicing portfolio on July 1.

For the first nine months of 2026, portfolio management recorded a pretax loss of $128 million, compared with pretax income of $202 million in the same period last year. Adjusted net income totaled $57 million, down from $66 million.

FOA ended the third quarter with $118 million in cash and cash equivalents, up from $85 million at the end of June. The company attributed the increase to cash generation from originations and capital markets activity.

Total equity stood at $307 million as of Sept. 30, including $259 million attributable to common stock. Book value was $28.08 per common share.

The company said it expects to complete a $60 million paydown of senior secured notes in November. Looking ahead to the final quarter of 2026, chief financial officer Matt Engel said the company expects funded volume to reach $3.1 billion to $3.4 billion, a range “supported by consumer demographics, our product breadth, and ongoing conversion improvements.”

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Ripple has returned 700 million XRP worth $875 million at the current price to escrow after its November token release, strengthening the bullish narrative as institutional interest in the coin continues to grow. The latest transactions leave 300 million XRP outside escrow, while exchange-traded funds and corporate treasuries maintain huge exposure to the token.

Ripple released 1 billion XRP through two transactions of 500 million tokens on November 1. The company subsequently returned 700 million XRP to escrow through three transactions of 100 million, 500 million, and 100 million tokens.

Ripple just locked another 700 million $XRP in escrow across three transactions.100M + 500M + 100M XRP.That's 700 million XRP moved into escrow, worth roughly $875M at the displayed transaction prices. https://t.co/gZkSewa4x7 pic.twitter.com/XS7J0K2jNT

The sequence leaves a net 300 million XRP outside escrow from the monthly release. Ripple’s escrow system, established in 2017, allows up to 1 billion XRP to become available each month, with unused tokens typically returned to new time-locked contracts.

The latest re-lock means 70% of November’s gross release has returned to escrow, limiting the amount remaining outside the contracts. But the monthly escrow cycle remains an important supply metric for XRP price watchers, particularly when compared with institutional demand and exchange balances.

Institutional exposure to XRP continues expanding through regulated investment products. Six US spot XRP ETFs held approximately 1.17 billion tokens as of the end of last week.

Bitwise and Franklin Templeton remain among the largest XRP fund holders, while corporate treasury strategies are creating another channel for institutional accumulation. Evernorth, on the other hand, has built a treasury holding of 473 million XRP, positioning itself around institutional XRP exposure and potential ecosystem strategies.

These developments give XRP holders another demand narrative alongside Ripple’s monthly escrow management. ETF holdings also provide a measurable way to track if institutional investors continue maintaining their positions during periods of price weakness.

The project is developing a Bitcoin Layer 2 powered by the Solana Virtual Machine, aiming to bring faster transactions, smart contracts, and decentralized finance to Bitcoin. Its planned infrastructure includes a BTC bridge, high-speed execution, and settlement back to Bitcoin’s main network.

The institutional opportunity is substantial. US spot Bitcoin ETFs have opened regulated investment channels for traditional investors, while banks and financial firms increasingly explore tokenization and blockchain-based settlement. Bitcoin Hyper is targeting the next step: making Bitcoin more usable within financial applications instead of leaving it idle in wallets and investment products.

That creates an interesting parallel with XRP. Ripple is building institutional payment and stablecoin infrastructure around the XRP Ledger, while Bitcoin Hyper aims to unlock programmable finance around Bitcoin. With the presale approaching its November 22 closing window, the countdown is now a major part of the HYPER story. Once the window closes, buyers will have to wait for the planned launch and subsequent market availability.

The final stretch is bringing the project’s infrastructure pitch, staking incentives, and launch countdown together as we watch for the next Bitcoin Layer 2 narrative to gain traction.

#5527. AI cloud startup Applied Compute raises $350M after reaching key revenue milestone

Applied Compute Inc., a fast-growing provider of artificial intelligence infrastructure, has raised $350 million in funding at a $3.25 billion valuation.

The startup announced the deal on Monday. Prominent angel investor Elad Gil led the round with participation from Nvidia Corp., Shopify Ventures, HubSpot Ventures and more than a dozen others.

Applied Compute operates a cloud platform that developers use to train large language models and perform inference, the process of running the models to provide responses to queries. Additionally, it has a team of machine learning researchers that can lend customers a hand with their projects. The group takes on tasks such as creating quality evaluations for newly developed models.

The software stack that AI researchers use to train LLMs usually comprises two main components. One creates multiple copies of the model, assigns a different task to each one and turns the results into training data. The other component uses that training data to refine the LLM’s weights. The two components usually run synchronously, which means that each one has to wait for the other to complete its work before launching.

Applied Compute’s platform uses a more efficient training approach called asynchronous reinforcement learning. It enables a training stack’s data generation and weight adjustment components to run at the same time, which speeds up LLM development. Additionally, the platform supports a second optimization method called self-distillation. It removes the need for teacher models, specialized neural networks that researchers use to supervise LLM training runs.

A built-in AI assistant automates repetitive aspects of customers’ work. It can, for example, summarize what new skills an LLM learned during a training run. Uncovering that information usually requires researchers to review lengthy reasoning logs.

Applied Computing’s platform also lends itself to running inference workloads. An autoscaling engine automatically adjusts the amount of hardware allocated to a model based on user traffic. A so-called online RL feature uses the prompts that the LLM receives to fine-tune its weights periodically, which keeps it aligned with customer requirements.

The company offers its training and inference features alongside a model router called Shift-1. It enables coding agents to send each user request to the LLM that can fulfill it in the most cost-efficient manner. Furthermore, it can split complex tasks among multiple LLMs.

Applied Computing disclosed in its funding announcement that its annualized recurring revenue has topped $100 million. The company, which launched less than 18 months ago, counts Microsoft Corp., DoorDash Inc. and other major tech firms as customers. It will use the newly raised capital to grow its market presence and buy more infrastructure.

“Training, inference, and routing are the first pieces of a much larger stack,” Applied Compute founders Rhythm Garg, Yash Patil and Linden Li wrote in a blog post. “We’re building the AI infrastructure every company will need to fully own their intelligence, from the models themselves to the systems that run, monitor and secure them.”

#5525. Google offers tepid response to accusations it would hold Search hostage if schools restrict AI tools

Google LLC today faced a barrage of criticism after the company warned that if schools restricted their students from using its artificial intelligence tools, the same students wouldn’t be able to use Search.

The fallout came after the company announced a slew of new products for classrooms. Teachers and schools were told that the new AI tools would come with features that will allow for limitations or complete blocks of the features, but if teachers or schools should take that route, students would not be able to use Google Search. Some media described it as rather cunning behavior from the tech giant.

“After listening to schools, teachers, leading researchers, and policymakers, we are now updating our approach to controls for Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search,” Google said in a blog post. “Access to these products will be entirely off for K-12 student accounts until school administrators explicitly turn them on.”

A New York Times article followed the announcement and explained that where schools have banned the use of AI or if they limit AI in the classroom, the students would not have access to Search. Since Google’s suite of products are a mainstay in classrooms all over the U.S., the backlash was imminent.

“Google is trying to use its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools,” New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani wrote on X. “No corporation should have the power to dictate how we teach our children. Our public schools exist to serve students, not to grow the profit margins of Big Tech.”

Sen. Bernie Sanders from Vermont was equally chastising, writing on X, “Google is threatening schools” and using what amounts to “extortion.” Lina Khan, former chair of the U.S. Federal Trade Commission, was similarly unimpressed, writing that Google was trying to, “coerce schools into adopting AI.”

Google was quick to respond. In a post on X, the company said its new policy is about giving schools more control over how students use AI. Gemini chatbot, Gemini Notebook, the company explained, will be turned off by default, but “schools are in control.”

“We are also updating Search for schools to make it better for learning,” Google added. “Specifically, AI Mode and AI Overviews will offer step-by-step guided learning through problems, so that students don’t get quick answers to schoolwork.” The company explained that it was aware of the dangers of students embracing the “AI shortcut” and effectively not engaging their brains.

However, Google seemed to ignore the basis of the criticism regarding Search not being available when AI functions were turned off. Given the company has found itself under the gun many times in recent years for its business tactics, and in light of studies showing overuse of technology can have a harmful impact on children, the response seemed to critics tepid at best.
