#5523. SEO or PPC? How to Choose Between Long-Term Growth and Instant Traffic on Your Website

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Every business owner eventually faces the same marketing crossroads: invest in search engine optimization (SEO) or spend money into pay-per-click (PPC) ads.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Every business owner eventually faces the same marketing crossroads: invest in search engine optimization (SEO) or spend money into pay-per-click (PPC) ads. Both strategies aim to get your business in front of potential customers on search engines, but they work in fundamentally different ways.

SEO builds long-term, cost-effective organic traffic through content and keyword optimization, while PPC delivers immediate, measurable results through paid campaigns. Choose SEO if you have time to invest and want sustainable growth. Choose PPC if you need fast visibility or compete in a crowded market. Many businesses combine both for balanced results.

SEO focuses on earning organic (unpaid) rankings by optimizing your website’s content, structure, and authority. PPC, on the other hand, involves paying for ad placements that appear above organic results, charging you each time someone clicks.

Choosing the right approach, or the right blend of both, can significantly affect your marketing budget, timeline, and overall business growth. This guide breaks down how each strategy works, compares their key differences, and helps you decide which fits your goals.

SEO is a long game. By optimizing your website for relevant keywords and producing high-quality, valuable content, you build sustainable visibility in search engine results pages (SERPs) over time.

One of SEO’s biggest advantages is cost efficiency. While it requires an upfront investment in content creation, technical optimization and link building, the cost per click decreases significantly as your organic traffic grows. You’re not paying for every visitor, you’re earning them through relevance and authority.

The tradeoff? Patience. SEO results typically take three to six months to materialize, and competitive industries may take even longer. Search engine algorithms also evolve constantly, meaning your rankings can shift based on factors outside your direct control.

PPC campaigns offer what SEO can’t: speed. Launch a campaign today, and you can start driving traffic and conversions within hours. This makes PPC an attractive option for product launches, seasonal promotions or businesses that need quick wins.

PPC also gives you granular control. You decide your budget, target audience, ad messaging and even the specific times your ads appear. This level of precision allows for rapid testing and optimization based on real performance data.

The downside is cost. PPC requires ongoing spend, and in competitive industries, cost-per-click rates can climb quickly. The moment you stop paying, your traffic stops too—there’s no lasting equity built the way there is with organic rankings.

When deciding between SEO and PPC, four factors matter most:

The right choice depends on your business goals, timeline and budget.

Choose SEO if you have the patience to invest in long-term growth and want a cost-effective strategy that keeps paying off after the initial work is complete. This approach suits businesses planning for sustained visibility rather than quick wins.

Choose PPC if you need immediate traffic, are launching a new product, or operate in a highly competitive market where organic rankings are difficult to achieve quickly. PPC is also useful for testing messaging and offers before committing to a long-term content strategy.

Consider combining both strategies if you want comprehensive coverage. Many businesses use PPC to generate quick wins while building their organic presence through SEO, creating a balanced approach that captures both immediate and long-term opportunities.

Neither SEO nor PPC is universally better, the right choice depends on your budget, timeline and business goals. SEO rewards patience with cost-effective, lasting visibility, while PPC delivers speed and control at a higher ongoing cost.

Most successful businesses don’t choose one over the other. Instead, they use a hybrid approach, leveraging PPC for immediate visibility while building long-term equity through SEO. Start by evaluating your current resources and goals, then test which strategy — or combination — moves the needle for your business.

Is SEO cheaper than PPC?Yes, it can be, over the long term. SEO requires upfront investment in content and optimization, but once rankings improve, you don’t pay per click. PPC requires continuous spending to maintain visibility.

How long does it take to see results from SEO?SEO typically can take three to six months to show meaningful results, depending on your industry’s competitiveness and the quality of your optimization efforts.

Can I use SEO and PPC together?Yes. Many businesses combine both strategies, using PPC for immediate traffic while building long-term organic visibility through SEO.

Which is better for a small business with a limited budget?SEO often makes more sense for limited budgets since it doesn’t require ongoing ad spend. However, a small, targeted PPC campaign can help generate quick traction while your SEO strategy develops.

What happens if I stop paying for PPC ads?Your traffic and visibility from those ads stop almost immediately. Unlike SEO, PPC doesn’t build lasting equity — it only works while you’re actively paying for it.

Every business owner eventually faces the same marketing crossroads: invest in search engine optimization (SEO) or spend money into pay-per-click (PPC) ads. Both strategies aim to get your business in front of potential customers on search engines, but they work in fundamentally different ways.

SEO builds long-term, cost-effective organic traffic through content and keyword optimization, while PPC delivers immediate, measurable results through paid campaigns. Choose SEO if you have time to invest and want sustainable growth. Choose PPC if you need fast visibility or compete in a crowded market. Many businesses combine both for balanced results.

SEO focuses on earning organic (unpaid) rankings by optimizing your website’s content, structure, and authority. PPC, on the other hand, involves paying for ad placements that appear above organic results, charging you each time someone clicks.

#5522. OpenAI hires Uber President Jill Hazelbaker to lead communications, filling a critical role that was curiously vacant for 10 months

OpenAI has hired one of Uber’s highest ranking executives to oversee its global communications efforts, filling a key role that had been vacant for nearly a year as the AI company navigates a challenging political landscape and moves closer to an initial public offering.

Jill Hazelbaker is joining OpenAI as chief corporate affairs officer, the company announced on Tuesday. Hazelbaker, who had been president and chief corporate affairs officer at ride hailing giant Uber, will work alongside OpenAI’s leaders to “deepen public understanding of AI and strengthen trust in its mission,” the company said.

She will report to OpenAI co-founder and president Greg Brockman and starts in early December, OpenAI told Fortune.

“As AI becomes part of more people’s lives, how we communicate, engage, and earn public trust has never been more important,” Brockman said in the announcement, citing Hazelbaker’s experience and understanding of the “opportunities and responsibilities that come with building technology at global scale.”

Hazelbaker is a well respected communications professional in the technology industry. She has served as Uber’s President and Chief Corporate Affairs Officer for the past 11 years, and previously held senior leadership roles at Snap and Google. She is replacing Hannah Wong, who served as OpenAI’ chief communications officer (CCO) until January 2026. Since then, OpenAI’s Chris Lehane has been leading the team in the interim.

In the ten months since Wong’s departure, OpenAI has experienced a series of public controversies—most notably when its AI agents hacked the company Hugging Face during training in July. The 11-year old company has been criticized for not being sufficiently transparent and communicative about its operations, at a time when public concerns about AI’s potential harms to society, the labor market, and the environment are rising. Backlash to the massive AI data centers being built across the U.S. has emerged as one of the key issues in the midterm elections taking place on Tuesday.

In September, OpenAI told Fortune it was not rushing to fill the role, and was focused on getting the right candidate. Over the summer, it ramped up its search by hiring an executive recruiting firm.

OpenAI offered Hazelbaker the position in the spring, but she turned it down, as Fortune reported in September. Sources suspected her close relationship with Uber’s CEO Dara Khosrowshahi, desire to be on the East Coast for her family, and already high salary played a role in her declining the role.

It appears OpenAI has now made Hazelbaker an offer she cannot refuse.

Hazelbaker will remain on the East Coast, but will spend time in San Francisco, where OpenAI is headquartered, the company told Fortune.

“The work of building public trust has never been more consequential,” Hazelbaker said in the announcement, describing AI as the “most profound technological shift of our lifetime.”

#5521. AMD beats expectations as agentic AI sparks its data center revenue growth engines

Shares of the chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices Inc. rose more than 5% in late trading today after it delivered solid third-quarter earnings and revenue today, with data center sales almost doubling from a year ago.

The company reported earnings before certain costs such as stock compensation of $2.09 per share, easily beating Wall Street’s forecast of $1.95 per share. Revenue for the period jumped 45% from a year earlier, to $13.38 billion, ahead of the $13.09 billion analyst consensus estimate. All told, the company’s net income for the quarter came to $3.47 billion, up 77% from the previous year when it posted a profit of just $1.96 billion.

The star performer in the quarter was AMD’s data center business unit, which accounted for 64% of its overall revenue, up from just 47% one year ago. After spending years trying to compete with Nvidia Corp.’s graphics processing units for artificial intelligence market share, the company’s traditional central processing units or CPUs are suddenly back in vogue thanks to the emergence of agentic AI applications such as Meta Platforms Inc.’s Muse. Autonomous AI agents can run much more efficiently on CPUs than they can on GPUs, boosting demand for the chips.

Looking ahead, AMD expects its server revenue to double year-over-year in fiscal 2027, with AI growth likely to accelerate even faster than the company projected just three months ago. “Adoption is just starting and we expect demand to grow sharply as agents are deployed more broadly and take on more complex work,” AMD Chief Executive Lisa Su (pictured) said on a conference call with analysts.

AMD’s data center story isn’t all about CPUs, though. The company also sells GPUs, including bundles of them shipped inside data center-ready rack-scale systems called Helios, and that system’s popularity is growing fast.

Su said Anthropic PBC, OpenAI Group PBC, Microsoft Corp., Oracle Corp. and Meta are all using AMD Helios systems in their data centers. Last week, Meta said its first Helion racks are already up and running as it revealed that AMD invested $1 billion in its latest equity offering.

The chipmaker has also committed to a $5 billion investment in Anthropic, which last week revealed the long-awaited prospectus for its upcoming initial public offering.

AMD delivered its latest earnings report just days after its rival Intel Corp. did the same. Intel also posted strong data center revenue growth, but its stock fell more than 30% on Friday on weak guidance and concerns about its ability to meet demand for its products.

But Su said AMD had no such problems. Last month she made a high-profile visit to Taiwan, where she held meetings with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. and a number of supply chain partners, and said after the trip that the company plans to substantially increase its supply in the coming year. “We have worked across our supply chain to secure the wafers, substrates, advanced packaging, memory and other key components needed to support much higher growth next year,” Su added.

AMD’s results will go some way toward reassuring investors who have become increasingly nervous about the direction of the AI industry and whether the hundreds of billions of dollars being spent on it each year is actually going to generate a return on their investments, said eMarketer analyst Jacob Bourne. “The results are a test of AMD’s own performance and the broader AI trade, and its data center and revenue beats will encourage investors after the recent semiconductor selloff,” he added.

Though AMD is far from immune to the recent volatility that has afflicted AI-related stocks, its future still looks increasingly rosy for now. “Demand for AI computing is not going to fall off a cliff, and AMD has the competitive products and major customer relationships to capitalize on that demand,” Bourne said.

Strength in the data center unit is helping AMD to ride out difficulties in its traditional market for personal computers, which is the reason for Intel’s poor outlook. During the second quarter, global PC shipments fell 4% from a year earlier, with buyers dissuaded by the rising cost of components such as memory chips, according to data from Counterpoint Research.

Along with Intel, AMD is a leading manufacturer of the x86 CPUs that power most of the world’s computers and laptops. The company reports PC chip revenue within a segment that also includes its chips for games consoles, and that unit saw its revenue decline 8% from a year earlier, to $3.7 billion. Gaming revenue fell 40% from the previous year.

For the current quarter, AMD is targeting revenue of abouot $17 billion at the midpoint of its guidance range, ahead of the Street’s $16.2 billion consensus estimate. The company also sees its gross margins coming in at 55%, just below the Street’s forecast of 55.3%.

AMD was busy on the acquisition front during the quarter. In September it revealed it’s going to buy World Labs Inc. for $8.2 billion in an all-stock deal. The San Francisco-based AI lab, founded by the AI industry luminary Fei-Fei Li, has developed world models that can simulate 3D environments to support the training of intelligent robots and other physical AI applications.

The company also acquired a startup called Taalas Inc. that makes specialized model-specific integrated circuits, which are essentially chips that can be customized to run a specific AI model more efficiently. That acquisition should help to boost AMD’s position in AI inference. AMD also invested in the AI image generation model maker Stability AI Ltd., which raised $76 million in funding in August.

#5520. What Clients Need Before They Trust You With Sensitive Work

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Your clients, and potential clients, need to know that they can trust you with their confidential information.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Confidentiality is essential. Without proper protection, sensitive personal or business information can become public. Cybersecurity tools and practical safeguards are critical for protecting confidential data. What assurances do your clients need before trusting you with sensitive work?

Every company seeks credibility. Building a strong reputation takes years, but a data breach or employee error can erase it instantly.

Business plans are drafted with intricate details on how a service or product will be offered. Features and benefits are discussed at length, alongside profit projections. However, few business proposals address building and protecting the company’s reputation. Why? Because entrepreneurs assume if they provide a quality product or service, that consumer trust will follow.

When I started my transcription company, I quickly realized protecting sensitive data would be our top priority. Our service is not a simple transaction. Clients entrust us with audio or video files containing sensitive information. Whether the content is for a select audience or public release, we safeguard every file as if it were confidential.

Handling sensitive data requires safeguards both inside and outside the company. Companies often require new hires to sign non-disclosure agreements (NDAs), but reputations can still be damaged if employees violate these agreements and share confidential information.

Recent headlines report charges against a foreign national accused of planting listening devices in a corporate boardroom. This case involves unauthorized recording of confidential information at a major AI company planning to go public. Both executives and future shareholders need assurance that sensitive information will remain secure.

Clients need assurance that their information will be protected. While some businesses still accept cash, most rely on electronic payments, and customers expect trusted vendors to handle their data securely.

The same applies to transcription. Secure file upload and transfer are essential. I frequently remind clients not to email files. Work for legal and medical clients must comply with CJIS and HIPAA requirements to protect sensitive data. Any breach would harm our reputation.

Industries like legal, medical and technology must protect sensitive data, but every business should prioritize customer data protection. Safeguarding information, from credit card transactions to medical histories, matters just as much across all sectors.

No matter your industry, reassure customers and clients that protecting sensitive data is a top priority. Here are a few ways to convey the importance of safeguarding customer info:

Clients and customers lose trust in companies for various reasons. Often, companies don’t realize this erosion until sales decline or complaints rise, making recovery harder. Key reasons for lost trust include:

Unfortunately, many customers are skeptical of marketing claims because products or services sometimes fail to meet expectations. When this happens, customers incur extra costs to resolve issues, and companies lose revenue through replacements or additional service.

Ethical decline is another concern. Clients become frustrated when companies fail to deliver on their promises, which underscores the importance of consistent, honest communication.

When discussing service commitments, I strive for clarity in writing, email and phone conversations. However, clients may sometimes overlook or misunderstand service details, either by not listening or reading disclosures. Following up and confirming information by email helps protect both parties.

The greatest cost of a data breach is reputational damage. While ransom payments and IT expenses are straightforward to calculate, the long-term reputational impact can cost millions over several years.

Minimizing data breach risk should be a top priority for every company. For this reason, my company employs only U.S.-based individuals who undergo comprehensive criminal background checks.

Many hackers and scammers who obtain confidential information operate overseas. I am often surprised when competitors use contractors abroad to transcribe files. Clients should know who can access their data and where those individuals are located.

Every company, regardless of size, should maintain an up-to-date data breach plan. Hackers often target small businesses as entry points to larger networks. I recommend a six-step plan:

Developing a comprehensive data breach plan requires specialized expertise. However, I recognize the importance of data security and take extensive measures to protect the sensitive information our clients entrust to us. Ultimately, all data is important to your clients and customers.

Regardless of the cause, how your company responds to failure is crucial. Mistakes happen, and even the most diligent employees or companies can “drop the ball.”

When mistakes are made, transparency matters. Be honest and admit your mistakes. Even the most irritated customer can moderate their views when a company admits its errors.

Recently, I was dining at a restaurant with high ratings for its food and service. Nonetheless, four- and five-star reviews aren’t worth much when your experience is going south. From the moment I entered the restaurant, nothing went well.

First, the host could not find my reservation, even after I provided the confirmation number. After being seated, we waited 10 minutes for our server. To speed things up, we ordered all courses at once, and the server assured us he would pace the meal appropriately.

Despite these efforts, the dining experience did not improve. When the server noticed my frustration, he brought the manager, and both apologized. The manager comped our meal, offered a premium bottle of wine and gave me a $100 gift certificate. This response changed my perspective, and when I returned the following week, the manager personally thanked me for giving them another chance.

A disappointing restaurant experience is minor compared to a multi-million-dollar mistake or data breach. However, the fundamentals of response remain the same.

Transparency and honesty are essential, but customers will only give companies a second chance if they believe their mistakes can, and will be corrected. Most importantly, customers want to feel that your company genuinely cares about them.

Confidentiality is essential. Without proper protection, sensitive personal or business information can become public. Cybersecurity tools and practical safeguards are critical for protecting confidential data. What assurances do your clients need before trusting you with sensitive work?

Every company seeks credibility. Building a strong reputation takes years, but a data breach or employee error can erase it instantly.

Business plans are drafted with intricate details on how a service or product will be offered. Features and benefits are discussed at length, alongside profit projections. However, few business proposals address building and protecting the company’s reputation. Why? Because entrepreneurs assume if they provide a quality product or service, that consumer trust will follow.

#5519. Apple warns rogue AI agents could ‘conceal’ and ‘manipulate,’ causing unintended consequences for its business

Apple is cautioning that rogue AI agents that “conceal actions” or hide or manipulate information could pose a threat to its business if they access systems without authorization and cause damage.

The warning by the world’s second most valuable company came in an annual filing Tuesday, a day after Apple reported its fourth-quarter financial results. In the risk factors section, Apple expanded its warnings about artificial intelligence. Apple’s caution underscores the risks tech giants and other companies are projecting after a string of AI safety incidents in recent months, which have prompted companies to release new security features and debate regulatory measures.

In its 10-K filing, which is made each year following the end of its fiscal year, Apple said “artificial intelligence agents and other technologies can take actions autonomously, including interacting with internal or external systems that in some cases they may not be authorized to access, executing or altering code, sending communications, and completing transactions.”

Such technologies, the iPhone maker said, “may behave in unintended or unpredictable ways, including by taking actions that were not directed, instructed or authorized, exceeding permissions, defying directions or resisting instructions.” And it noted that autonomous AI agents that go rogue could “conceal actions, hide, withhold or manipulate information, or generate inaccurate or deceptive outputs.”

Apple is the latest to warn about risks posed by AI agents. Google parent Alphabet also pointed out the risks posed by rogue agents in a recent filing. Google, however, was more pointed about the potential consequences, writing that during AI model testing, it had observed unexpected behavior, including agents taking actions outside their intended scope, which could ultimately lead to “severe or catastrophic security and societal incidents, or negatively affect human rights.”

The risks outlined by companies follow several major cybersecurity incidents involving AI models, most notably this summer’s attack by OpenAI agents on AI company Hugging Face. In Anthropic’s IPO prospectus, made public last week, the company listed many risk factors, including incidents in which its models gained unauthorized access to real-world systems during security testing. It also estimated that 5% to 7% of its revenue this year came from customers later found to be violating its usage policies.

Executives at Microsoft and other major tech companies have called for a greater focus on securing AI agents. Microsoft recently announced a set of controls to detect, monitor, and restrict AI agents, including cutting their permissions or stopping them if they behave suspiciously. Chief executive Satya Nadella has argued that companies should treat agents as potential insider risks and put security controls outside the AI model rather than trusting the model to police itself.

In its 10-K filing on Tuesday, Apple also outlined other pressures, including memory and storage component shortages that it said will intensify. It also said demand for cloud computing, storage, and other AI infrastructure has produced “constrained supply, extended lead times, and increasing costs” that could affect its AI rollout. Its research and development spending rose 32% year over year, driven by higher infrastructure-related costs, including AI investments.

Apple shares dropped roughly 2% on Tuesday after the company said its margins would continue to be squeezed by memory chip costs and after it showed slowing growth in its Services segment. Ternus, on his first earnings call as CEO, largely stuck to scripted marketing points and offered few details about Apple’s plans for personalized AI agents.

#5518. Supermicro and Arista Networks crush expectations as AI infrastructure wins again

Growing nervousness about spending on the artificial intelligence boom has made technology stocks increasingly volatile this year, but all it takes is one good quarter to reignite investor confidence, as Super Micro Computer Inc. and Arista Networks Inc. both showed today.

The companies are still relatively small fry in terms of the bigger AI picture, but as key data center infrastructure providers, they have shown consistently strong revenue growth over the last couple of years, and neither looks to be slowing down.

Indeed, Supermicro’s sales shot up by an incredible 298% in its latest quarter as it powered its way to yet another impressive revenue beat. The server maker reported fiscal 2027 first-quarter earnings before certain costs such as stock compensation of $1.81 per share on sales of $19.95 billion, cruising past Wall Street’s guidance of $1.23 per share in earnings and $17.35 billion in sales. After-hours, the company’s stock gained more than 6%.

Meanwhile, Arista delivered third-quarter earnings of $1.20 per share on revenue of $3.66 billion, up 58% from a year earlier, surpassing the Street’s target of $1.08 per share in earnings and $3.33 billion in revenue. Its stock moved higher too, and rose more than 9% in the late-trading session. The company is a major supplier of networking equipment for AI data centers, helping to link together massive clusters of graphics processing units and other high-powered chips.

Supermicro Chief Executive Charles Liang (pictured) said his company continues to sell its servers and storage solutions as fast as it can build them. “Supermicro’s transformation into a total AI and IT data center solution provider continues to accelerate,” he added.

Investors were looking for signs that Supermicro may face headwinds in the coming months, with the impact of rising component costs being one of their major concerns. But the company’s results seem to have reassured doubters that supply issues could impact its profitability. Notably, Supermicro said its gross margin rose to 12.8% in the quarter, higher than the 9.3% margin recorded in the same quarter one year ago.

Supermicro’s guidance for the current quarter was impressive too. The company said it’s looking for earnings of between $1.66 and $1.90 per share on sales of between $19.5 billion and $21.5 billion in its second quarter. That’s much higher than the Street’s forecast, which calls for earnings of $1.14 per share and sales of $18.1 billion.

Arista’s 58% revenue growth was the biggest year-over-year jump since the company went public back in 2014, and it could well break that record again if its guidance holds true. The company said it’s looking for fourth-quarter earnings of between $1.26 and $1.30 per share on sales of $3.95 billion at the midpoint of its range. That would represent growth of 59%. The guidance was better than expected, with Wall Street looking for earnings of just $1.16 per share on sales of $3.65 billion.

Arista Chairperson and Chief Executive Jayshree Ullal told analysts that even she was surprised by how well the company did in the prior quarter. “This strong momentum across customer sectors highlights our increased relevance for the generative and agentic AI era,” she said.

#5517. Meta says automation wrongly took down No Kings and a Senate candidate’s page. It’s automating more anyway

Meta has spent the last year handing more of its content moderation to artificial intelligence. In the last few weeks, Facebook and Instagram’s parent company has fended off election-interference accusations in Brazil and the U.S. It has largely blamed these errors on its automated systems.

Those accusations have come from a sitting president, a national protest movement and a U.S. Senate candidate. Each landed as Meta, a Fortune 500 company that reported $201 billion in revenue last year, speeds up a shift from human reviewers to large language models.

Meta announced in March that it would roll out more advanced AI content-enforcement systems. By June, large language models had replaced human reviewers for about half of review requests, with a goal of 90% or more automation for some violation categories by the end of 2026, according to the Financial Times. Meta told the paper its models make 13% fewer errors than human reviewers and catch 10% more violations; some employees have warned that the shift is happening too fast with too little oversight.

In 2018, ahead of elections in Brazil and the U.S., Facebook set up a “war room” of more than two dozen experts to fight election interference. Eight years later, both countries are voting again, and Meta now calls its war room the Election Operations Center. But more of the work of policing its platforms has shifted from people to software.

According to an October report by the Institute for Strategic Dialogue, a research organization, platforms are increasingly relying on “crowdsourced and automated systems” rather than human oversight. The report found that platforms have disclosed little about how these systems work or are tested, and said: “relying on them as the primary means of oversight during a fast-moving election cycle remains an untested proposition.”

This fall’s cases show what happens when those systems misfire in the middle of an election, and why Meta’s explanations have satisfied few affected people.

Meta did not respond to Fortune‘s request for comment.

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won a fourth term in an Oct. 25 runoff despite what his campaign said were Meta’s efforts to restrict his online reach. Meta blamed technical errors.

Lula’s campaign went to Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court on Oct. 10, accusing Meta of favoring opponent Flávio Bolsonaro through biased algorithms and AI restrictions. In that petition and later filings, the campaign cited cases in which Meta’s automatic translation rendered comments such as “Flávio futuro presidiário!!” (“Flávio, future prisoner!!”) as “Flávio future president!!” and alleged that Meta restricted sharing for some of Lula’s posts.

The newspaper Folha de S. Paulo reported that Meta staff acknowledged in internal messages that Lula’s accounts were restricted compared with Bolsonaro’s.

On Oct. 15, the court ordered Meta to treat both candidates equally under threat of a daily fine of 500,000 reais, about $98,000. After finding Meta’s initial response insufficient, the court on Oct. 19 gave the company 24 hours to prove it had not restricted either candidate.

Meta’s filing listed 17 measures, Reuters reported, including human review within two hours of any automatic restriction on the presidential campaigns’ ad accounts. The company denied treating the candidates unequally and said the problems arose from technical errors. Bolsonaro’s campaign later joined the case, saying it had also been treated unfairly.

Brazil’s electoral prosecutor’s office told the court that Meta had not fully complied with the rulings, including a requirement to explain how its AI tool treats content about each candidate. It argued that errors varied by candidate, undermining Meta’s explanation of technical errors.

Lula won the runoff with 51.8% of valid votes. The electoral court has yet to decide whether to fine Meta, and federal prosecutors, who opened an inquiry into account takedowns on Oct. 14, filed a civil suit against Meta on Oct. 21.

On Oct. 17, during the fourth national No Kings day of action, aimed at encouraging early voting, Meta suspended the coalition’s Instagram account, MS NOW reported. Organizers said the account went down at about 1:30 p.m. ET, at the height of the day’s events, for about 90 minutes. Even after it became viewable again, administrators couldn’t access it for several hours.

The coalition also said on Threads that it had received reports that “#NoKings and early voting content was inaccessible, restricted, or seemed suppressed across Meta platforms.”

Meta’s explanation changed overnight. That day, Meta’s vice president of communications, Andy Stone, attributed the suspension to unusually high rates of posting, sharing or commenting. The next day, he wrote on X that Meta’s network security systems had detected “the use of a Claude tool reading profiles, posts, and hashtags” in intense bursts, and that the company’s “automated protections” had wrongly taken the account offline.

“We want to reiterate our sincere apology for the error,” Stone wrote. The coalition’s social media team later told Ars Technica it had used Claude, Anthropic’s AI model, to search keywords and hashtags to track online conversation.

The coalition sent an open letter to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg asking whether Meta had communicated with the Trump administration about the event or the 2026 midterms. It also asked how Meta’s “whitelist protocols,” which protect certain high-profile accounts from automated removal, treat Trump and his allies compared with No Kings and other “civil society efforts to encourage voter participation.”

In an Oct. 21 reply, the coalition posted that Meta apologized again and offered a meeting with its technical experts. The coalition answered with a second letter saying the company had not given a substantive response and demanding a meeting with Meta leadership.

On Oct. 22, five Democratic senators led by Chris Van Hollen of Maryland demanded Meta’s records of any communications with the Trump administration about No Kings and called the company’s “shifting explanations” alarming. On Oct. 30, the coalition said it met with senior Meta executives, but the meeting ended without substantive commitments to change Meta’s practices or establish safeguards.

On Oct. 27, Instagram took down a Spanish-language account that Florida Democratic Senate candidate Angie Nixon’s campaign had created to reach Latino voters, while the campaign was posting from a get-out-the-vote rally in Osceola County.

“We are calling on Meta to immediately restore the page and provide an explanation for its removal,” Nixon posted on X, sharing the suspension notice Instagram had sent. The account was back online by the next morning.

A Meta spokesperson told Newsweek that because the account was created only a week and a half earlier, “our systems automatically and mistakenly assessed it to be impersonating the Nixon for Senate campaign.”

The anti-Trump organizing movement 50501, which stands for 50 protests, 50 states, 1 movement, linked the suspension to the No Kings incident in an Instagram post demanding “transparency and accountability beyond technical explanations.”

Meta’s Oversight Board, a Meta-funded but independent body that reviews content moderation decisions, criticized “recurring enforcement failures in Meta’s election integrity efforts.” It cited the No Kings suspension and the “overenforcement” of Meta’s fraud policies against Lula ad accounts. The statement did not suggest either incident was politically motivated, and Meta is not bound by it.

Attorneys general from 13 states and the District of Columbia have asked Meta to explain the No Kings suspension and describe how it distinguishes “legitimate political activity” from “harmful ‘bot’ traffic.” Reps. Robert Garcia of California and Jamie Raskin of Maryland, the top Democrats on the House Oversight and Judiciary committees, requested a briefing by Nov. 9.

“We need records explaining how this happened and whether anyone in the Trump Administration had a hand in it,” Raskin said.

None of these demands carries the force of law. In Brazil, the electoral court’s decision on a fine and the prosecutors’ suit will test whether a government can compel answers. In the U.S., that depends on today’s vote: if Democrats win the House, Garcia and Raskin would be in line to chair committees with the power to subpoena answers to some of these same questions.

#5516. Dave’s Hot Chicken’s CEO Was Handed a $100 Bill and 3 Words of Advice by His Boss at a Valet Stand. Those Words Are Still How He Runs the Company Today.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Jim Bitticks spent years watching his boss give generously to the people around him. He says that habit is a big part of how Dave’s Hot Chicken grew.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Jim Bitticks had a crisp $10 bill ready for the valet. Then Bill Phelps handed the man $100.

The parking lot was only about 30 feet away. Retrieving the car had taken less than a minute. Bitticks looked at his own tip and told Phelps he could have at least let him go first.

Phelps pulled out another $100 bill and handed it to Bitticks.

In January 2026, Bitticks became CEO of Dave’s Hot Chicken, moving up from president and chief operating officer. He succeeded Phelps, who became executive chairman.

Asked what he learned from his predecessor, Bitticks talks about taking care of employees beyond their salaries and benefits.

“I’ve seen Bill pay people’s student loans off,” Bitticks says.

Phelps once upgraded a private jet to make room for an hourly graphic artist named Eddie. Earlier, while Bitticks was working at Blaze Pizza, where he rose to chief restaurant officer, a manager called about $200 Phelps had left in a tip jar. She worried he had meant to leave $2.

Bitticks asked Phelps’ longtime business partner Elise Wetzel about it.

“That’s Bill Phelps, generous to a fault,” she told him.

Bitticks sees a connection between those gestures and the company Dave’s Hot Chicken has become.

“I think a lot of the Dave’s success story is connected to sort of that willingness to be generous to others,” he says.

That includes sharing experiences and giving people opportunities to learn. When asked about building the team behind the company’s growth, Bitticks starts with believing people can develop the skills they need if someone gives them training and a chance.

He estimates that about 60 of roughly 75 corporate support employees had worked with the leadership team at Wetzel’s Pretzels, Blaze Pizza or Carl’s Jr.

The team has grown across brands because people who worked together before have brought one another into the next opportunity. Bitticks now leads a company staffed largely by those familiar faces, with firsthand knowledge of what they can do when given room to grow.

The graffiti at Dave’s Hot Chicken connects a restaurant in Dublin to a parking lot in Los Angeles.

For Bitticks, that recognizable identity travels alongside something the company cannot export: a franchise partner’s knowledge of the local market. The company initially heard warnings about entering the United Kingdom. An experienced restaurant operator saw an opportunity instead.

“We know how to do U.K.,” Bitticks recalls the group saying.

The partner backed that confidence with its choice of real estate, combining two neighboring souvenir shops into a corner restaurant on London’s Shaftesbury Avenue. Artwork, construction and marketing helped turn the location into the brand’s highest-volume restaurant for roughly a year, according to Bitticks.

Dave’s also opened in Dublin and signed a deal to expand into 10 additional European countries, including Italy, Poland and Germany.

“The whole model is built around franchisees that know their market,” Bitticks says.

What guests recognize when they arrive comes from a different kind of expertise.

Dave’s began in 2017 as a chicken stand in a Los Angeles parking lot, with street graffiti on the brick wall behind it. When the founders opened their first permanent restaurant, they wanted to preserve that energy. They hired two graffiti artists who were friends of the founders to bring it inside.

The artists have worked with the company’s design and construction team to give new restaurants a family resemblance without repeating the same room.

“Every single location you go to at Dave’s isn’t exactly the same as another, but feels related,” Bitticks says.

He compares the restaurants to his four children. They look different, but people can tell they belong together. Bitticks says the artists had completed about 98% of Dave’s locations, expanding their team and training others internationally to keep up with growth.

European franchisees bring their local expertise to the business while preserving the visual identity guests associate with Dave’s. A London operator can find the right corner. The design team makes it recognizable as Dave’s.

#5515. In Democrats’ second Senate flip of the night, South Carolina rejects the senator Trump hand-picked

South Carolina voters look like they’re choosing a Republican governor and a Democratic senator on Tuesday night. Only one of them was just called, and that’s the one that beat out President Donald Trump’s pick.

Democrat Annie Andrews, a now-former pediatrician, defeated Sen. Darline Graham, as called by CBS News, NBC News and Decision Desk HQ. She is the first Democrat to win a Senate race in South Carolina since Fritz Hollings in 1998, in a state Trump carried by 18 points in 2024.

On the same ballot, Republican Alan Wilson held a narrow lead in the governor’s race into Tuesday evening, but the race was not yet called at time of publication. Graham ran roughly 10 points behind him on the margin. Ticket-splitting has been rare elsewhere tonight, but in South Carolina, enough Republicans backed Wilson for governor and Andrews for Senate to cost Graham the seat.

Democrats’ first Senate flip of the night came in North Carolina, where former Gov. Roy Cooper defeated Republican Michael Whatley for the seat held by retiring Sen. Thom Tillis, becoming the first Democrat to win a Senate race in the state since 2008.

Trump was involved at every step of Graham’s rise. After Lindsey Graham died in July, Trump lobbied Gov. Henry McMaster to appoint his sister, a political newcomer, to finish the term. She first described the job as a chance to finish her brother’s work. Days later, Trump posted “RUN, DARLINE, RUN!” on Truth Social and promised his “complete and total endorsement.” She announced her campaign on Fox News three days after that.

His endorsement got her through the primary, but barely at that. She was forced into a runoff with Republican Rep. Ralph Norman, which she won by less than 5 points.

As the general election tightened, Trump came back. He rallied for her in Pendleton on Oct. 21 and in Rock Hill a week later. “Lindsey is watching, and very proud of her!!!” he posted the morning of the Rock Hill rally. On Election Day, he called her “a spectacular person, and a true American Patriot.”

The rallies gave her a short-term lift. A Citadel poll found Andrews trailing by one point before the Pendleton rally, and Graham’s support 7 points higher among voters surveyed afterward. A New York Times/Siena poll in the final week showed the race tied.

South Carolina Republicans warned about Graham for months. In October, Dorchester County Republican Party Chairman CJ Westfall, a critic of her primary campaign, told CNN he expected Wilson to win by 10 to 12 points and Graham by just two to four. Slate’s Ben Jacobs reported that many in the party resented that she got the seat through nepotism, with Trump backing her because of his relationship with her brother. Some of them organized a write-in campaign for Norman.

Party money followed Trump into the state anyway. Senate Republicans’ main super PAC sent reinforcements to a seat it had never needed to defend. American Mission, the Republican arm of the AI industry’s Leading the Future super PAC network, put about $2.7 million behind her.

Andrews, meanwhile, made room for Republicans. She rarely campaigned with national Democrats, and a week before the election she picked up the endorsements of two former governors: David Beasley, a Republican, and Jim Hodges, a Democrat.

Notably different than her brother, she made clear she wouldn’t run against Trump. “I’m willing to work with anyone, including the president,” she said last week.

Lindsey Graham ran against Trump in 2016 but became, as Fox News put it, one of his biggest supporters in the Senate by 2020. That year, Democrats spent more than $100 million trying to beat him and lost by 10 points. This year, Andrews raised $10.8 million, 60% of it from small donors.

#5514. Tech Moves: Xbox COO’s sudden departure; SeekOut leadership shakeup; Fred Hutch names VP

Tech Moves covers notable hires, promotions and personnel changes in the Pacific NW tech community. Submissions: [email protected]

by Lisa Stiffler on Oct 27, 2026 at 2:08 pmNovember 2, 2026 at 1:05 pm

— Xbox Chief Operating Officer Helen Chiang has suddenly left Microsoft after 21 years with the company, just months after landing the role in July. Her past roles include leading Mojang and the Minecraft franchise.

Verge first reported the news on Friday, citing a memo from Xbox CEO Asha Sharma that did not disclose the reason for her departure.

An Xbox spokesperson was likewise mum on details. “We don’t discuss individual personnel matters. We’re grateful for Helen’s years of service and wish her well,” the company said in an email to GeekWire.

In response to speculation around her departure, Chiang offered a LinkedIn post on Nov. 2 refuting rumors that she left because of leaks to the media, to take a role with a competitor, for poor behavior or because she was passed over for a larger role.

“My story is about staying true to your core values, especially when it is hard. That’s the legacy I hope to leave behind,” Chiang wrote, without providing specifics.

Xbox has undergone a massive reorganization that included Chiang’s appointment, roughly 3,200 job cuts through the fiscal year — about 20% of the Xbox workforce — the spinoff of four game studios and a plan to dramatically flatten management.

— Seattle-based tech leader Philip Su has joined Anthropic as a member of technical staff on beneficial deployments. The management role focuses on AI applications in global health, life sciences, economic mobility and education.

Su started his tech career with 12 years at Microsoft and later worked for Facebook. He has launched multiple ventures, including Audere, a global health software nonprofit, and Superphonic, a podcast player. In 2021, he worked at an Amazon fulfillment center to experience the holiday rush.

Su also created and leads an annual course for University of Washington computer science students on how to maximize their personal and professional growth.

— More leadership changes are underway at SeekOut, a Bellevue-based recruiting startup launched in 2017. The company announced Monday that co-founder John Tippett is now president, moving from his role as chief client officer.

In April, SeekOut CEO and co-founder Anoop Gupta retired and passed the reins to enterprise software veteran Sean Thompson. In August, co-founder and chief technology officer Aravind Bala took over as CEO. Thompson is now listed as an adviser to the board.

Tippett will lead day-to-day operations and work with Bala “on the company’s direction,” according to a press release. SeekOut said it wants to integrate AI tools into customers’ operations to reduce recruiters’ workload.

SeekOut is No. 68 on the GeekWire 200, a ranked index of the Pacific Northwest’s top startups.

— Fred Hutch Cancer Center has appointed Michael (Mick) Merritt as vice president of strategy and partnerships, effective Dec. 7.

Merritt joins from Penn Medicine, where he was chief operating officer of Penn Signature Services. He has more than 25 years of experience in academic medicine, consulting, strategy, business development and operations.

— Industrial wastewater treatment startup Membrion has named Alexander Demihovsky as director of applications engineering. He joins the Seattle-based company from Xylem. His past employers include Evoqua Water Technologies and Bechtel National.

“Alex helps turn customer needs into viable project plans, mitigate execution risks and develop competitive proposals,” the company said.

— Marine geothermal energy startup Endurance Energy has named Marty Calvert as the director of turbomachinery. Calvert joins the Seattle startup from Blue Origin. He was previously a turbomachinery engineer at NASA for more than 13 years.

Endurance completed its fifth deployment to the ocean floor last month, testing Adélie, a 100-kilowatt geothermal generator named for a penguin.

#5513. Autonomous site reliability engineering startup Traversal bags $120M in funding at a $1B valuation

Traversal Inc., a startup that’s trying to automate site reliability engineering tasks with artificial intelligence agents, seems to be closing in on that goal after raising $120 million in fresh funding, bringing its valuation to $1 billion.

The newly minted unicorn’s round was led by Kleiner Perkins, Redpoint Ventures and Khosla Ventures, three of Silicon Valley’s highest-profile venture capital firms, whose names should give it the credibility it needs to accelerate its growth plans. Sequoia Capital – another big VC name – also participated in the round, alongside Battery Ventures and Amex Ventures.

AI might have made the job of software developers much easier than it used to be, but for the site reliability engineers tasked with maintaining the infrastructure to run that code, it has only made life much more difficult. The influx of AI-generated code has put infrastructure engineers under intense pressure, and they’re struggling to keep up.

According to a report earlier this year by Splunk Inc. and Oxford Economics, enterprise downtime costs have risen more than 50% in the last two years, draining up to $600 billion annually from businesses worldwide. That’s because software developers have increased their code output by around 180% over the same timeframe, which means those poor infrastructure engineers are forced to work harder than ever to match their growing output.

Enter Traversal, which is coming to the rescue with a highly promising autonomous site reliability engineer that’s designed to assist human specialists by diagnosing, remediating and preventing information technology infrastructure problems. Instead of just keeping watch and firing off alerts to human engineers when an outage occurs, Traversal actively investigates any issues that pop up and does its best to fix them so as to ease their ungodly workload.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Anish Agarwal said there’s an urgent need for a specialized AI site reliability engineer, because not even the best general-purpose large language models have been able to show they’re up to the task. He points to the ORCA-bench benchmark that his company co-developed alongside researchers from Cornell Tech and Columbia University. It reveals that even the most advanced frontier models barely achieve 25% accuracy on medium-difficulty SRE tasks, with their hallucination rates often exceeding 40%.

“Site reliability engineering is one of the hardest problems in applied AI because every company’s software environment is different, and with downtime costing companies as much as $600 billion a year, the stakes are clearly enormous,” Agarwal said.

Traversal’s AI far surpasses what the best frontier models can do. It’s designed to be deployed in enterprises’ IT environments, where it sits and analyzes massive volumes of operational telemetry, including logs, metrics and traces, so as to establish a baseline for normal behavior. When problems occur, it uses causal machine learning to identify the root cause of the issue, and then works out a solution so all the human engineer has to do is accept its recommendation to restore normal service.

Agarwal’s background in causal machine learning is the key to Traversal’s AI SRE’s much higher accuracy. It’s an AI discipline that combines causal inference with machine learning to identify cause-and-effect relationships, rather than relying on statistical correlations. In essence, it enables Traversal’s models to simulate the effects of various actions, interventions and policy changes have on IT infrastructure, so it can quickly work out what the likely cause of a problem is.

Agarwal said the company is striving to build a “superintelligent AI SRE” that can finally help enterprises to keep pace with the rapid velocity of their AI-enabled developer teams. And he believes it’s well on the way to achieving that goal. “After two years refining our technology, we’re seeing customers expand how they use Traversal across increasingly complex production environments,” he said.

In the last year, Traversal has grown its revenue more than nine-fold and its number of monthly active users has multiplied by 20. Some of its best-known customers include Pepsi Co., DigitalOcean Holdings Inc., Nubank and Harvey AI Corp.

Traversal’s momentum is impressive, but Agarwal said the company is only just getting started. With $120 million in the bank, it’s going to accelerate hiring within its engineering, go-to-market and research and development teams so it can get closer to its goal of building a superintelligent AI SRE.

Bitcoin could be approaching another major historical turning point as Americans prepare to vote in the 2026 midterm election. The crypto market has struggled through a difficult October, but previous midterm elections delivered surprisingly strong returns over the following year.

Bitcoin gained an average of 53.7% during the 12 months after the 2014, 2018, and 2022 midterms. With BTC trading at the $78,000 level ahead of the November 3 vote, we are watching to see if history offers another bullish signal.

Bitcoin and its midterm election pattern have coincided with major market transitions. However, the short-term aftermath was often painful and is leaving us with an important question. Could 2026 finally deliver a smoother recovery?

Bitcoin’s performance following the previous three U.S. midterm elections paints a good picture for long-term holders. BTC gained 24.1% during the year following the 2014 election. BTC then advanced 43.4% after the 2018 midterms and 92% following the 2022 vote.

The immediate aftermath also tells a different story. Bitcoin fell 27.5% during the 90 days following the 2014 election and plunged 46.5% after the 2018 vote. The 2022 election delivered a more favorable 90-day return of 22.6%.

These contrasting outcomes show that the Bitcoin midterm election pattern is more compelling over longer periods, not in the short term.

Now, the 2026 election arrives during a different phase of Bitcoin’s market cycle. Previous midterm elections occurred during years when Bitcoin was still approaching major cycle lows. In 2014 and 2018, the crypto market continued falling after Election Day before eventually recovering. The 2022 election also preceded another decline, partly driven by the FTX collapse.

Bitcoin’s current setup could be different if the June low near $57,803 ultimately holds. BTC has already rebounded from that level, potentially placing the market in an early recovery phase heading into the midterms.

#5511. How to Decide Whether to Build In-House, Buy an Existing Solution or Partner With Another Company

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

When should a company build, buy or partner? Here’s what you need to know.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

The challenge of when a company needs to develop a capability it doesn’t currently possess poses a management question. The analysis starts with a financial comparison. Management calculates the cost of developing internally, compares it with the price of purchasing an existing solution and selects the option with the more attractive projected return.

The analysis, however, runs the risk of reducing a strategic decision to a procurement exercise. In practice, companies can choose to build the capability themselves, buy it through a product, platform or acquisition, or partner with another organization that already possesses it.

I’ve encountered versions of this problem across banking, fintech, technology, construction and financial services, including technology modernization and system conversions, M&A work and the development and pricing of financial products.

The details and economics widely vary, but the strategic question underneath is consistent. Companies should assess what they actually need and then work towards the best answer to fulfill that need based on a larger strategic vision.

Building internally makes sense when a capability is sufficiently important to competitive differentiation that management wants to control how it evolves.

This can apply to technology, intellectual property, operating processes or specialized expertise. If a capability determines why a customer chooses the company over competitors, then an outside provider may limit the ability of the company to differentiate. Internal development allows the company to shape the capability around its strategy rather than shaping its strategy around what the market offers.

Leaders, however, generally underestimate what “build” entails. Building does not end when a system launches, the new steam is assembled or the capability becomes operational. The organization has also chosen to maintain it, staff it, improve it and keep it relevant as the business changes. A company may have the capital to build a function, but it requires continued management attention, technical talent and operating discipline.

Buying can compress years of development work. In simple terms, that means purchasing an established technology platform or service rather than creating one internally. At the other end of the spectrum, it can mean acquiring a company because the desired capability, people, intellectual property, customers, volume, distribution or market position can be difficult to produce organically.

The financial analysis of an acquisition naturally focuses on purchase price, expected return, opportunity cost and integration challenges. Strategically, management should also determine exactly what it is buying and why. What value is the company trying to solve through inorganic growth or acquisition?

The second stage of buying includes integration. A company can acquire an asset immediately without immediately acquiring the ability to use the new asset well. Systems may have to connect, processes may change, and employees may need to adopt an entirely new operating model. The objective is to determine what advantage buying produces and how quickly it can be absorbed and transitioned into an operating advantage.

The third option is partnership. This approach allows companies to access expertise, distribution, technology or operating capabilities without assuming full ownership. That can be particularly useful when the capability matters to the customer proposition but does not itself need to become a core institutional competency.

Financial services provide many examples of this logical framework. Banks and finance companies frequently leverage technology providers, payment systems, capital providers, third-party complementary products or specialized services. Creating these components internally would consume enormous resources without necessarily improving what makes the company distinctive.

The same logic applies beyond financial services. A manufacturer may partner for logistics. A technology company may rely on specialized infrastructure. A growing business may use an outside provider for a function that would be expensive to build but does not meaningfully distinguish the company in the market.

Partnerships work best when companies have clearly defined value propositions and can find mutually beneficial arrangements that add value.

A disciplined build-buy-partner decision can be organized around several questions.

First, how important is this capability to differentiation? The closer it sits to the reason customers choose the company, the stronger the argument for ownership or significant control.

Second, how quickly does the organization need it? Build may produce a better long-term fit but arrive after the market opportunity has passed. Buying or partnering can create speed when timeliness matters.

Third, does the company possess the talent to own it? Capital alone doesn’t create capability. Management has to attract, retain and lead the people who operationalize ideas.

Fourth, what is full economics? Build costs include maintenance and continued development. Acquisition costs include integration. Partnerships may require recurring payments.

Fifth, how much control does the business actually need? Leaders sometimes demand ownership when contractual rights, service standards or a well-designed partnership would provide sufficient control at a substantially lower organizational cost.

Finally, what does this choice require the company to become? Every internal capability creates another area that leadership must manage well. Every acquisition adds complexity. Every partnership creates an external dependency that must be governed.

Each of the three options has pros and cons that largely depend on the functional needs of the business. There is no right option when costs and opportunities coexist, depending on the company’s strategy and fundamentals. The main point is that all three options require careful analysis and thought before operationalizing.

The challenge of when a company needs to develop a capability it doesn’t currently possess poses a management question. The analysis starts with a financial comparison. Management calculates the cost of developing internally, compares it with the price of purchasing an existing solution and selects the option with the more attractive projected return.

The analysis, however, runs the risk of reducing a strategic decision to a procurement exercise. In practice, companies can choose to build the capability themselves, buy it through a product, platform or acquisition, or partner with another organization that already possesses it.

I’ve encountered versions of this problem across banking, fintech, technology, construction and financial services, including technology modernization and system conversions, M&A work and the development and pricing of financial products.

#5509. ‘Lawyer up’: Democrats take the House, and warn Trump’s family businesses are first in line for subpoenas

Democrats won control of the House on Tuesday night, NBC News and MS NOW projected. The win gives them limited power over President Donald Trump’s agenda and much broader power to investigate the businesses his family runs.

Democrats needed a net gain of just three seats, and they got there with wins in Republican-held suburban and swing districts.

In New Jersey’s 7th District, Democrat Rebecca Bennett, a former Navy helicopter pilot, defeated Rep. Tom Kean Jr., CNN projected, and the AP also called the race. In Virginia’s 2nd, former Rep. Elaine Luria flipped the seat held by Rep. Jen Kiggans, Decision Desk HQ projected. In Colorado’s 8th, former state lawmaker Manny Rutinel flipped one of the toss-up seats after campaigning on lowering costs and opposing the administration’s immigration crackdown. And in North Carolina’s newly redrawn 11th, Democrat Jamie Ager defeated Republican Jennifer Balkcom.

Democrats also held three Florida seats that Republicans had redrawn to flip. With races still being called, NBC’s Decision Desk estimates Democrats will finish with about 248 seats, a 61-seat majority, while CNBC’s election desk projects at least 235.

Trump, who had urged supporters to treat the midterms as a referendum on his presidency, responded on Truth Social: “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!”

Rep. Robert Garcia of California, who will chair the House Oversight Committee in the new Congress, marked the win with a two-word message in a statement and on X: “Lawyer up.” His office said he has vowed to take on what it called the “Trump Crime Family,” along with corporate corruption, abuses at the Department of Homeland Security and ICE, and the cover-up of the Epstein files.

Democrats can now pass bills with a simple majority, but passing a bill in the House doesn’t make it law. Trump has threatened to “veto everything” if Democrats win Congress, and overriding a veto takes two-thirds of both chambers. That’s a margin Democrats won’t have in either one.

That limits what House Speaker-in-waiting Hakeem Jeffries can deliver on his four stated priorities: reversing Trump’s Medicaid cuts, extending Affordable Care Act subsidies, restoring Congress’s authority over tariffs and ending the war with Iran, NBC reported. Each would need Trump’s signature or a veto-proof majority. What the House can do is refuse to pass Trump’s priorities, including spending bills. That gives Democrats leverage in every budget fight for the next two years.

Subpoenas don’t need the president’s signature. Committee control comes with the power to compel documents and testimony from the administration, and from private companies and individuals too.

Garcia has said his panel will focus on “Trump family corruption,” including the president’s cryptocurrency ventures, which have earned him more than $1 billion. He told Punchbowl News the committee will look at the family’s crypto deals, Donald Trump Jr.’s business dealings, and Trump family members like Jared Kushner “sitting on boards and getting contracts.” He also promised “quick action” on alleged pay-to-play arrangements involving former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and Corey Lewandowski. Garcia has said administration officials, including acting Attorney General Todd Blanche, could face subpoenas on “day one” of the Democratic majority.

World Liberty Financial, the Trump family’s crypto company, is likely to be first. Democrats have focused on an Emirati royal known as the “Spy Sheikh,” who bought a $500 million stake in the company last year, while it seeks a national bank charter that an arm of the Treasury Department must approve. House Democrats had already asked Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to investigate the deal. Until now, all they could do was ask.

Democrats have also said they’ll look at Trump’s pardon of a Binance co-founder who helped the Trump family launch a stablecoin. Garcia has asked the Pentagon’s inspector general to investigate whether companies that brought Eric Trump or Donald Trump Jr. into their ownership or onto their payroll were rewarded with defense contracts. Those companies have collected more than $725 million in loans, grants and awards since Trump took office, according to Oversight Democrats.

The scrutiny could reach companies outside the Trump family. Corporate donors to Trump’s White House ballroom and companies that did deals with Trump family members are expected to be among the first targets, with inquiries starting as early as February. Democrats expect the White House to resist, and plan to subpoena private entities with ties to Trump directly to get around it. In Trump’s first term, the White House slow-walked document requests and claimed executive privilege, and that strategy could return.

The White House has dismissed the plans. Democrats’ “only agenda is to continue their decade long witch hunt against President Trump,” spokeswoman Lauren Bis told Newsweek before Election Day.

#5508. A new pal for Pluto? Rubin Observatory finds its first dwarf planet candidate

by Alan Boyle on Oct 27, 2026 at 7:54 pmOctober 27, 2026 at 8:23 pm

Astronomers sorting through data from the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile have found an icy world that has a good chance of joining Pluto in the solar system’s retinue of dwarf planets.

University of Washington astronomer Mario Jurić joined the astronomer who made the discovery, Matthew Holman of the Harvard & Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics, to announce the findings today at a meeting of the American Astronomical Society’s Division for Planetary Sciences in Spokane, Wash.

Jurić, the Rubin team’s solar system lead scientist, said the observatory’s capabilities made it possible to detect and characterize the new dwarf planet candidate, known as 2026 ED138.

“Rubin is giving us an unprecedented capacity to explore the sky through a combination of speed, depth, and precision,” Jurić said in a news release. “And the discovery is just the beginning: Once we identify a new object, we can search back months, and sometimes even decades, finding it in images where nobody knew to look. This ability to both discover and ‘precover’ objects is transforming how quickly and accurately we can determine their orbits and understand the distant solar system.”

2026 ED138 traces a tilted orbital path that takes it well beyond Pluto, the solar system’s best-known dwarf planet. It’s currently at a distance of 46 astronomical units, where 1 AU equals the average distance between Earth and the sun. Pluto, by comparison, is currently about 40 AU from the sun.

Astronomers suspect ED138 formed billions of years ago closer to the sun before being flung into a wider orbit by gravitational interactions with Neptune.

Based on an analysis of its distance, brightness and assumed composition, ED138 is thought to be somewhere between 600 and 1,500 kilometers (373 to 932 miles) in diameter. At that size, an icy object should possess enough gravity to pull itself into a round shape — satisfying the primary physical criterion for a dwarf planet.

ED138 may be Rubin’s first dwarf planet candidate, but it almost certainly won’t be the last. Thanks to the observatory’s Simonyi Survey Telescope — named after the family of Seattle software billionaire Charles Simonyi — the Rubin team detected more than 11,000 new asteroids even before June’s official start of a 10-year survey of the southern sky.

Rubin’s researchers analyze the data from those scans to find objects of interest — ranging from asteroids to gamma-ray bursts — and track them over time. On Oct. 13, Holman was running data through a search code that he developed with Kevin Napier, a colleague at the Center for Astrophysics. ED138 stood out due to its exceptional size and brightness.

“My first reaction was one of excited disbelief,” Holman said. “Objects like this are very rare, so I immediately started checking whether I or the code had done something wrong.”

To confirm the discovery, Holman, Jurić and their colleagues found 30 archived observations of ED138 dating back to March 4. The Asteroid Institute’s ADAM Precovery service found still more images of the object, going back to 2016, in the archives of a different astronomical survey.

The precovery data confirmed that ED138 was a special case.

“Finding an object this big, roughly 1,000 kilometers across, is something that happens maybe once in a generation,” Jurić said. “It’s the largest trans-Neptunian object found in about 20 years, and Rubin turned it up while we were still commissioning the telescope.”

In 2006, the International Astronomical Union defined dwarf planets as planetary objects that are big enough to crush themselves into a roundish shape — technically speaking, into a state of hydrostatic equilibrium — but not big enough to clear their orbital neighborhood.

So far, the IAU has classified five solar system objects as dwarf planets — including Ceres in the main asteroid belt, plus Pluto, Eris, Haumea and Makemake in the region beyond Neptune. 2026 ED138 joins a host of other celestial objects that are thought to be dwarf planets but haven’t yet been added to the IAU’s official list.

“The official list hasn’t moved since 2008,” Jurić told GeekWire in an email. “I’m not sure if there’s an active process that reviews candidates, and what are the timelines.”

Jurić and his colleagues hope additional observations will boost ED138’s chances of attaining true dwarf planethood.

“The next step in building the case would be to prove it’s round (in hydrostatic equilibrium),” he wrote. “The means to do that would be directly through occultations (and there’s a good chance of that, given it’s in a dense stellar field), and then thermal measurements plus modeling and light curves (or the absence of variability).”

#5507. James Talarico wasn’t born the last time a Democrat won a Texas Senate race. At 37, he won one despite $200 million from Elon Musk to stop him

Democrat James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton in Texas’s Senate race, NBC News and Decision Desk HQ projected. The 37-year-old is the first Democrat to win a Senate race in Texas since 1988, when Lloyd Bentsen won his last term, six months before Talarico was born. He is also the first Democrat to win any statewide office there since 1994.

Elon Musk spent more than $200 million to help elect Paxton, according to a New York Times analysis cited in Fortune’s tally of his political giving. Most of it went through the Senate GOP’s main super PAC, Senate Leadership Fund. Musk gave SLF $75 million on Sept. 9 and $83 million on Sept. 23, and each time, SLF moved nearly the same amount into a new entity called Texas PAC the next day, the Texas Tribune reported. His trust also gave $10 million to Lone Star Liberty PAC, the main outside group backing Paxton.

The money came after Talarico had outspent Paxton on the airwaves for months. By the end of September, outside groups led by SLF had spent more than $217 million on ads in the race. Trump’s main super PAC added $10 million, its first major outlay of the midterms.

Talarico relied mostly on his own campaign. By early September he had raised $72 million to Paxton’s $16.8 million, and he finished the cycle as the most prolific fundraiser in the country. He made Musk’s spending part of his message. “This Senate seat doesn’t belong to Elon Musk,” he said on the trail.

Paxton reached the general election by beating Sen. John Cornyn, a four-term incumbent, in the May runoff. He won by nearly 28 points after Trump endorsed him. Cornyn had warned that a Paxton nomination could cost Republicans $150 million to $200 million to hold the seat, the Texas Tribune reported. Paxton was impeached by the Texas House on bribery and corruption allegations in 2023 and acquitted by the state Senate. After losing the runoff, Cornyn called Paxton “lazy” and said he would help Republicans elsewhere instead of raising money for him. Paxton never agreed to debate Talarico, making this the first Texas Senate race since 2000 without a debate between the major-party nominees.

Talarico, a state legislator and Presbyterian seminarian, ran on affordability and corruption. He argued that Paxton had served wealthy donors while Texans struggled with the cost of groceries, housing and health care. The race also turned on masculinity and anti-transgender attacks, the 19th reported.

It was the second time Tuesday night that a Republican whose path to the nomination ran through Trump lost a seat his party had held for decades. Earlier, Democrat Annie Andrews defeated Sen. Darline Graham in South Carolina.

Texans voted early in record numbers. Early voting reached 40.5% of registered voters, the highest midterm early-turnout rate on record in modern Texas. Talarico built his lead in the suburbs. In partial returns, he was winning Tarrant and Collin counties, which Trump carried by 5 and 11 points in 2024. Trump won Texas by 13.7 points two years ago.
