#5449. Opinion: San Francisco is delivering, while Seattle is still deliberating

by Joe Nguyễn on Nov 3, 2026 at 9:47 amNovember 3, 2026 at 9:47 am

Editor’s note: GeekWire publishes guest opinions to highlight a range of perspectives on issues shaping the tech and startup community. To submit a guest column, email [email protected].

How can a region care so much, spend billions in tax dollars and yet leave people losing faith in its future?

In Seattle, that question has become painfully familiar. People see suffering and disorder on their streets with little reason to believe help is coming. Business owners wonder whether the city values their presence or understands what it takes to keep their doors open. Even people who love this place are beginning to speak about its problems as permanent.

That growing resignation took us to San Francisco. We wanted to understand how a city so many had written off was giving people reasons to believe in its future again.

I expected to come home impressed with San Francisco. Instead, I came home with a deeper appreciation for Seattle. And an anger I am still trying to reconcile.

Seeing San Francisco make progress reminded me that Seattle has the talent and resources to do the same, perhaps even better. That is what made me frustrated. We should not have to accept people suffering on our streets and businesses struggling to stay open as conditions beyond our ability to change.

Not long ago, San Francisco had become a warning about what happens when a prosperous city loses its way. Less than two years into Mayor Daniel Lurie’s administration, that story has begun to change. Reported crime fell 22 percent in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier. According to Kidder Mathews, office vacancy declined to 26 percent in the third quarter from 31 percent in the prior year.

San Francisco still has profound problems, and the suffering we saw on its streets cannot be erased by encouraging statistics. But the people we met shared a confidence that their work could change the city’s direction. They understood what they were working toward and could explain what would happen next. Their optimism comes from seeing progress and believing they can build on it.

And I kept wondering why that felt so refreshing.

Seattle has extraordinary talent and resources, with public servants who care deeply and service providers doing demanding work under difficult conditions. Our business community helps shape the world. With that much ability and commitment here, we should feel confident that we can make our own neighborhoods safer and more welcoming.

Yet we often seem more resigned to our limitations than confident in our possibilities.

I recognize that habit because I have worked inside it. As a legislator and state agency director, I saw good intentions fall short when leaders avoided hard decisions and failed to hold people accountable for results. Even small obstacles became accepted excuses when no one took responsibility for overcoming them.

Throughout the trip, I kept looking for a more complicated explanation for the difference between San Francisco and Seattle. Eventually, the answer became impossible to miss.

Leaders expected the institutions they led to deliver results and took responsibility for making that happen. The unsettling part was how unfamiliar something so basic had come to feel.

San Francisco offered examples of what happens when leaders refuse to accept failure.

“Perhaps the most consequential thing we have lost is the expectation that we can do better.”

One example was Mayor Lurie’s response to open-air drug markets. The previous administration had already brought police, public health officials and other agencies together, but people we met described meetings that produced more updates than action. Lurie took that existing structure and gave it a clear purpose. Participants were expected to make decisions and take responsibility for carrying them out, then return with evidence of what had changed on the streets.

This approach helped illuminate a problem that is also familiar to Seattle. Officers encountering someone dangerously intoxicated often have no appropriate place to take them. Leaving the person on the street puts them and others at risk, while taking them to jail does little to address their need for care and would remove scarce law enforcement officials from patrol for hours.

San Francisco opened the RESET Center to fill this gap. Eligible individuals are able to receive brief medical supervision and stabilization, followed by connections to services. The center opened within ten months of the decision to proceed. It is a limited response to a larger crisis, but it gives people an option they lacked.

Across our conversations, leadership meant staying with a problem until the next step became possible. That requires something more uncomfortable than calling for accountability. It requires accepting that evidence may challenge an approach we have previously defended.

If we believe Seattle is a progressive city, we should ask whether our policies deliver the progress we promise. That means questioning our assumptions and changing programs when results fall short. Reconsidering an approach can feel like abandoning our values, but those values should compel us to change when people are still in need of help.

The business community must reconsider its own habits too. We often avoid politics even as public decisions shape our future. In San Francisco, business leaders helped set the agenda and backed leaders willing to act. If we want better outcomes here, we must help shape the decisions that produce them.

Government, in turn, must make clear that businesses belong here. A shop owner asking for a safe doorway and a person in crisis outside that door both deserve a response. A capable city should be able to care for both.

People form their judgment of a city through these encounters. They notice whether someone answers. They notice whether anything changes.

Over time, those experiences become confidence or despair.

San Francisco reminded me that resignation can lift. People can begin expecting more when they see reasons to believe their efforts matter.

Seattle has so much worth believing in. What we need is leadership willing to turn that promise into something people can feel.

Perhaps the most consequential thing we have lost is the expectation that we can do better.

What might we accomplish if we recovered it?

Read the full series, starting with Part 1.

#5448. PancakeSwap's 69% CAKE Emission Cut Would Make CAKE Less Deflationary

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Cutting CAKE emissions by 69% sounds like the most token-friendly move PancakeSwap could make. But run last week's burn figures through "The Flip," and CAKE's net deflation doesn't speed up. It falls by about 30%.

That's the part missing from coverage of the vote, which is currently running about 98% against. Reports have focused on the drop from 22,500 to 7,000 CAKE per day. They haven't covered the burn the proposal removes to fund higher LP payouts. I rebuilt the supply math using PancakeSwap's own weekly burn breakdown. The result is more interesting than a straightforward "cut emissions, good for CAKE" story.

The Flip governance vote is a binary For/Against vote. It opened on October 21 at 08:07 UTC and closes on October 24 at 08:07 UTC. As of Thursday afternoon, the vote page showed:

One address, 0x3D...e1ad, cast 765,559 votes against, about 61% of all voting power used so far.

That share has fallen as more voters joined, and the result would be lopsided even without that wallet. Excluding it, "Against" still has more than 95%. With only 32 votes cast, though, this is mainly a verdict from a small group of large veCAKE holders, not a broad community poll.

The proposal, first posted on PancakeSwap's forum on October 14, has two parts.

Emissions: Daily CAKE emissions would drop from 22,500 to 7,000, with the remaining 7,000 going to a new ecosystem fund called the Pantry. The cut happens in two stages: first to 11,000 per day, then to 7,000 once CAKE reaches its Tokenomics 3.0 goal of about a 20% supply reduction.

PancakeSwap estimates LPs would have earned about $62 million more if this split had applied to 2025 volume.

Here's PancakeSwap's burn report for the week ending October 20, as published in its weekly update:

Current emissions are 22,500 per day, or 157,500 per week. That puts this week's net deflation at about 201,000 CAKE.

Now apply The Flip to the same week. The v3 and Infinity burns are mostly gone, while v2 and "Other" stay, leaving about 190,000 CAKE of weekly burn. At stage one, emissions fall to 77,000 a week, so net deflation drops to about 113,000 CAKE, a 44% decline. At stage two, emissions fall to 49,000 a week, and net deflation recovers only to about 141,000 CAKE. That's still 30% below where it is today.

The emission cut saves 108,500 CAKE a week at full rollout. But the removed v3 and Infinity burn totaled 168,600 CAKE that week. The burn being given up is larger than the emissions being saved.

The previous week tells the same story. Working backward from the week-over-week changes, the burn was about 530,000 CAKE: roughly 272,000 from v2 and 191,000 from v3. Net deflation was about 373,000. Under The Flip, it would have been about 249,000 at stage two, which is 33% lower.

There's one real offset. The non-stablecoin part of the new 12% treasury fee still funds buybacks, and PancakeSwap hasn't said how large that is. So my figures are a floor, not an exact forecast. It's also possible that higher LP payouts attract more liquidity and volume, and the team projects up to 30% more liquidity. That would increase v2 burns over time.

PancakeSwap's own estimate, based on 10 weeks of activity, is that v2 burns alone would keep CAKE net deflationary by about 190,000 CAKE a week after emissions. That's plausible, and CAKE would keep shrinking. But it's still a slower pace of deflation than what CAKE has been running at, sold under the headline of a 69% emission cut.

The final cut to 7,000 a day depends on reaching the 20% supply reduction target. CAKE supply is 329,915,408, down 11.5% from 372,837,045 in April 2025. The roughly 20% target sits near 298.3 million, which leaves about 31.6 million CAKE still to burn.

Coverage has suggested stage two could arrive about 12 months after stage one. Here's how long 31.6 million CAKE actually takes at stage-one net deflation:

Hitting the target in 12 months would require about 608,000 CAKE of net deflation every week. That's more than CAKE's gross burn in either recent week. On these numbers, stage one could stay in place for years. The "69% cut" headline is really a 51% cut for the foreseeable future.

LPs aren't the ones voting this proposal down. Voting power comes from veCAKE, which means locked CAKE, not liquidity positions. LPs are the group that stands to gain the most, with an 88% fee share.

veCAKE holders have different incentives. Today, they direct the 22,500 daily emissions through gauge voting, and an ecosystem has grown around that control. The Flip would reduce that budget to a 7,000-a-day fund managed by PancakeSwap's team. It would also cut the burn support that has been shrinking supply. For someone holding CAKE for its scarcity, The Flip gives up a definite burn today in exchange for a possible liquidity gain later.

That's why the vote is so one-sided. The people being asked to approve The Flip aren't the people it pays. If it fails on Saturday, I'd expect the next version to keep some v3 burn share. Otherwise, the emission cut doesn't do what the headline suggests.

#5447. October 29, 2019

Chan Park feels like “an eternal nomad.” He has since age 12, when he moved from Korea to the U.S., where he attended middle school in Minnesota, followed by high school in New Jersey, followed by college in New Hampshire. Then he really began to bounce around. Park worked as a trader in New York out of college, embraced the ski-bum life in Utah, then headed to Asia for Uber, where he spent six years, running its expansion team, then managing its entire Southeast Asia business out of Singapore.

More specifically, he was responsible for eight countries across the region, and 350 people, which didn’t give him a lot of time to organize his home. But he wasn’t overwhelmed by the chaos. Instead, he says that in Singapore, something unusual happened. “There’s this huge culture of landlords furnishing space to attract expats,” explains Park. “The furnishings aren’t super high-end, but they’re well-designed and well put together, and it enabled me to be basically moved in as soon as I put my clothes in the closet.” Suddenly, coming home was a treat — a new sensation for him. “For the first time, I was proud to host friends for dinners and barbecues and to just open the door and relax.”

Park knew his U.S. friends could benefit from the same experience, and before long, he was talking with his Dartmouth classmate turned product and industrial designer Christian Talmage about forming their own company. Enter Oliver Space, which provides a lot of what that Singaporean landlord delivered to Park. It furnishes places for busy professionals, making moving into a new home as easy as hanging up their clothes.

The now year-old service is available in the Bay Area only. And Oliver Space employs just a dozen people so far. But the company has already gained enough traction to attract $6.8 million in seed funding from an interesting array of investors, including Mayfield, Abstract Ventures, investors Jana Messerschmidt and April Underwood, Opendoor founder Eric Wu, and Kevin and Julia Hartz of Eventbrite, among others.

Now, Oliver Space just has to grow as quickly, or more so, than other furniture-as-service startups to recently attract funding.

Nuvation, a year-old, New York-based cancer drug startup led David Hung, has raised $275 million in Series A funding. Omega Funds led the round, joined by Aisling Capital, Altitude Life Science Ventures, Baupost Group, Boxer Capital, EDBI, ECOR1 Capital, Fidelity, Pavilion Capital, Perceptive Advisors, Redmile Group, and Surveyor Capital. Hung founded Medivation, later selling it to Pfizer in a $14 billion deal. He more recently headed to the biotech startup Axovant, where things “went very wrong,” notes FierceBiotech. More here.

PeerStreet, a six-year-old, L.A.-based platform for investing in real estate-backed loans, just raised $60 million in Series C funding. Colchis Capital led the round, joined by earlier backers Andreessen Horowitz, World Innovation Lab, and Thomvest Ventures. Forbes has more here.

Robinhood, the six-year-old, San Francisco-based company behind a popular commission-free stock-trading app, tells Axios it has raised $50 million in new Series E funding from DST Global, closing out a $373 million Series E round at a $7.6 billion valuation that was announced in July (then as a $323 million round led by DST). Don’t be surprised to see that extra money spent on ads to compete with Charles Schwab, ETrade, and TD America. Here’s why.

Scopely, an eight-year-old, L.A.-based free-to-play mobile gaming company, has raised $200 million in Series D funding at a $1.7 billion valuation. NewView Capital led the round, joined by CPPIB, Baillie Gifford, and earlier backers Greycroft, Revolution Growth and Sands Capital Ventures. Skift has more here.

Burst Oral Care, a 2.5-year-old, Venice, Ca.-based maker of sonic toothbrushes, has raised more than $20 million led by Volition Capital, with participation from a small group of seed investors. More here.

Candy.com, a 10-year-old, Braintree, Ma.-based online candy retailer, has raised $31 million in funding for a new supply chain business called Green Rabbit that it built to manage its own temperature-sensitive confectionary products. CelLink, a seven-year-old, San Carlos, Ca.-based maker of flexible electric circuit tech for auto and energy applications, has raised $22.5 million in Series B funding from RBVC, Ford Motor Co., and BMW i-Ventures. More here.

ESS, a seven-year-old, Wilsonville, Ore.-based maker of energy storage systems, has raised $30 million in Series C funding. Breakthrough Energy Ventures and SoftBank Group’s SB Energy co-led the round, joined by Energy Ventures, PTT Global Chemical, BASF Venture Capital, Cycle Capital Management, Presidio Partners Investment Management, IPM Group, and Pangaea Ventures. GreenTechMedia has more here.

Fountain, a five-year-old, San Francisco-based automated gig and hourly hiring platform, has raised $23 million in Series B funding led by DCM. IDNow, a five-year-old, Munich, Germany-based identity verification company that enables consumers to verify their identity online, using their smartphone, tablet or webcam, has raised $40 million from Corsair Capital. TechCrunch has more here.

PierianDx, a five-year-old, St. Louis, Mo.-based clinical genomics informatics startup, has raised $27 million in Series B funding. ATW Partners and SJF Ventures co-led the round, joined by earlier backers Health Catalyst Capital, Inova Health Systems, RTI International, and ARUP Labs. More here.

Ribbon, a two-year-old, New York- and Charlotte, N.C.-based company that empowers buyers to make all-cash offers on homes, has raised $30 million in Series B funding led by earlier backer Greylock Partners, along with an additional $300 million in debt from Goldman Sachs (an amount that may be increased by $220 million, says the company). The round brings Ribbon’s total equity and debt funding to $555 million. Last year, it raised a $225 million in Series A round from Greylock, Bain Capital Ventures, NFX, and Nyca Partners, all of which just re-upped. The RealDeal has more here.

Scratchpay, a three-year-old, L.A.-based lending company focused around veterinary care, has raised $15 million in Series B funding and another $50 million in debt. Companion Fund led the equity piece, with participation from TTV Capital, FJ Labs and Struck Capital. The $50 million warehouse facility comes from Credit Suisse. More here.

Twistle, an eight-year-old, Seattle-based mobile-health platform that helps clinical teams streamline care pathways by automating follow-up and surveillance, has raised $16 million in Series A funding co-led by Health Enterprise Partners and Memorial Care Innovation Fund. More here.

WeFarm, a four-year-old, London-headquartered marketplace and networking site for small-holder farmers in Kenya and Uganda, has raised $13 million in Series A funding led by earlier investor True Ventures, with participation from AgFunder, June Fund and other earlier investors LocalGlobe, ADV and Norrsken Foundation. TechCrunch has more here.

ALICE, a six-year-old, Menlo Park, Ca.-based simulation platform for construction that leveraging AI to analyze a project’s building requirements and generate more efficient construction plans, has raised $8 million in Series A funding led by Merus Capital, with participation from Foundamental, Blackhorn Ventures and Lightspeed Venture Partners. More here.

Become, a three-year-old, San Mateo, Ca.-based business lending marketplace that caters to small and mid-size businesses, has raised $10 million in Series A  funding, along with $2.5 million in venture debt. The equity piece was co-led by Benson Oak Ventures and Magenta Venture Partners, with participation from RIO Ventures Holdings, iAngels and Entrée Capital. The debt funding was provided by Viola Credit. TechCrunch has more here.

Fireflies.AI, a five-year-old, San Francisco based meeting transcription and collaboration tool, has raised $4.6 million in seed funding led by Canaan. Other investors in the round include F7 Ventures and angel investors April Underwood, Slack CMO Bill Macaitis, and Salesforce director of search Susan Kimberlin. VentureBeat has more here.

KOIO, a 4.5-year-old, New York-based direct-to-consumer Italian leather sneaker label, just raised $6 million in funding. Founders Fund led the round, joined by Acton Capital Partners and Brand Foundry. The company has now raised $9 million altogether. More here.

Manime, a two-year-old, a Palo Alto, Ca.-based company making custom-fit gel nail adhesives, has raised $2.6 million in seed funding led by Canaan, with participation from Trinity Ventures, Techstars and NFX. TechCrunch has more here.

mPower Technology, a four-year-old, Albuquerque, N.M.-based solar cell startup, has raised $2.5 million in Series A funding from Sun Mountain Capital. More here.

Quill, a two-year-old, San Francisco-based no-frills enterprise messaging startup led by Stripe’s former creative director, has quietly raised two rounds of funding, reports TechCrunch. It closed a $2 million seed round led by Sam Altman, with participation from General Catalyst, followed by a $12.5 million Series A round at a $62.5 million post-money valuation led by Index Ventures. More here.

Recount Media, a months-old, Bay Area-based video venture that was founded by journalists John Heilemann and John Battelle and says it will deliver bite-size “remixes” of the day’s biggest political stories, has raised $10 million in funding. Backers include Union Square Ventures, Jay-Z’s Arrive venture fund, Kevin Durant’s Thirty Five Ventures, Robert Wolf’s 32 Ventures, True Ventures, SV Angel, and a couple of individual angel investors. Vanity Fair has more here.

Searchable.ai, a three-month-old, San Francisco-based stealthy search startup focused on the enterprise, has raised $2 million in seed funding led by Defy Partners. Other investors in the round include Paul English, co-founder of Kayak; Wayne Chang, co-founder of Crashlytics; Brian Halligan, co-founder and CEO of HubSpot; Jonathan Kraft, president and COO of the Kraft Group and the New England Patriots; MIT professor Edward Roberts; Eric Dobkin, founder and chairman emeritus of Goldman Sachs Global Equity Capital Markets; and Susquehanna International Group. TechCrunch has more here.

Socially Determined, a nearly three-year-old, Washington, D.C.-based healthcare data analytics startup, has raised $7.3 million in Series A funding from Ziegler Link-Age Funds, ProMedica, 3M, OSF HealthCare, and LRVHealth. More here.

#5446. Tech Moves: Microsoft loses a CVP to AWS and gains one from Alteryx; Lila Bio and BECU name execs

Tech Moves covers notable hires, promotions and personnel changes in the Pacific NW tech community. Submissions: [email protected]

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 3, 2026 at 10:28 amNovember 3, 2026 at 2:30 pm

— After more than 33 years at Microsoft, Mazhar Mohammed has left to become vice president of AWS Streaming and Messaging at Amazon.

Mohammed joined Microsoft as a software design engineer on Windows NT straight out of a master’s degree program. Over the decades, he also worked on messaging, mobile services and partner experience for cloud services. He most recently served as corporate VP for the commerce and fraud protection platform.

His LinkedIn post was short and to the point. Mohammed said he was “happy to share” the news, and the post featured a photo of an Amazon box with the message “Alexa, play ‘New Beginnings.’”

— Microsoft has named Chad Thompson as CVP of Agent Cloud, a group within the company developing technology that allows businesses to deploy AI agents and put them to work across their organizations.

“My view: enterprise is where AI pays off. Not in demos, but in measurable results. Lower costs, faster cycle times, better decisions, and work that gets done without someone pushing it along,” Thompson wrote in a LinkedIn post.

Thompson joins from Alteryx. He previously spent six years at Amazon, departing as general manager of Amazon Glow. Other past employers include Smartsheet, Exasol and Adobe.

— Gail Carpenter has been named as VP and chief financial officer of Global Entertainment and Advertising at Amazon. She was most recently CFO of Worldwide Stores Finance and has been with the company for 11 years.

— Seattle biotech startup Lila Bio has appointed Kimberly Ma as chief development officer. The company spun out of Nobel laureate David Baker’s lab at the University of Washington and is using AI to design new proteins that can treat cancer with targeted radiation therapy. Last year it announced a collaboration with pharmaceutical giant Eli Lilly to develop therapies for solid tumors.

Ma has 20 years of experience in oncology drug development, most recently as a leader at Abdera Therapeutics. She also worked at RayzeBio, where she led the clinical operations team and supported the company’s IPO and its $4.1 billion acquisition by Bristol Myers Squibb in 2024.

— The not-for-profit credit union BECU has named Geoffrey Fonga as VP of AI transformation. The member-owned organization is based in Tukwila, Wash.

“For years, I helped organizations adopt and scale AI as an advisor and a vendor,” Fonga said. “Now I get to do the harder, more rewarding part: leading that transformation from the inside.”

Fonga joins from DataRobot. He previously held leadership roles at McKinsey & Company and Wells Fargo.

— Andre Woodson Jr. has taken a new role at Amazon as manager of U.S. state and local policy communications and external affairs. Woodson was previously a regional field communications manager and has been with the company for more than 12 years.

— Hanna Grene has left Microsoft, where she served as global go-to-market and innovation leader for energy, to join Xcel Energy. She will lead the company’s newly established Enterprise Growth and Commercialization group, effective Nov. 16.

— Seattle-based RevealDx,which is developing AI technology for detecting potentially cancerous lung nodules, has made two leadership appointments:

— Enterprise software company LogicGate has named two new leaders to the business, which is headquartered in Chicago and has multiple C-suite executives based at its Bellevue, Wash., office. Steve Smith has joined as managing director of Europe, the Middle East and Africa, and Amanda Meglemre as general counsel.

— Former Cisco and Microsoft security executive Edna Conway was appointed to the advisory council for Known, a Bellevue, Wash.-based tech company building accountability infrastructure for AI agents. Conway was with Cisco for 20 years before joining Microsoft in 2020 as VP and chief security and risk officer for Azure infrastructure.

— Avalanche Energy, a Seattle-based startup building fusion devices, has named Chris Riegel as head of talent acquisition. He joins from HiringKit, an HR company that Riegel co-founded. Former employers include Amazon and Unity Technologies.

In addition to chasing fusion, Avalanche is leading a team tackling DARPA’s nuclear battery challenge and launching FusionWERX, a commercial-scale testing facility for fusion technologies in Eastern Washington.

— Julie Averill, former chief information officer at lululemon and REI, has joined the UW Foundation Board, which helps raise philanthropic support for the university.

— Technology Alliance has appointed Jen Oleson, a senior director at Seattle-based consulting firm Slalom, to its board. Oleson will serve on the organization’s Research Capacity Committee.

— Ben Helsel has left Premera Blue Cross to join Kaiser Permanente, where he’ll serve as VP and general manager of commercial markets in Washington.

The festivities take place Thursday, Dec. 10, with the main event running from 6 p.m. to 10 p.m. at The Shop at 2233 6th Ave. S. in Seattle’s SoDo neighborhood.

Dress to impress, break out your holiday flair, or keep it geek chic. Cocktail attire is welcome, but there are no fashion rules at this party.

A big thank you to our returning presenting sponsor, First Tech Federal Credit Union, and our 2026 sponsors, including Microsoft, Wilson Sonsini, Zoox, University of Washington, ALLtech, WTIA, Turkish Airlines, Washington State University and Prime Team Partners. #5444. October 31, 2019

Album VC, a Lehi, Utah-based early-stage venture firm that’s been known until now as Peak Ventures, just gathered up $75 million in capital commitments for its third early-stage fund.

The development shows investor confidence in Album’s young team, which came together in 2014 after the founder of Zinch — a site connecting colleges and students that sold to the ed-tech company Chegg in 2011 — decided to try his hand at investing in other startups.

As that founder, Sid Krommenhoek — who stayed on with Chegg for several years, running its international efforts — explains it, “I thought I’d do another startup. But I also knew from our own experience in struggling to raise money the need for more capital in Utah, and I thought having that operator-entrepreneur perspective could be useful.”

A first fund, like many in the industry, was more of an experiment, though it was a decent $23 million, thanks largely to the support of Chegg CEO Dan Rosensweig, who was early to commit capital to the fund. A second ($56 million) fund followed when Krommenhoek and John Mayfield — a friend who joined him from a marketing role at Qualtrics — began investing more seriously in their backyard and beyond.

They were soon joined by a third investor, Diogo Myrrha, who began as a principal with the firm and is now a general partner. Explains Krommenhoek of one of the many things that binds the three Brigham Young University grads, “We all came into Utah’s orbit when it wasn’t necessarily a place where you could live out your career, but that’s changed.”

Arranta Bio, a months-old, Watertown, Ma.-based contract development manufacturing organization focused on the biotech industry, has raised $82 million in funding, including from Ampersand Capital Partners and Thermo Fisher. More here.

B8ta, a four-year-old, San Francisco- and New York-based operator of an experiential retail-as-a-service platform, has raised $50 million in Series C funding led by Evolution Ventures, with participation from Macy’s, Khosla Ventures, and Peak State Ventures. Retail Touchpoints has more here.

Tmunity Therapeutics, a four-year-old, Philadelphia, Pa.-based biotherapeutics company trying to propel a series of cancer-fighting cellular therapies through clinical trials, has raised $75 million in Series B funding led by Andreessen Horowitz. Other investors in the round include Kleiner Perkins, Westlake Village BioPartners, Gilead Sciences, The University of Pennsylvania, Be The Match BioTherapies and BrightEdge Venture Fund. More here and here.

Vindex, a months-old, New York-based esports infrastructure platform founded by a former Activision Blizzard vice president, has raised $60 million in Series A funding from unnamed investors. ESPN has more here.

Crunchbase, a 12-year-old, Bay Area-based private company information database that spun out of TechCrunch in 2015, has raised $30 million in Series C funding led by OMERS Ventures. Earlier investors also participated in the round, including Emergence Capital, Mayfield, Cowboy Ventures, and Verizon Ventures. TechCrunch has more here.

CytoVale, a six-year-old, San Francisco-based med-tech startup focused on re-imagining diagnostics using cell mechanics and machine learning and applying this first to sepsis, just raised $15 million in funding. Breakout Ventures and Blackhorn Ventures led the round. More here.

dotData, a year-old, San Mateo, Ca.-based data science automation platform, has raised $23 million in Series A funding led by JAFCO, with participation from Goldman Sachs and NEC Corp. VentureBeat has more here.

Freetrade, a four-year-old, London-based startup offering a mobile app for zero-commission trades and professional advice, has raised $15 million in Series A funding, including from Draper Esprit. TechCrunch has more here.

#5443. Jumbo Series A Rounds Hiding The Real Squeeze On Seed Startups

Global startups have closed at least 114 Series A rounds of $100 million or more so far this year, Crunchbase reported in late September, and more than 70% of them went to AI companies. For most seed founders, that headline is a warning.

U.S. startups closed 272 Series A rounds in the third quarter, according to Crunchbase data, about 28% fewer than the 377 a year earlier. Seed held up better, at 984 rounds vs. 1,059. The megarounds hide how few A rounds are getting done.

Seed checks keep growing. The median U.S. seed round was about $3 million last year, 3x its 2018 level, according to Crunchbase. Yet only 24% of companies that raised a $1 million-plus seed in 2023 have moved past seed, and just 16% of the 2024 cohort, down from 55% or higher through 2020.

Uncork Capital‘s Andy McLoughlin told Crunchbase News that Series A investors now expect $2 million to $3 million in ARR, sometimes $4 million, and the time from seed to A has stretched past two years. If a seed won’t carry you to that bar with six months to spare, a smaller round is the better deal.

A bigger seed isn’t required. Take Atomic, a New York-based supply chain planning software company founded in 2023 (and not an MGV portfolio company). It raised a $3 million seed, right at the median, in April 2025, led by Madrona and DVx Ventures, then closed a $12.5 million Series A led by Madrona and Klass Capital about 17 months later.

Funds of $100 million to $500 million typically lead the Series A. Figure out which ones lead at your stage and when their current fund closes, then send the right partners updates for a year before you ask for anything.

The Series A bar is now a revenue bar, which makes it a go-to-market problem first. Most seed companies I meet have a stronger product than sales motion.

At MGV, our work starts with a first session we call Sales Jumpstart: we interview the founders and their team. We then score the company on our proprietary matrix: where it is today, where it should be, and what it needs to become a scalable go-to-market machine.

From there, founders work through workshops on outbound reach, qualification, profiling, the funnel, objection handling, hiring assessment, compensation plans, fundraising, deck building, storytelling and investor intros, with mentoring alongside.

A company at $2 million in ARR with a sales process a new hire can run is a better Series A candidate than one at $3 million built on founder-led deals nobody else can repeat. The founders who make it are already planning for the round after this one.

#5442. Amazon rewrites its software engineering playbook for an era when AI writes the code

by Todd Bishop on Nov 3, 2026 at 12:26 pmNovember 3, 2026 at 12:36 pm

Last month, a small team inside Amazon Web Services called Velocity Labs went from concept to the public release of a new open-source AI model in less than a week.

The group, whose existence hasn’t been previously reported, was formed in April. Velocity Labs has about 35 people, most of them in Seattle. The idea is to think beyond Amazon’s normal product-oriented approach, building quick prototypes in areas of AI that the company sees as underexplored and increasingly important to customers.

“We have noticed how the open-source community, and some of our competitors, experiment with new ideas, and deliver initial products fast,” the company says in job listings. “With Velocity Labs we are building an organization that can move faster, explore more, and make sure AWS is at the cutting edge of innovation in agentic AI.”

Inside the group, scientists and engineers work together, and they’re encouraged to cross over: engineers engage in research, and scientists do engineering work.

Velocity Labs is an example of the ways Amazon is trying “to create organizations that we think are going to be better suited to working with this new set of tools,” said Marc Brooker, an AWS vice president and distinguished engineer who leads the team.

For the vast majority of Amazon’s developers, he said, AI agents now write almost all the code that would have previously been written by hand.

Redefining the role: The team is part of Amazon’s larger rethinking of software development for the AI era, laid out in revised guidelines that the company’s engineering leaders sent to its developers earlier this year.

A letter that accompanied the guidelines, published last week under the byline of Michael “Terk” Terkowitz, a VP and distinguished engineer in Amazon’s stores business, advises engineers to learn AI now and to stay close to their customers and products.

The letter acknowledges that as Amazon has grown, some engineers and managers have become “less connected to their customers and business.”

Amazon has never published its underlying role guidelines for software engineers, and it declined to provide a copy of the revised version for this article. Brooker, one of the authors of the accompanying letter, said in an interview that the update emphasizes measuring engineers and teams by outcomes rather than inputs.

“We had seen these anti-patterns in the industry of folks really focusing on how many tokens are you spending, how many lines of code are you committing,” Brooker said, explaining that those kinds of measures don’t equate to customer value.

Asked whether AI use is part of performance reviews or promotions, Brooker said, “Not directly in a metrics sense.” It could factor in, he said, to the extent that it makes someone a stronger performer.

The letter doesn’t dismiss usage metrics entirely. Amazon has found that they “correlate well with the outputs that matter” and expects that to continue “for some time,” it says.

But what’s important, the letter says, is to use them “with care and judgement.”

Amazon engineers have described pressure to use AI tools. Three developers told The New York Times last year that managers were pushing them to use AI, raising output goals and becoming less forgiving about deadlines, with some coders saying their jobs had begun to resemble warehouse work. Amazon has set a goal for more than 80% of its developers to use AI each week, the Financial Times reported.

In May, Amazon shut down an internal leaderboard called KiroRank — which ranked employees by how much they used Kiro, the company’s AI coding tool — after finding that some were using the tool excessively just to climb the rankings, the FT reported.

Asked whether that episode was part of the impetus for the revised guidelines, Brooker said he didn’t recall the leaderboard or the details surrounding it.

“If your work does not benefit from current AI tooling, that is a finding, not a failing. Document why, share it with your community of peers, bring it to your manager, and work to find solutions.”

Letter accompanying the revised SDE role guidelines

How the work has changed: Two years ago, most Amazon developers were still writing their code by hand, Brooker said. Today, “for the vast majority of our developer population, almost all of their implementation code is agent generated rather than human written,” he said.

“That is a massive change in the way of working for software engineers,” he said.

Brooker said he used to spend much of his time in a traditional code editor or the command line, and now spends a lot more of it working with agent tools such as Kiro, Kiro Crew and Anthropic’s Claude Code, calling it “a complete change of tools.”

For the company, the transition hasn’t been seamless. In March, Amazon acknowledged that an engineer who followed inaccurate advice from an AI agent contributed to one of several outages on its retail site, though the company disputed a Financial Times report that junior and mid-level engineers would need senior engineers to sign off on AI-assisted changes.

Amazon also pushed back on an earlier FT report that a 13-hour disruption to an AWS service in December happened after engineers let its Kiro AI coding tool make changes, and the tool decided to “delete and recreate the environment.” Amazon blamed user error — a misconfigured role — and said it has since added safeguards, including mandatory peer review for production access.

Still, the letter acknowledges that today’s AI tools won’t help in every situation, and it says that’s OK as long as engineers can explain why.

“If your work does not benefit from current AI tooling, that is a finding, not a failing,” the letter says. “An engineer who can explain where AI does not yet help their work is demonstrating the judgement we are asking for.”

Inside Velocity Labs: The group is part of the agentic AI division led by Swami Sivasubramanian, which has organized much of its work around small teams of six to eight people, as GeekWire reported in June. Velocity Labs also includes the developers behind Strands, AWS’s open-source toolkit for building AI agents.

The model that Velocity Labs released last month, Strands Decider 2B, is designed to make quick, narrow decisions inside AI agents, such as which tool to use or where to route a request. It’s based on Qwen, an open model from Alibaba, and was released Oct. 1 along with the recipe used to train it.

Brooker built the original version on his own GPU at home after the startup TypeSafe AI unveiled Jev, a similar decision model, on Sept. 15, he wrote on his blog. “Every line of code was written by an agent,” he wrote, though he tried to make sure “the core ideas and insights were mine, or at least I understood them.”

Brooker described the team’s turnaround as less than a week from concept to public release. OpenAI announced a similar hosted service, its Decisions API, the same week, TechCrunch reported.

Brooker credited the team’s speed to its small size and a high level of trust: each person takes ownership of a piece of a project and asks for help when needed. He expects Amazon to create more teams like it, though not across the whole company.

Impact on jobs: Amazon has cut roughly 30,000 corporate jobs since late 2025. CEO Andy Jassy has said he expects AI to shrink the company’s corporate workforce over time.

At the same time, AWS CEO Matt Garman said in April that Amazon is “hiring just as many software developers as we ever had,” Business Insider reported. An Amazon spokesperson told the publication that more than 11,000 interns and early-career software engineers would join the company globally this year.

Asked whether AI will mean fewer engineers at Amazon, Brooker said, “I don’t think it changes the number of engineers.” The company wants engineers who take ownership, are curious and can learn quickly outside their areas of expertise, he said.

AI isn’t the right answer for every problem, Brooker said.

If the right tool is “an AI agent powered by a cutting-edge model, fantastic,” he said. However, he added, if it’s “three lines of Python code, that’s great too.”

In just a few weeks, AWS re:Invent brings advanced and expert-level sessions on the services you build on every day, from serverless and containers to databases and developer tools. Go hands-on with new launches the same week they’re announced, and hear directly from the engineers who built them. Experience the depth you won’t find anywhere else.

#5441. Filing: Amazon’s previously announced layoffs include 95 jobs in Washington state

by Todd Bishop on Nov 3, 2026 at 6:11 pmNovember 3, 2026 at 6:13 pm

A notice made public Tuesday evening, disclosing about 95 Amazon job cuts in Washington state, is part of the company’s previously reported layoffs in its retail business, not a new round of reductions, a spokesperson confirmed.

The filing lists software engineers, product managers and program managers among the affected employees. Most are based in Amazon’s Seattle offices, but others work in Bellevue and Redmond, at warehouses in Sumner and Pasco, or remotely.

Reuters reported in early October that Amazon was laying off fewer than 1,000 corporate employees, mainly in its Stores unit, which runs the company’s e-commerce business. Amazon confirmed to GeekWire at the time that “hundreds” of Stores employees were affected. The notice covers only employees based in Washington state.

“We’ve adjusted parts of our Stores business because we believe this structure will better enable us to deliver on our priorities,” Amazon said in a statement at the time.

Most affected employees were notified in October, including 43 on or about Oct. 7, when the Stores cuts were first reported. Others received notice in September or as early as July 3, according to the filing.

The federal Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification (WARN) Act requires large employers to give workers and the government advance notice of mass layoffs. Washington’s version of the WARN Act generally requires 60 days’ notice when a covered employer eliminates 50 or more jobs within 30 days across its Washington operations, excluding part-time employees.

Amazon has made a series of smaller filings under the state law in the past year, including notices covering 121 jobs in August, 57 tech jobs earlier in the summer and 84 jobs last December.

The latest notice covers employees at 17 Amazon offices and warehouses in Seattle, Bellevue, Redmond, Sumner and Pasco, plus 15 remote workers in the state.

The list also includes risk managers, several directors and other senior employees. Employees who land other jobs inside Amazon before their separation dates won’t be laid off, the notice says.

The Stores cuts were much smaller than Amazon’s major corporate cutbacks since last fall. The company eliminated about 14,000 corporate roles globally in October 2025, including 2,303 in Washington, followed by another round in January that included 2,198 Washington employees.

#5439. Series B Funding Is Up, But Fewer Deals Are Getting Done

More money, fewer rounds. That, in short, is the state of U.S. Series B startup funding in 2026, as venture capital investment continues to concentrate heavily around a handful of AI hotshots.

Crunchbase data shows that so far this year, investors have poured around $48 billion into financings around the Series B stage 1, the highest tally in years. Yet round counts are below year-ago levels and are on track for a multiyear low.

One trend driving capital concentration is a sharp decline in small and mid-sized Series B rounds.

So far this year, less than a third of deals in our sample set 2 were for under $30 million. By contrast, between 2021 and 2025, rounds in this range accounted for about half of deals, per Crunchbase data.

The smallest Series B deals have gotten particularly scarce. This year there were just 26 rounds under $10 million in our sample set.

On the flip side, really large Series B rounds are quite popular.

At least 110 companies have raised rounds of $100 million or more around this stage so far this year. That’s roughly a quarter of all deals.

Of these, the largest by far was a $12 billion round 3 for Prometheus, Jeff Bezos’ physical AI startup that launched last year.

Model developer World Labs, led by AI pioneer Fei-Fei Li, was tied for next-biggest fundraiser, closing on $1 billion in February. Nuclear energy startup Valar Atomics also secured $1 billion in Series B funding across tranches this year, with Sequoia Capital as lead investor.

For  a wider snapshot, below we put together a sample list of more of this year’s biggest U.S. Series B recipients.

Meanwhile, one of the least surprising findings from our analysis of Series B recipients is that it was a heavily AI-focused group.

So far this year, about two-thirds of Series B funding has gone to AI-focused startups, per Crunchbase data. In 2025, by comparison, about half of investment went to companies in AI categories.

AI companies were also heavily represented by round count. So far in 2026, more than half of all reported U.S. Series B deals have been for AI companies.

Overall, the numbers point to a bullish climate for Series B investment, particularly for AI startups with demonstrated traction. The environment looks particularly favorable for companies that have already raised considerable sums at Series A and seed.

Even so, these don’t look like the best of times for startups seeking smaller Series B rounds. Seems like in the current AI-driven cycle, investors are increasingly focused on big checks for high-valuation companies.

May include rounds that have characteristics of Series B financings but were not explicitly announced as Series B deals.↩

Sample included U.S. Series B rounds of $1 million or more.↩

Prometheus did not publicly announce its $12 billion funding round as a Series B, but reports from multiple sources, including an Axios post, described it as Series B.↩

#5438. Sector Snapshot: Travel Tech Funding Heads Toward Multiyear Low Despite AI Push

Travel demand appears to be holding up, but at the same time, investor appetite for travel tech startups has cooled. Even a wave of startups promising to improve travel with AI hasn’t managed to reverse the funding slowdown, a review of Crunchbase data shows. Whether uncertainty over how AI will reshape travel planning and booking is contributing to that pullback remains an open question.

Startups in the travel tech space have raised $2.2 billion this year through the third quarter, according to Crunchbase data. The largest funding recipients span a wide range of categories including hotel management software, travel booking platforms, alternative accommodations and corporate events. The mix also includes electric aviation, travel finance and insurance, and consumer hospitality businesses, reflecting a broad definition of travel tech.

The broad trend: Investors are making far fewer bets on travel startups than immediately before and after the COVID-19 pandemic, Crunchbase data shows. This year could be the lowest since at least 2018 when it comes to dollars raised and deal count.

AI is a recurring theme among the largest funding recipients, with many using it to perform functions such as automating hospitality operations, personalizing bookings and streamlining travel planning.

The numbers: In the first three quarters of 2026, startups in the travel tech space have raised $2.2 billion globally across just 302 funding rounds, Crunchbase data shows. That’s down fairly significantly so far from the $3.7 billion raised in 2025. Deal volume is on track to fall for a third consecutive year — pointing to a market where investors are putting more money into fewer companies.

Funding and deal volume in recent years remain far below past levels. In 2021, for example, funding in the sector topped $12 billion. That’s a bit surprising considering that so much travel was halted in the midst of the COVID-19 pandemic. But even prior to the pandemic, funding and deal totals were much higher — totaling $9.4 billion across 1,277 deals in 2018 and $10.4 billion across 1,190 transactions in 2019.

Even travel industry researcher Skift noted the funding downturn in a recent newsletter, saying: “Though it’s too early to say whether this is a long-term market movement, it’s a clear sign of the times.”

Interestingly, several of the year’s largest deals involved startups headquartered outside of the United States.

The year’s largest funding recipient through the third quarter was Mews, which raised a $300 million Series D in January led by EQT Growth, with participation from Atomico, HarbourVest Partners, Kinnevik, Battery Ventures and Tiger Global Management. The Amsterdam-based hospitality software company helps hotels manage reservations, payments and operations, and says it plans to expand its use of AI agents to automate workflows. The financing valued the company at $2.5 billion.

Chinese electric aircraft developer Aerofugia raised about $144 million in February in a financing led by CITIC Securities, joined by New Alliance Capital, Vertex Ventures China and other investors. Chengdu-based Aerofugia, also backed by automaker Geely, develops electric passenger aircraft that take off and land vertically, often called flying taxis.

Montreal-based Stay22 secured a $122 million minority growth investment from Summit Partners in February. The startup uses AI to help publishers, creators and event organizers turn their audiences’ interest in travel into bookings and affiliate revenue.

Home-swapping platform Kindred announced an $85 million Series C led by Index Ventures in February. The San Francisco-based startup operates a members-only network where travelers exchange stays in one another’s homes. Its announcement also included a $40 million Series B co-led by New Enterprise Associates and Figma CEO Dylan Field, bringing the combined funding disclosed that day to $125 million.

Another large deal went to Paris-based Naboo, which announced a $70 million Series B in February led by Lightspeed Venture Partners with participation from Notion Capital, Isai and Ternel. The company uses AI to help businesses source venues, organize corporate events and manage related purchasing and payments.

Several travel startups have found buyers in 2026, including companies developing AI tools for planning and booking trips. Amadeus acquired corporate travel AI assistant SkyLink in February, while Expedia acquired AI trip-planning startup Layla in July. Both deals illustrate a trend of established travel companies buying startups to expand their AI capabilities.

Expedia also completed its acquisition of venture-backed Tiqets, a booking platform for museums, attractions and experiences, in February.

On the IPO side, a potentially prominent prospective exit fell through. Travel experiences platform Klook withdrew its planned U.S. offering in October after having filed last November.

Still, the downturn in startup funding and dearth of IPOs in the sector hasn’t affected one of the bigger now-public players in the space. Corporate travel booking and expense management platform Navan has seen its stock rise nearly 60% this year. Formerly called TripActions, it began trading on Nasdaq under NAVN in October 2025. Its stock closed at $27 on Oct. 28, up about 58% this year from its Dec. 31 closing price of $17.08. It was also 8% above its $25 IPO price, meaning much of this year’s gain recovered from losses following the listing.

#5436. CFTC Sets December 14 Deadline to Rewrite "Actual Delivery": Where Exchanges Are Exposed

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The clock is officially ticking on the Commodity Futures Trading Commission’s (CFTC) attempt to overhaul its regulatory grip on retail digital asset trading.

While corporate press releases focused on preliminary announcements, the formal publication of Federal Register Document 2026-20888 under RIN 3038-AF80 establishes a strict deadline: public comments close on December 14, 2026.

That date anchors an urgent operational check for digital asset exchanges, custodians, and margin trading desks. While crypto media outlets like The Defiant and TFTC covered the high-level regulatory announcement, this breakdown maps the ANPRM’s exact per-question mechanics directly against the concrete exchange structures they expose. The Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM) represents the Commission’s first attempt to replace its piecemeal enforcement stances with a binding, notice-and-comment framework for "actual delivery" under Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Commodity Exchange Act (CEA).

Responding by December 14 is not merely an exercise in policy debate; it requires market participants to confront the exact legal and technical mechanics where their existing architectures remain exposed.

Under Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the CEA, any leveraged, margined, or financed retail commodity transaction falls under full CFTC futures regulation unless "actual delivery" occurs within 28 days. Centralized exchanges historically operate in a regulatory gray area by executing off-chain, book-entry updates in internal databases and claiming those entries fulfilled delivery requirements.

The proposed Regulation CTX directly targets that operational model. Through the questions inside the ANPRM 2026-20888, the Commission reveals four critical vulnerabilities that exchanges must address before the comment window shuts:

In its analysis of the proposal, law firm Fenwick & West highlights that the ANPRM leaves open a crucial question regarding how the 28-day actual delivery exception applies to fully-paid transactions maintained entirely on an exchange’s internal ledger.

If an exchange's user agreement or onboarding terms contain broad margin or financing language, the CFTC signals that every transaction on the platform, even fully-paid spot trades could be swept into the CTX umbrella. Without explicit actual delivery, an exchange keeping user assets on internal book-entry databases risks having its entire spot book reclassified as an illegal, unregistered derivatives venue.

The ANPRM questions whether off-chain ledger entries can ever satisfy actual delivery without an explicit on-chain transaction. If the CFTC mandates on-chain settlement, exchanges relying on centralized databases to match order books at high speeds will face severe throughput bottlenecks and surging gas costs.

The notice probes what constitutes true "possession and control" by the buyer. The CFTC specifically asks whether a customer maintains full control if an exchange retains administrative keys, emergency pause functions, or liquidation authority. If retaining risk-management hooks breaks the delivery exception, platforms cannot claim actual delivery while maintaining centralized control over user balances.

Recognizing that instant on-chain delivery for high-frequency retail leverage is technically impractical, the Commission seeks feedback on Alternative CTX framework models. The notice asks whether leveraging registered Futures Commission Merchant (FCM) structures, strict account segregation, and proof-of-reserves audits can provide a viable compliance pathway for platforms choosing not to settle every trade on-chain.

Because this ANPRM RIN 3038-AF80 precedes a formal Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM), the CFTC is using the December 14, 2026 window to gather empirical data on how exchanges manage custody, leverage, and settlement. Platforms can review the docket materials directly via the CFTC Innovation page.

Exchanges relying on internal ledgers to offer retail products must submit technical feedback demonstrating how their custody models preserve user protection. Once the CFTC translates these questions into binding NPRM language, the legal definition of "actual delivery" will solidify, leaving non-compliant exchanges directly vulnerable to federal enforcement actions.

Bitcoin price fell sharply as renewed Iran conflict fears collided with a wave of crypto hacks, giving us a fresh market shock. Reports of US strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island revived concerns about oil supplies, while a string of security breaches continued to undermine confidence across the digital asset industry.

The sell-off comes as we are grappling with weak crypto sentiment, falling ETF flows and uncertainty surrounding global markets. Bitcoin is now caught between geopolitical risk and a growing security crisis within its own industry.

The latest reported US strikes added uncertainty to an eight-month conflict that has disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Oil prices edged higher after the reports, with Brent crude trading near $105 per barrel today.

The Iran narrative returned to the forefront after reports that US forces struck Qeshm Island, near the Strait of Hormuz. The US officials themself described the strikes as defensive, but the development threatens to complicate diplomatic efforts between Washington and Tehran. The two sides have continued contacts aimed at ending the conflict, but no breakthrough has emerged.

❗️ US OFFICIALS CONFIRMED WASHINGTON BOMBED IRAN'S QESHM ISLAND FEW HOURS AGO IN A SERIES OF 'LIMITED STRIKES' — WSJ pic.twitter.com/Yy3C0ysWPQ

The Strait of Hormuz remains a major concern for global markets. The waterway previously carried around one-fifth of global oil and natural gas supplies, making any disruption a potential threat to energy prices and inflation.

Higher oil price could complicate the outlook for central banks and keep financial conditions tight. That would leave risk assets, including Bitcoin, vulnerable if investors shift toward cash and safer investments.

Asian equities also retreated today as investors weighed geopolitical risks, technology-sector weakness and uncertainty ahead of US midterm elections. Reuters reported that MSCI’s Asia-Pacific index excluding Japan fell 1.4%, while South Korean shares dropped as much as 4.1%.

Customers withdrew billions of dollars following the incident, raising questions about confidence in centralized trading platforms.

The exchange said it would cover the losses, while withdrawals later began stabilizing. However, the incident has added another source of uncertainty for traders already navigating a fragile market.

The Binance breach is not an isolated case. Recent attacks have also hit Mercado Bitcoin, Polymarket and infrastructure providers serving crypto platforms.

Mercado Bitcoin disclosed a security incident involving customer-related systems, while Polymarket experienced unauthorized withdrawals through a compromised third-party provider. The incidents have renewed concerns about the security of exchanges, wallets, and services connected to crypto applications.

A wave of attacks has also targeted older BTCPay Server installations and a vulnerable WordPress crypto-payment plugin, according to recent security reports.

The timing is particularly damaging. Crypto markets need fresh capital and confidence to sustain a recovery, but repeated breaches risk pushing investors toward self-custody or away from the sector altogether.

Bitcoin price now depends on whether geopolitical tensions ease and crypto-specific fears begin to fade. A diplomatic breakthrough between the US and Iran could reduce pressure on oil markets and improve appetite for risk assets. However, another escalation around the Strait of Hormuz could renew inflation concerns and trigger further selling across equities and crypto.

Bitcoin also needs to show that the recent security incidents have not triggered a deeper withdrawal of capital from the industry. Binance’s outflows and the latest exchange breaches will remain important sentiment indicators.

For now, the Iran story is unfolding alongside a wider Bitcoin and crypto confidence test. If the sell-off continues, Bitcoin could face another challenge to its recovery. If geopolitical fears cool and the hacking fallout remains contained, buyers may get an opportunity to step back in.

Can BTC stabilize despite pressure from both global markets and the industry’s own security failures?

#5432. Binance Resumes Withdrawals After Major Hack as Michael Van De Poppe Predicts Bitcoin Crash

Binance is seeing massive withdrawals after it restored its withdrawal system. Van de Poppe believes Bitcoin is set to fall to $74,000 because of market sell-offs.

Binance announced that it has restored its withdrawal system after the historic hack that compromised its hot wallet.

In its official X account, the exchange told its customers that withdrawals are now enabled for several networks, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, XRP, BSC, Dogecoin, and many others.

The world’s largest crypto exchange, Binance, suffered what appeared to be the largest crypto heist on record on Oct. 29, 2026. Hackers stole $6.3 billion, but the company managed to freeze $2.54 billion.

The exchange, co-founded by Chinese-Canadian entrepreneur Changpeng Zhao (CZ), suspended deposits and withdrawals on the day of the attack. The firm assured clients that users’ funds are safe and that it would cover all losses from the hack.

On Saturday, the FBI released an official statement revealing that North Korea was responsible for the breach that led to the theft of $6.3 billion from Binance on Thursday.

That evening, Binance announced it successfully restored 90% of the crypto assets lost in the breach. The firm said it used its own reserves, including the SAFU and internal treasury, to fully cover customer losses so clients would not lose their capital.

Today, Binance announced its withdrawal system is back to normal, and customers can withdraw any amount without delay. According to data shared this evening by CryptoQuant, over $4 billion in assets have been withdrawn from the exchange since withdrawals resumed after the $6.3 billion hack.

Meanwhile, crypto analyst Michael van de Poppe believes Bitcoin is likely to fall toward $74,000 as customer outflows and a wider market sell-off weigh on investor sentiment. Bitcoin currently trades at $77,789 following Binance’s security breach, and the analyst is watching whether support around $76,200 and $76,800 holds.

He warns of broader impacts, as persistent, massive withdrawals could trigger a plunge in BTC’s value toward $74k. The selling momentum could push BTC lower from current levels due to high-leverage BTC shorts and expectations of a relief rally.

#5431. Zest’s new AI agent finds restaurants and books reservations over text

Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.

Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE.

Zest, the restaurant discovery app that launched earlier this year, is already thinking about a future where mobile apps are no longer the primary interface. On Thursday, the startup introduced a new feature: a personal AI-powered “restaurant concierge” that lives in your text messages, similar to other popular AI agents like Instinct or Poke.

The launch reflects a broader shift in how startups are thinking about AI, as conversational AI agents take on tasks that had previously required users to launch stand-alone mobile apps. For Zest, that means bringing its restaurant recommendations into texts, then allowing users to immediately take the next step of booking a table.

“The agent is the product now,” explains Zest founder and CEO Mario Gomez-Hall. “You text it, and it answers from your own history and your friends’. It doesn’t need weeks of conversation to learn you because it starts from where you’ve actually been,” he said.

Originally founded in November 2024, with $1.8 million in pre-seed backing from Alexis Ohanian at 776 and Steve Jang at Kindred Ventures, the app’s unique feature is that it links up with users’ credit cards to track where they’re actually eating out to get a sense of their tastes and interests. With this data on hand, Zest can make tailored suggestions of what places you might like to try next, whether that’s in your own city or suggestions of places to try when you’re traveling.

The credit card data used by Zest’s app is imported via the financial services company Plaid, which is used by banks and other fintech and budgeting apps. Zest says it focuses only on those transactions in the food and drink categories when making its personalized map and lists.

The startup’s latest idea is to tackle the same problem — where should I go to eat? — from a new angle. It will now make its suggestions from inside a text message thread and can turn to AI to do things like check availability and make the reservation for you through connected services like OpenTable, Resy, and SevenRooms.

To work, users will text the Zest concierge at (212) 470-6067. What’s even better is that Zest can be dropped into a group chat, where it can blend everyone’s tastes to find places the whole group will love. Here, it can also settle indecision with an in-thread voting feature and then can book a table for the group without leaving the conversation.

Users can ask Zest for recommendations based on a number of factors, like cuisine, craving, occasion, dietary restrictions, or neighborhood, and can ask questions about the restaurants, like how busy the place may be, or whether it offers Wi-Fi, and more. Plus, you can ask Zest to send you the menu to help you make a decision.

In TechCrunch’s tests, the AI worked fairly well, offering a list of suggestions for new places matched to our tastes that also fit particular conditions, like time of day, party size, location, and other factors. While finding an open table is something other apps have offered for years, there’s a convenience factor in being able to just text back and forth about the various options and have it tell you the available booking times.

The company began testing the concierge last month, but decided to hold the launch until it could add the booking capabilities; over time, the startup is considering moving Zest beyond restaurants to offer recommendations for businesses, shopping, and more.

By shifting to texts, Zest hopes the company can scale beyond its initial thousands of users and generate revenue.

“Booking and ordering are the first revenue lines. Zest books your table through OpenTable or Resy today, with food ordering coming, and there are transactions there to participate in,” said Gomez-Hall. “The reason that gets interesting is that Zest learns your taste faster than a general assistant does, because it starts from where you’ve actually been instead of asking you questions. That’s worth something well beyond dinner,” he added.

#5430. More Money, Fewer Checks: These 3 Charts Show The Divide Behind VC’s Record Funding Year

Startup capital is both more abundant than ever this year and yet scarcer. That contradiction has become increasingly visible in 2026 when analyzing Crunchbase data, and the trend continued through Q3.

Our data shows that despite record venture capital spending in 2026 — nearly $680 billion through Q3 — investors are writing fewer checks to seed and early-stage companies, the businesses one typically thinks of when we talk about startups.

One of the best ways to visualize this dichotomy is by looking at how much of the record global venture funding this year went to funding rounds across different tiers: less than $100 million, $100 million to just under $1 billion, and $1 billion and more.

As illustrated above, the funding surge this year is concentrated in those largest rounds, while the smaller-round market has essentially flatlined since 2023.

The massive surge in billion-dollar-plus rounds in Q1 and Q2, of course, was thanks to record-setting financings for OpenAI and Anthropic. But it’s not just those two companies concentrating capital at the top. About one-third of Q3 funding went to just 27 companies raising billion-dollar-plus rounds.

In North America, the largest startup market, deal counts have trended downward over several years, even as venture investment soared.

In Q3, reported deal counts in North America fell 16% year over year and 14% quarter over quarter, reaching the lowest quarterly total since 2023, even as North American funding dollars jumped 50% year over year to $92 billion. The contraction is concentrated in seed and early-stage deals — North American late-stage counts actually increased year over year.

Series B is a particularly stark illustration of the dollars-up-but-deals-down trend. Series B marks the stage when startups are maturing: they typically show some growth and traction but still have plenty of upside potential. But while dollars invested in U.S. startups at the Series B stage hit a multiyear high so far this year, deal count is on track to hit a multiyear low.

It’s a similar story among seed and Series A startups, with money concentrating into larger rounds even as deal count dips.

Anthropic, the biggest venture-backed private company of all, is slated to go public this month in a potential $2 trillion IPO, offering a prominent test of public investors’ appetite for the companies driving this venture boom.

A strong public-market reception could reinforce venture investors’ willingness to finance enormous AI bets, while a disappointing debut could put unicorn valuations under pressure.

But neither outcome guarantees that funding will reach a wider pool of startups. The real measure of a broader startup recovery we’ll be watching: whether deal counts start to rise alongside the dollars.

#5429. Satlyt takes another step toward turning satellites into space data centers

Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.

Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE.

Naturally, Rama Afullo’s first reaction was, “Let’s GOOOO,” he said. His company, Satlyt, is building software to turn existing satellites into data processing networks, similar to the orbital data center concept. And he just took another step closer to that.

After 13 months of work, the company had a successful test earlier this month. Working with the University of Houston on a NASA-funded research project, the test showed how the startup’s software can spread out tasks among computers while in orbit based on communication and available compute.

He said the goal is to create software that connects to multiple satellites to share computing assignments. Users of the system “will only need to define permissions, priorities, and operating limits,” while the software will make decisions within those limits, Afullo told TechCrunch. Its software is already on three satellites in orbit and the first step to that vision was this test. While the test used NASA-funded research, the agency has not yet selected it for any particular mission or chosen it to deploy its technology.

Afullo said NASA missions face the same constraints that Satlyt hopes to address — “limited computing resources, intermittent communication, and the need to get useful information back to people.”

In this test, the company created a simulated network with four computers, four users, and eight services. The software then assessed how to assign and run tasks on those computers, accounting for compute and communication availability. One physical computer aboard a spacecraft ran the experiment, evaluating a simulated network of four computing hosts, then returned the results to Earth. The test proved that Satlyt’s software can generate plans on hardware in orbit, but more testing will be done to see how those computers transfer information amongst each other in practice when multiple physical computers are used.

“The finding is a trade-off,” he said. One approach worked best, though it required more computing power than the others.

Still, Satlyt which was in the top five of TechCrunch Disrupt Battlefield this year, calls this a win. “It’s a building block toward satellites sharing computing work,” he said.

NASA already has a technology network designed to move data through space even when communication links face delays. It started using this tech earlier this year and has already tested it on aircraft.

Afullo, who previously worked at Google and SpaceX, founded Satlyt in 2024 to turn spacecraft into virtual data centers. Its software helps operators run AI and other applications onboard, processing data closer to where it is collected and reducing dependence on downlinks, where satellites send data back to Earth, and ground-based analysis.

For example, if a spacecraft sees a wildfire on Earth, such software can help it transmit relevant information much faster. “The goal is to get useful answers to people sooner and make better use of limited communication windows,” he said. “This experiment tested one planning component of that broader capability.”

Satlyt said it still needs to test its own software under various workloads, hardware, and connectivity conditions. They also found an issue in how their software was time-referencing delays, Afullo said — it was stamping it as arrival time (the time it arrived) rather than elapsed delay (how long it took to arrive), which is a different metric.

It doesn’t mean the experiment failed, however. “The software development, onboard execution, and return of outputs succeeded,” he said.

But Afullo said much work remains. “We also need usable communication links, permission from participating operators, secure transfers, resource scheduling, and recovery when a connection of computers becomes unavailable.” Satlyt is also researching applications beyond low Earth orbit, including supporting 4K video streaming from the Moon through its NASA-funded work.

“Our next technical steps are broader validation and integration, followed by demonstrations of computing work shared across separate spacecraft,” he said. “Longer term, we want developers to build applications for space without having to rebuild the infrastructure for every mission. That’s what virtual AI data centers in space mean to us.”
