#5397. Polymarket Hit by Massive Hack

A massive security breach has reportedly seen nearly 1,000 accounts on the crypto-based prediction market Polymarket drained, with the attack leading to losses of more than $2.6M.

Blockchain analyst Conor Grogan revealed that a total of 995 accounts were hit by the attack, resulting in losses of roughly $2.65 million.

Polymarket has seen 995 accounts drained by a hacker, for $2,654,211.42. Largest losses were 341k and 307k Hacker has converted all funds to POL (most likely to avoid freezing) https://t.co/PjT2QhgBSa

The two biggest losses detected by Grogan were $341K and $307K.

Moreover, the analyst also revealed that the attacker has converted all stolen funds into Polygon's native token (POL). This move might have been made to avoid having the funds frozen.

"If you are a @Polymarket user lock your account. I just got drained $800,000," a trader warned via X.

The trader also claimed that a friend lost another $600K and warned users not to interact with the website.

As noted by blockchain investigator StarPlatinum, the attacker stole roughly $2.68M in just one hour.

The data shows that at about 17:05 UTC, an empty wallet began receiving funds.

At 17:25 UTC, the wallet had amassed roughly $412K.

However, the figure jumped to $2.02M at 17:50 UTC and reached roughly $2.68M at 18:05 UTC.

In total, the attacker has amassed some 28.6M POL tokens, as noted.

So far, it appears that the attack might have occurred due to a hack of a third-party JavaScript component that was embedded in the Polymarket website.

It's not the first time that the popular prediction market has faced a massive hack leading to a multimillion-dollar security breach.

We've identified & fixed an issue impacting our international platform, Polymarket⁠.com. One of our 3rd party providers was compromised, and we have referred this to relevant law enforcement. Anyone who has been impacted will be made whole. Out of an abundance of caution, we have temporarily halted trading & are working to bring the platform back online.

In June, Polymarket also faced a similar hack. The attack happened when hackers compromised a third-party vendor and injected malicious JavaScript into the frontend of Polymarket.

In total, some $2.94 million was stolen from at least 11 wallets.

Now, Polymarket has reportedly confirmed that the security breach occurred due to a hack of a third-party service provider.

The company also vowed to make every affected user whole. In other words, users who suffered losses due to the attack will be compensated.

#5396. Solana Validator Admission Ticket: Who Fell Short After Alpenglow, and How Marinade Responded

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

StakeThat +MEV went into one of Solana's first Alpenglow epochs with about 137,000 SOL staked with it and 0.8169 SOL in its vote account. The new admission ticket required 0.8198 SOL. It was 0.003 SOL short.

That's the first post-activation picture of Solana's Validator Admission Ticket. Most stake made it through without trouble, but a small group of validators keeps dropping in and out, often by amounts smaller than a typical transaction fee. At least one large stake program changed its delegation code hours before activation so its stake wouldn't stay with those validators. Marinade's published validator snapshots for epochs 1063 to 1067 show who fell short and what happened next.

According to Solana's BLS Pubkey and VAT page, Alpenglow has been active on mainnet since epoch 1064, which began around 13:36 UTC on October 21. From then on, each validator's vote account pays a 0.8 SOL Validator Admission Ticket at the start of every epoch. The fee is burned, and it pays for the following epoch. The first charge, at the start of epoch 1064, covered epoch 1065.

The rules are strict. If the fee can't be paid, Solana's page says, "your validator does not vote or produce blocks in the next epoch." Validators without a registered BLS key, or outside the top 2,000 by stake, are also excluded. Delegators to an excluded validator earn no inflation rewards for that epoch. The page also stresses that the balance "has to stay funded, not be funded once."

The vote account also has to stay above its rent-exempt minimum. In Marinade's data, the full requirement works out to 0.8197612 SOL.

Marinade publishes the inputs to its stake auction every epoch in a public pipeline repository. The input data checks whether each validator's vote account holds enough to cover the next epoch's ticket. Each snapshot covers about 670 validators and roughly 438 million SOL of stake.

Before activation, in the epoch 1063 snapshot, 33 validators holding 7.63 million SOL, or 1.74% of stake, were below the ticket balance. Once Alpenglow went live, that number fell quickly: 15 validators with 1.55 million SOL (0.35%) in epoch 1064, then 19 with 1.15 million (0.26%) in epoch 1065, the first epoch the ticket actually paid for. By epoch 1066 it was 13 validators with 790,000 SOL (0.18%), and by epoch 1067 just 8 with 710,000 SOL (0.16%).

The epoch 1063 count matches a figure in Marinade's own code history. A commit on October 21 notes that its new gate "refuses the 33 validators with vat_eligible false" in the 1063 snapshot.

The biggest pre-activation gaps were fixed in time. An unnamed validator with 2.05 million SOL of stake, Temporal Emerald with 1.23 million and Bitget Wallet with 593,000 were all below the ticket balance in epoch 1063. All three had topped up by the next snapshot. Of the 33 flagged before activation, 25 had recovered by epoch 1064.

So the fee didn't remove a large share of stake. The balance check affected less than 2% of stake at its peak, and about 0.16% by epoch 1067.

The validators that did fall short show a pattern: many of them nearly had enough.

Because the ticket is charged every epoch, a validator that tops up just enough to pass once will fail again an epoch later unless it adds more. Between epochs 1064 and 1067, between 3 and 11 validators fell below the threshold each epoch, while a similar number recovered.

The shortfalls also cut across setups. Every validator flagged in epoch 1067 runs either Agave 4.3.x, the client release the migration required, or the latest Firedancer build. Software readiness wasn't the issue. Keeping the balance funded was.

Solana offers a fix: routing block revenue to the vote account through solana vote-update-commission-collector. That keeps the account funded automatically, though the change takes two epochs to apply.

The bigger story is how stake programs reacted. Marinade, one of Solana's largest delegation programs, changed its auction code in pull request #153, merged at about 06:47 UTC on October 21, roughly seven hours before Alpenglow activated.

The change adds a new disqualifying condition, vatIneligible. A validator whose vat_eligible flag is false "gets no SAM and no backstop stake," because "Agave then pays its stakers no inflation rewards for the epoch." A null value never disqualifies a validator. The check currently tests only the SIMD-0357 balance, not BLS key registration.

The first version applied the rule only in Alpenglow epochs. Marinade's developers then caught a timing problem. Agave starts charging the ticket at the 1063-to-1064 boundary, and "a stake move made in epoch E takes effect in E+1," so the original rule "left Marinade stake on refused validators for epochs 1064 and 1065." The merged version refuses ineligible validators in every epoch.

The snapshots confirm it worked. In the epoch 1064 snapshot, 192,762 SOL of Marinade stake sat on ineligible validators, nearly all of it on one unnamed validator. By epoch 1065, that had dropped to 2,407 SOL, and by epoch 1066 to 10 SOL. A later commit gives the rule its own label and call to action in Marinade's interface, so operators can see why they've been excluded.

Marinade, in short, turned a protocol fee into a delegation rule of its own. A validator that misses one ticket loses an epoch of rewards, and it also loses Marinade stake until its balance recovers.

Before activation, Solana Compass reported that a community tracker flagged 45% of stake as not ready two days ahead of epoch 1064, mostly validators on Agave 4.3.0 and 4.3.1. The following day, that had dropped to 20.3%.

Marinade's snapshots show the software gap closing much as those warnings suggested it needed to. Stake on Agave 4.3.0 and 4.3.1 fell from 6.56% in epoch 1063 to 0.08% by epoch 1067. Firedancer operators, who had to switch to Agave for the migration, dropped from 11.0% of stake to 5.9% in epoch 1064. They then came back strongly, reaching 17.2% by epoch 1067, well above their pre-migration share.

The large readiness gap was about software and keys, and it was mostly closed by the time it mattered. The fee gap was always small.

For most delegators, nothing changed: more than 99.8% of stake sits with validators that keep their tickets paid. For those delegated to the few that don't, the cost is clear: no inflation rewards for that epoch, and in Marinade's case, stake moved elsewhere.

The protocol sets one requirement: 0.8 SOL in the vote account every epoch. Stake programs are now adding their own rules on top, starting with Marinade's. Validators that keep running near the threshold will keep losing epochs of rewards, and possibly delegations, until they keep a buffer or automate funding.

#5394. Hackers Target Crypto Users With Fake ChatGPT and Claude Apps

Cybercriminals have been using the hype surrounding artificial intelligence (AI) technologies to distribute cryptocurrency mining malware through fake desktop apps that mimic popular AI tools like ChatGPT and Claude.

In a recent report, cybersecurity vendor Check Point Research (CPR) said threat actors have been setting up fake GitHub repositories to advertise fake AI apps like GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus, among others.

The hackers have even set up dedicated GitHub.io sites that promote their fake AI apps and trick victims into downloading malicious files.

According to the CPR researchers, the attackers are using search engine optimization (SEO) manipulation to get their malicious sites to rank high on Google.

One of the most worrisome aspects of the campaign is how the attackers use legitimate software components from OpenAI and Anthropic to mask malicious activity.

The malicious ZIP archives that victims can download feature legitimate digitally signed executable files. These legitimate executables are bundled with malicious DLLs.

Once victims run the seemingly legitimate application, the malicious DLL gets loaded without their knowledge, thanks to the DLL sideloading technique.

This makes it very hard for victims to spot the attack since the malware relies on legitimate software to run its code.

At the end of the day, the attack leads to the installation of XMRig, a cryptocurrency miner that quietly uses the victims' resources to mine digital assets for the attackers.

Interestingly, the malware can also stop mining whenever it senses user activity so that it can evade detection.

In addition, CPR researchers discovered that the malware includes several techniques to make security investigations harder.

For example, it can pause execution for a very long time if it senses that it is not running under the expected executable file.

It also checks the keyboard language setting on a computer before going ahead with the infection.

The first GitHub repository for the campaign showed up in July 2026, and malicious downloads started popping up at the end of August.

At the moment, the payload is a cryptocurrency miner, but researchers have warned that YobaLoader can potentially be used to deploy other types of malware.

#5393. Massive $5.9 Billion Binance Hack Hits XRP, BTC, ETH and Other Tokens

Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, has been hit with a massive security breach. Blockchain analysts believe the hackers have stolen nearly $6 billion in crypto from wallets linked to the exchange.

According to blockchain analytics firm Glassnode, the suspected hack initially involved crypto worth $5.3 billion.

The hackers made some of the biggest transfers out of the crypto exchange, including an estimated $1.66 billion in Tether (USDT), 17,985 Bitcoin (BTC) worth about $1.45 billion, and $767 million in USD Coin (USDC).

Other crypto tokens involved in the suspected hack included Ethereum (ETH), XRP, Solana (SOL), and Tron (TRX).

According to Glassnode, the suspicious outflows occurred sequentially across various blockchains. XRP transfers came first, followed by SOL, BTC, and others.

Glassnode also noted that the exchange's BNB balance wasn't touched.

The total suspicious outflows are close to $5.9 billion.

The total losses aren't known yet. Analysts are sharing different estimates as they watch funds jump from one blockchain address to another.

Changpeng Zhao (CZ), Binance's co-founder and former CEO, acknowledged the apparent security breach. At the same time, he assured Binance's customers that they are safe.

"It does look like a hack on Binance," Zhao wrote on X.

User funds are safe! It does look like a hack on Binance. Appreciate the quick freeze from Tether (~$971m) and Circle (~$823m). I don't manage Binance (.com) anymore, but as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered.

The billionaire commended the quick response of stablecoin issuers Tether and Circle, which froze about $971 million and $823 million, respectively.

"I'm not running Binance (.com) anymore, but as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered," Zhao emphasized.

In his next post, Zhao admitted that the actual losses could be higher, even though an analyst estimated that about $1B in exposure remained after the assets were frozen. But he again reaffirmed that the losses would be covered.

The quick response from major stablecoin issuers was crucial.

Tether's CEO Paolo Ardoino revealed that the company had frozen over 1.567 billion USDT linked to the potential hack at Binance.

"Protecting the industry and our partners is our main priority," Ardoino stated.

Meanwhile, Circle's CEO Jeremy Allaire confirmed that the company had frozen over $800M in USDC in coordination with law enforcement.

Later on, Binance provided an update. The exchange confirmed that the total amount of frozen assets came to $2.54B. Binance also warned that this number could increase as the investigation is ongoing.

If the highest estimates of stolen funds are accurate, the Binance incident could be the biggest crypto hack ever.

In February 2025, the record was set when crypto exchange Bybit lost about $1.5 billion worth of Ethereum in an attack that was linked to North Korean hackers.

Following the suspected breach at Binance, the broader crypto market fell.

Bitcoin briefly dipped below $79,000. Ethereum fell below $2,300. XRP is down by almost 7%. Binance's native crypto token BNB dropped even harder. It dipped about 7% during the initial response.

#5391. Binance Reveals When It Will Resume Withdrawals After Historic Hack

Binance co-CEO Yi He has said the crypto exchange expects to restore withdrawal services within the next 48 hours.

"We're working on improving the withdrawal service and related address controls," she said.

According to Yi He, deposits are unaffected and are operating as usual.

However, Yi He didn't specify when withdrawal services would be fully restored.

This announcement was made after Binance temporarily paused deposits and withdrawals as it was looking into what appears to be the biggest crypto hack in history.

According to the crypto exchange, the estimated impact of the incident is around $6.3 billion. Crypto analytics firm Chainalysis has stated that the impact is around $6.4 billion.

Binance has already collaborated with blockchain partners to freeze about $3 billion of the affected funds.

Also, the crypto exchange has assured its customers that all losses will be covered by its Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) and company funds.

Binance has also released preliminary findings on what could have led to the security breach.

The crypto exchange claims that it could be the compromise of one of its DevOps engineers' laptops.

According to the exchange, the compromised laptop enabled the hacker to access a service container from which unauthorized withdrawal transactions were initiated.

However, the crypto exchange has also mentioned that no leaked wallet private keys have been found so far during the investigation.

Binance has already revoked authorization for the compromised address. The exchange is also collaborating with law enforcement agencies and blockchain intelligence firms to trace the stolen funds.

Binance has also promised to share a detailed technical report once the investigation is over. Also, it will release an updated Proof of Reserves after the security enhancements are completed.

However, crypto analytics firm Chainalysis claims that the record-breaking attack could have been carried out by North Korean hackers.

According to Chainalysis, investigators found that crypto funds stolen in the Binance hack have been mixed with crypto associated with last month's Bitget exploit.

According to Chainalysis co-founder Jonathan Levin, TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking group, could be the attacker.

Blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs also has high confidence that TraderTraitor is behind the attack.

The North Korean hacking group has been associated with a number of big crypto thefts, such as the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in February 2025.

But Binance hasn't made any official statement yet about the attacker. Binance's investigation is still in progress.

The plan, disclosed with Coinbase’s third-quarter results on Thursday, is worth about $1.31 billion at Thursday’s $160.59 close. Co-founder Fred Ehrsam and President Emilie Choi filed plans of their own, bringing the total to about 13.6 million shares, roughly $2.2 billion.

Armstrong replied on X that the plans only sell above price targets, “most of these are set for very high prices, a signal of how bullish I am.” The market didn’t take much comfort: every major crypto stock was down at least 6.8% in early trading.

Discover: Bitcoin Swings Less Than Coinbase and Oracle, Yet Crypto Stocks Move Up to 2.4 Times as Hard: Why?

A Rule 10b5-1 plan lets executives set up share sales in advance, with fixed rules on price and timing, so they can’t be accused of trading on inside information later. Coinbase’s quarterly filing and TipRanks’ breakdown show three new plans:

Armstrong’s plan can sell from November 16, 2026 through October 2027. It’s more than double his previous plan from the third quarter of 2025, which covered 3.75 million shares. Together, the three plans cover about 6% of Coinbase’s 223.7 million Class A shares.

Armstrong’s defense rests on the price targets, which Coinbase hasn’t disclosed. In the same thread, he wrote:

“Very few of the sales in my 2025 plan ever sold. I have the vast majority of my net worth in one stock: COIN. Even if this entire plan executed that would still be true.”

If the targets really sit far above today’s price, the plans won’t sell anything at $142. Traders will only know for sure from Form 4 filings, which start showing any sales after November 16.

The plans landed on a weak quarter. Total revenue fell 35% from a year earlier to $1.22 billion, transaction revenue dropped 44% to $590 million, and consumer spot trading volume fell 59%. Net income of $718.7 million came almost entirely from a $715 million paper gain on the crypto Coinbase holds. October looks no better: CNBC put fourth-quarter transaction revenue at just $165 million through October 25.

There was a bright spot: prediction markets passed $200 million in annualized revenue, and Armstrong said he’s “seeing signs that the market is turning.”

Coinbase led a broad selloff in crypto stocks on Friday morning. The rest of the group fell between 6.8% and 9.1%, more than twice as hard as Bitcoin, which was down 3.5% over 24 hours after Thursday’s $6.36 billion Binance hack.

Crypto stocks on October 30, 2026, about 10:05 a.m. ET, versus Thursday’s close. Sources: Yahoo Finance, Binance.

Two things stand out. Coinbase fell 3.2 times as hard as Bitcoin, well above the up-to-2.4-times range crypto stocks have shown against BTC this year. And the Nasdaq 100 fell only 2.5%, so the drop is specific to crypto rather than a broad tech selloff.

The Binance hack cuts both ways for Coinbase. Binance has paused withdrawals and is repaying users from its own reserves, which could push some traders toward a US-listed, regulated exchange. But a $6 billion theft also hits confidence in crypto trading generally, and Friday’s selling suggests investors are weighing that more heavily.

Wall Street hasn’t given up on the stock. TipRanks counts 19 Buy ratings, nine Holds and two Sells, with an average price target of $206.61, about 45% above Friday’s price. COIN is now 60.5% below its 52-week high of $361.40.

The daily chart since mid-May shows why $139 matters. Coinbase bottomed at $139.18 on June 26 and $139.11 on July 31, and both times it rallied. Friday’s low of $138.71 is the third test of the same floor, and the first to break it, even if only by 40 cents so far.

May 12 to October 30, 2026: COIN 1D chart. Source: Yahoo Finance (Nasdaq).

The stock is below both its 50-day EMA ($173.51) and its 200-day EMA ($189.59), and the 50-day has stayed under the 200-day throughout the five months on the chart. Friday’s drop also left a gap between Thursday’s $157.61 low and Friday’s $148.50 high.

For crypto stocks, Coinbase’s $139 floor is the line to watch next week. Armstrong says his plan only sells far above it, and the Form 4 filings from November 16 will show whether he’s right.

#5388. Cosmos Hub Approves Gaia v29 With 99.41% Support Ahead of October 28th Upgrade

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Proposal #1059 passed with 49.59% turnout as the chain counts down now to block 33,618,500 on October 28th, where validators are told to run the security-patched v29.0.1 binary, not the version named in the proposal.

The Cosmos Hub's latest upgrade drew almost no opposition. About 168.5 million ATOM voted on Proposal #1059, and only 2,335 ATOM voted No. Under that one-sided result is an unusual change: the Hub's stakers voted to remove the governance route that earlier generations of Cosmos proposals used to change the chain's own settings.

Proposal #1059 schedules the upgrade of the Cosmos Hub to Gaia v29.0.0. It finished voting on October 27 at 12:00 UTC with a PASSED result. The vote approves the upgrade, but the software has not run yet. The chain still has to reach the upgrade height, halt, and restart on the new binary. Until that happens, Gaia v29 is approved but not yet live.

On-chain records show 49.59% of staked ATOM voted, against a 40% quorum requirement. Yes took 99.41% of the vote, or 167,514,965 ATOM. No With Veto took 0.58% (982,855 ATOM), Abstain took 0.01% (14,360 ATOM), and No rounds to 0.00% (2,335 ATOM).

The veto share is the main number to watch in a Cosmos governance vote, because a large enough veto rejects a proposal even if Yes wins. At 0.58%, the veto bloc was far too small to matter. That fits the proposal's nature. It is a maintenance release that removes deprecated code and updates dependencies, and it has no economic or political stakes.

The forum discussion covered one governance point: a delegator's own vote overrides their validator's vote. A few large validators did not decide the result on their own. Delegators could have overridden them, and very few chose to vote differently.

The proposal names v29.0.0, but operators are not supposed to run that build at the upgrade height. On October 23, three days into voting, the Gaia team tagged v29.0.1 and updated the official forum post to recommend it.

The patch changes only one thing: it rebuilds Gaia with Go 1.26.10 instead of Go 1.26.7. That picks up the Go security fix tracked as CVE-2026-111943 (GO-2026-6809). The project's upgrade notes call v29.0.1 a non-state-breaking patch release, so it computes the same chain state as v29.0.0. Nodes that already installed v29.0.0 can switch at any time by replacing the binary and restarting.

Operators using Cosmovisor need to know one detail. The on-chain upgrade name stays v29.0.0, so the v29.0.1 binary still goes into the upgrades/v29.0.0/bin/ directory. If a validator names the folder after the patch version, Cosmovisor will not find the binary when the chain halts. The project's sample service configuration has automatic binary download turned off, which means each operator has to put the correct binary in place before the halt.

Gaia v29 removes the x/params module from the Cosmos Hub. That module is the original, centralized store for parameters, and it backed the legacy ParameterChangeProposal governance route. The release changelog lists the change under API-breaking changes: "The legacy ParameterChangeProposal governance route and cosmos.params.v1beta1.Query service are no longer available."

In practice, governance has already moved on. Each module now owns its parameters, and changes go through that module's own governance message. The legacy route remained as a fallback, and v29 removes it. The rate-limiting module was the last part of the Hub still wired to the old params subspace. In v29 it no longer depends on it.

The forum Q&A states who is affected. RPC providers, wallets, explorers, and governance dashboards should check whether they still call the params v1beta1 query service or create legacy parameter-change proposals. After the upgrade, those calls will fail on the Hub. For most users nothing changes. The proposal requires no token migration, and balances, delegations, and IBC assets are unaffected.

The second API-breaking item affects multisig accounts specifically. Gaia v29 moves the Hub from Cosmos SDK v0.53.4 to v0.53.8, and the changelog warns: "As of cosmos-sdk v0.53.8, --gas auto gas simulation is broken for multisig senders. Multisig transactions must specify a fixed --gas value until this is fixed upstream."

This matters in practice. The Hub's weekly update of October 22 said the problem applies to the Community Pool migration multisig. That multisig is handling a USDC.n migration spend that was moving toward an on-chain proposal during the same week. Treasury signers, custody desks, and DAO operators who build transactions with --gas auto will need to set gas by hand until the upstream SDK is fixed.

The same release also brings CometBFT from 0.38.23 to 0.38.25, the IBC rate-limiting middleware from 10.1.0 to 10.7.0, and runc from 1.2.8 to 1.3.6. It also moves the build toolchain from Go 1.25 to Go 1.26.

The upgrade handler, the code that runs once at the upgrade height, does more cleanup than the proposal summary describes. It first deletes everything in the deprecated provider store, the state left over from the Hub's time as an Interchain Security provider. Next it wipes the legacy x/params store. Last, it removes a receipt left behind by the earlier v28.3.1 balance migration.

The code also shows how cautious the Gaia team is about the upgrade. The stores stay mounted, and their contents are cleared as ordinary state changes. Unmounting them entirely could cause version-mismatch errors when nodes load the chain from disk. Gaia v29 has also run on the Hub's provider testnet since October 13, about two weeks before mainnet.

At 15:32 UTC on October 27, Mintscan showed block 33,618,500 as "not yet created". The chain was at block 33,604,199, with 14,301 blocks to go. At the recent average block time of 5.722 seconds, the Mintscan countdown for block 33,618,500 estimated the height for about 14:16 UTC on October 28. The forum's original estimate was 13:50 UTC. The real time depends on how fast blocks are produced over the next day.

When the chain reaches that height, block production stops. It restarts only after validators holding more than two-thirds of voting power are back online on the new binary. That makes the vote result only half the story. The other half is whether validators show up on v29.0.1 promptly, so that the halt lasts minutes rather than hours.

#5387. Crypto Developers Using Claude Via VS Code May Have Been Compromised: This Version Has a Backdoor

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

Developers using Claude AI through Visual Studio Code (VS Code) may have been exposed to a serious security threat after researchers discovered a malicious version of the popular coding assistant's extension.

According to an October 30 report from cybersecurity researchers at OpenSourceMalware, version 2.1.313 of the Claude Code extension contained a hidden backdoor that could enable attackers to remotely access infected computers.

The malicious version was identified in the Open VSX extension registry, where developers download tools for their coding environments.

The compromised extension reportedly looked and functioned like the legitimate Claude Code tool, making the threat particularly difficult to notice. However, researchers discovered additional malicious code designed to run automatically when the extension loaded.

Once activated, the backdoor attempted to establish a remote connection to an attacker-controlled server, potentially giving hackers access to the victim's computer.

More concerningly, the malware was designed to remain active even after the computer restarted.

This means simply closing VS Code or stopping work with Claude might not eliminate the threat.

Although the attack was not specifically designed to target cryptocurrency users, developers working on blockchain projects could face significant risks.

Their computers may contain sensitive information, including private keys, wallet credentials, exchange API keys, and access to cryptocurrency infrastructure.

If attackers successfully gained remote access, they could potentially obtain this information and use it to compromise wallets or projects.

However, researchers did not report confirmed cryptocurrency theft or identify any specific blockchain-related functionality in the malicious code.

The researchers confirmed malicious code in the analyzed Open VSX version but could not establish how it was introduced.

Importantly, the findings do not prove that Anthropic's official VS Code Marketplace release or its broader distribution systems were compromised.

Developers who installed version 2.1.313 through Open VSX should treat their systems as potentially compromised and investigate immediately.

Removing the extension alone may not be sufficient, as the backdoor was designed to persist independently.

The cryptocurrency market is going through the largest robbery in its history, but industry veterans manage to find a reason for harsh dark humor in it.

Former Ripple CTO and creator of the XRP Ledger network David Schwartz reacted to the Binance exchange hack with a caustic joke aimed at his main historical competitor, the Stellar (XLM) blockchain.

Schwartz commented on a post by EasyA co-founder Dom Kwok, who complained that hackers had wiped out his balances, leaving only Litecoin untouched. The former Ripple CTO, in turn, quipped: “These sick b*stards dropped an extra 517 XLM into my Binance account!”

The sarcasm is tied to a long-running corporate conflict: Stellar was created by former Ripple co-founder Jed McCaleb, and the idea that hackers forcibly “credit” victims with competitors’ tokens instantly went viral.

Despite Schwartz’s ironic tone, the blow landed directly on Ripple’s own ecosystem. The attackers instantly withdrew 233.46 million XRP tokens (about $296 million) from Binance’s hot wallets. It is impossible to return them: the XRP Ledger architecture excludes forced freezing of the native token at the protocol level.

However, with the company’s second asset, the situation turned out differently. Ripple Senior Vice President Jack McDonald announced that the company had detected the movement of stolen Ripple USD (RLUSD) stablecoin and urgently blocked the attackers’ addresses.

Binance co-founder Yi He has already publicly thanked the Ripple team for promptly freezing about $200 million in RLUSD funds, emphasizing that user funds are now protected (SAFU). While XRP showed the hackers absolute decentralization, the controlled RLUSD stablecoin became the main protection tool.

The incident itself became part of the historic Binance hack totaling $6.3–6.36 billion across 10 blockchain networks.

At the moment, the exchange, together with partners, has managed to freeze a total of about $3 billion across various ecosystems, and according to blockchain sleuths, the North Korean cyber group TraderTraitor (Lazarus) is behind the attack itself.

MetaMask is facing fresh questions about its future after Consensys launched a new institutional settlement network targeting banks, asset managers and financial market infrastructure providers.

The announcement puts Consensys’ institutional ambitions in the spotlight just weeks before its planned separation from MetaMask. The move could also leave the popular wallet competing independently while its former parent pursues Wall Street.

Introducing Sovereign Network Interoperability by Consensys.State-of-the-art interoperability that enables institutions to do business freely, settling securities, exchanging currencies and posting collateral across ledgers, without bridges or moving assets onto a shared…

Consensys unveiled Sovereign Network Interoperability at Devcon, introducing infrastructure designed to coordinate transactions across independently operated financial networks. Can MetaMask maintain its position as institutional blockchain adoption accelerates?

The new Sovereign Network Interoperability platform aims to help institutions settle securities, exchange currencies, and move collateral across separate blockchain networks.

Its bridgeless design keeps assets on their original ledgers while coordinating transactions between approved counterparties. Consensys says the system uses cryptographic verification to reduce reliance on additional trusted intermediaries.

The platform targets four major financial workflows, including securities settlement, wholesale payments, collateral mobility, and tokenized fund transactions.

Consensys plans to support Ethereum-compatible networks and protocols such as the Ethereum Economic Zone and Inter-Blockchain Communication. Canton connectivity is also planned.

The launch builds on Consensys’ existing institutional infrastructure, including Linea, Hyperledger Besu and Teku. The company is positioning itself as a technology provider for financial institutions seeking private, always-on blockchain settlement.

The institutional launch arrives as Consensys prepares to separate its consumer and enterprise operations into two companies.

Under the September restructuring plan, Consensys Software Inc. will rebrand as MetaMask, with Joe Lubin serving as chairman and CEO. The protocols and institutional infrastructure business will move into a newly formed company retaining the Consensys name. The separation is expected to be completed by the end of 2026.

Today, MetaMask begins its next chapter as an independent company.Consensys Software Inc., the company behind MetaMask, is rebranding as MetaMask, fully focused on the consumer platform. The protocols and institutional infrastructure businesses, including Linea, are becoming a…

MetaMask will focus on consumer finance, expanding beyond its traditional wallet functions into payments, savings, trading and access to financial instruments.

The company has reported more than 100 million downloads across approximately 190 countries. Its Money Account product also signals an ambition to become a self-custodial financial platform.

Still, the split creates uncertainty around how resources, intellectual property and shared development capabilities will be allocated.

Consensys has not disclosed separate revenue figures, financing arrangements or detailed asset allocations for the two businesses. This leaves MetaMask facing a strategic challenge. It must continue developing its consumer platform while Consensys builds infrastructure aimed at some of crypto’s largest potential customers.

The institutional settlement push also highlights a potential opportunity for Bitcoin Layer 2 projects seeking to expand beyond payments and decentralized finance.

Bitcoin Hyper is one project positioning itself around this idea, combining a Bitcoin Layer 2 design with a wallet and an execution environment intended to support faster transactions and applications.

Different route. Stronger vision. That's the Hyper way. ⚡️https://t.co/VNG0P4GuDo pic.twitter.com/jyimj70P5J

Its longer-term opportunity could extend into settlement infrastructure if the network develops the security, interoperability, and compliance features institutions require.

The project has raised more than $33.2 million in its presale, with HYPER priced at just $0.0136. It also offers 35% staking rewards, while the planned network uses a canonical BTC bridge, transaction batching, and zero-knowledge proofs to settle Layer 2 activity back to Bitcoin.

Bitcoin Hyper is also developing a wallet and broader application ecosystem. Its testnet explorer is live, with additional wallet, bridge, and staking features listed among upcoming milestones. The token launch has been announced for November 26, and exchange listings and full network rollout are planned.

If Bitcoin Hyper can deliver reliable BTC transfers, secure settlement, and applications suited to financial institutions, its infrastructure could eventually compete for use cases now being developed on Ethereum-compatible networks.

That would put Bitcoin Layer 2 projects in a different conversation, not simply as faster payment rails for retail users, but as potential infrastructure for tokenized assets and cross-network settlement.

In the technology sector, ongoing strong demand for generative AI, increasing adoption of enterprise and cloud AI, accelerating capital expenditure cycles among major cloud providers, and sustained investor interest in AI leaders would create a highly favorable environment for companies central to AI infrastructure development, such as NVIDIA.

Under this highly speculative scenario, and assuming supportive market conditions return, Nvidia (NVDA) could reach $550 to $850, with a stretch target of $1,200+ by January 1, 2027.

This remains pure speculation and entertainment, not a realistic base-case outlook. The catalyst would require extraordinary coordination among multiple governments and national AI programs that is currently highly unlikely.

#5379. Nearly Half of the Stolen Binance Basket Had a Freeze Button

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Tether, Circle and Ripple could freeze their tokens within hours of the Binance theft, and they did.

There is no one to call for the stolen bitcoin, ether and TRX, which makes up most of the money Binance is unlikely to get back.

In most hacks, the stolen total is the headline. In the Binance breach, the more useful number is how much of the stolen money could be stopped.

On-chain trackers estimate the stolen basket at more than $5.6 billion. Binance itself has put the estimated impact at $6.3 billion and says nearly $3 billion is frozen. That freeze was possible only because of how the stolen money was made up.

Almost half of it was in tokens whose issuers can freeze them. The rest was in assets that no company, foundation or council can stop on their main blockchains.

That second half explains why recovery stalled at about $3 billion despite a fast industry response. It is also the part Binance will most likely have to pay for itself.

The per-asset breakdown from on-chain trackers is:

Sorting by whether the issuer can freeze the token gives a near-even split:

That one division shaped everything that happened after the theft.

The response on the freezable side was unusually fast:

The pattern is the same in every case. A company that issues a token on a public blockchain usually keeps a way to block specific addresses from moving it. Critics see that power as a central point of control, but in this theft it worked. Within hours, the largest dollar-value block of the stolen money could not be moved.

There was one notable intervention outside the token issuers. On Arbitrum, the Arbitrum Security Council took emergency action and moved 74,559,805 ARB and 8,425 ETH, about $30.5 million, out of an address connected to the exploit.

It shows that some layer-2 networks keep emergency powers their base layers lack. The amount was small next to the size of the theft.

The other half is a different story. Bitcoin has no issuer. Ether on Ethereum's main network has no admin key. TRX is Tron's native coin, and no token issuer sits between the holder and the blockchain. Once these assets reached the attacker's wallets, stopping them depended on exchanges refusing deposits and investigators tracking the funds, not on any freeze function.

Together, the $1.45 billion in BTC, $875 million in ETH and $234 million in TRX make about $2.56 billion. That is close to Binance's own numbers: about $3 billion frozen out of a $6.3 billion estimated impact leaves roughly $3.3 billion still in play, and most of it is in assets nobody can freeze.

The bitcoin figure is the most contested part of the basket. Some BTC moving out of Binance-linked wallets during the incident may have been Binance moving its own reserves to safety rather than attacker withdrawals. So the true unfreezable total could be lower than $2.56 billion, but the split between the two groups is unlikely to change much.

The attacker appeared to understand this difference and acted on it right away.

On-chain records show the main sweep on Ethereum used an EIP-7702 delegation. This feature lets a regular wallet hand control to a smart contract. Within minutes, the drained hot wallet's contents, including more than 1.6 billion USDT, had moved to attacker-controlled addresses.

The clearest example of the next step is on Aave. According to Aave's governance forum update from risk manager LlamaRisk, one wallet in the exploiter's cluster acted between 20:58 and 21:01 UTC:

That trade left freezable USDT locked inside Aave as collateral and gave the attacker wrapped ether, which no issuer can freeze. The position stays over-collateralized, and LlamaRisk said it "does not put Aave suppliers at risk." The ETH, however, was already gone.

Aave responded on a large scale. Between 21:42 and 23:04 UTC, its guardian multisigs froze:

The freezes blocked new deposits and borrowing. Reports also describe stablecoins being swapped for ETH on Uniswap.

The race was easy to see in the timeline. Each hour before an issuer froze its token was another hour to swap that token for ether. Tether and Circle reacted within the first hour, so most of the stablecoin stash was frozen before it could be converted.

A freeze stops the attacker, but it does not put money back in Binance's accounts. Frozen tokens stay locked at the attacker's addresses until the issuer decides what to do with them. In past cases, issuers have destroyed frozen tokens and reissued the same amount to the rightful owner, usually after legal or law-enforcement checks. That process takes time, and each issuer has its own procedure.

Binance has said that its initial investigation points to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop. According to the company, that laptop let the attacker reach a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. Binance said it found no evidence that wallet private keys were leaked, and that it has revoked the affected address authorization and is working with law enforcement and blockchain intelligence firms.

Deposits and withdrawals were suspended while security checks continue. Binance has not yet given a date for reopening them.

Binance has said it will cover all losses using its SAFU fund and its own money. Grouping the stolen basket by freezability gives a rough picture of what that bill could be.

The roughly $3 billion that is frozen should eventually be recovered, depending on how and when each issuer releases or reissues the tokens. The bitcoin, ether and TRX are another matter. Unless exchanges block deposits and investigators recover funds as they are laundered, that part is effectively gone. It accounts for most of the money Binance will have to cover from its own reserves.

The theft also raises a question for the whole industry. The assets that limited the damage were the issuer-controlled tokens that crypto purists often criticize. The assets that caused the real loss were the ones built so that no one can stop them. Exchanges have long decided hot-wallet sizes by liquidity needs. After this theft, they may also consider which assets in those wallets can still be stopped once they leave.

While the FBI and the U.S. Secret Service investigate the theft of $6.3 billion from Binance wallets, a public discussion between Elon Musk and the exchange’s founder Changpeng Zhao (CZ) unfolded on the X platform. The spat highlighted an unexpected irony: Musk decided to troll the crypto exchange in the midst of the crisis, but in response received a harsh reminder that his own assets had become Binance’s main argument in the dispute over solvency.

The reason for the dispute was a meme by one of the users, which ironically compared CZ’s public promises to cover the losses with Sam Bankman-Fried’s famous tweet on the eve of the FTX collapse: “FTX has enough to cover all client holdings.” Elon Musk reacted to this comparison with an awkward emoji (😬), launching a wave of trolling directed at the exchange.

@elonmusk @HuaweiMate6 Elon, have a lot of respect for you, but bad time to troll. Please stop. Our SPCX shares (from our $500m investment in your Twitter takeover) are worth more than a billion. Would appreciate if you show a little support. Thanks!

The reaction of the Binance founder followed immediately: “Elon, have a lot of respect for you, but bad time to troll. Please stop.” As a counterstrike, Zhao, right in the discussion thread, reminded Musk whose money exactly he had used to buy Twitter in 2022. At that time, Binance provided the billionaire with $500 million. By October 2026, these investments had transformed into a stake in the aerospace giant SpaceX (SPCX) with a market value of more than $1 billion.

Trying to shame Musk and at the same time prove the stability of the exchange to the audience, Zhao disclosed internal calculations right there in the dispute thread. According to him, of the $6.3 billion in stolen funds, about $3 billion was promptly frozen by stablecoin issuers, and another part is covered by the SAFU reserve fund. The actual balance gap is about $2 billion, exactly half of which is potentially covered by this stake.

“Gap is about $2b, we have $1.x billion in SPCX alone. The remaining gap is (still painful, but) manageable,” Zhao replied to Musk, adding at the end: “Would appreciate it if you show a little support. Thanks!”

To finally shift the focus away from security problems and put Musk in his place, Binance co-CEO Yi He harshly intervened in the discussion. She published an ironic open address to Zhao, taking a veiled jab at the head of SpaceX: “Reporting to the major shareholder: Our company’s revenue for the year is sufficient to cover the losses, so we do not yet need to sell the SpaceX shares you are bullish on.”

Zhao himself later explained that he pulled out the data on the SPCX stake in the dispute with Musk exclusively to demonstrate the platform’s safety margin, so that he “can be less worried.” The owner of X himself has so far left the attacks of Binance’s leadership unanswered.

The exchange plans to resume withdrawals within 45–48 hours after the completion of internal checks, and the four-year-old investment has de facto turned into the main stash with which Binance is now protecting itself from market panic.

#5377. Crypto Stocks Lost Up to 54% in October as Hedge Funds Erased Every AI Stock Purchase Since 2025: Why Did Bitcoin Miners Fall Hardest?

All reviews, research, news and assessments of any kind on The Tokenist are compiled using a strict editorial review process by our editorial team. Neither our writers nor our editors receive direct compensation of any kind to publish information on tokenist.com. Our company, Tokenist Media LLC, is community supported and may receive a small commission when you purchase products or services through links on our website. Click here for a full list of our partners and an in-depth explanation on how we get paid.

Crypto stocks start November after an October that cost them up to 54%, more than six times Bitcoin’s drop, as Goldman Sachs data showed hedge funds sold enough AI stocks in five sessions to wipe out all their net AI buying since early 2025.

That matters for crypto because the biggest losers weren’t the exchanges. They were Bitcoin miners, which have spent two years renting their power and data centres to AI companies and now trade like AI infrastructure.

Cipher Digital (CIFR) fell 53.9% between the September 30 and October 30 closes, and IREN lost 41.4%. MARA and Riot dropped 40.2% and 36.4%. Bitcoin, tracked by BlackRock’s IBIT, fell 8.4% over the same days, and the S&P 500 barely moved.

The exchanges caught up later. Coinbase and Robinhood held up through the hedge fund selling streak, then lost 17% and 16% in the second half of the month, much of it on Friday after the Binance hack and Coinbase’s results.

So were crypto stocks sold as crypto, or as AI?

JUST IN: Hedge funds are pulling money out of US stocks at fastest pace ever

Hedge funds sold AI stocks for five straight sessions, from October 8 to 14, on Goldman Sachs’ prime brokerage data. Most of it was funds dumping shares they already owned, about 3.5 times the pace of new short bets, and roughly $20 billion of tech stock went out over two weeks.

Goldman Delta-One head Rich Privorotsky put the problem in one line: computing demand “can grow exponentially, but the capital available to finance it cannot.”

That line describes the miners. Cipher, IREN, Hut 8, TeraWulf and Core Scientific have all signed deals to host AI computing, and IREN’s AI cloud revenue of $70.5 million overtook its Bitcoin mining revenue of $66.7 million for the first time last quarter.

The selling streak shows who traded as what. From the October 7 close to October 14:

Every miner fell harder than chip stocks in the week hedge funds dumped AI, Cipher more than three times as hard, while Bitcoin hardly moved.

The miners, then the trading venues, then the Bitcoin holders. Over the full month, the order lines up with how much of each business looks like AI or trading volume, and how little looks like Bitcoin itself.

Strategy is the tell. A company that is mostly a pile of Bitcoin fell in line with chip stocks (-14.2%), not with miners, and Circle, which earns interest on stablecoin reserves, fell least of all.

The trading venues had their own problem. Most of Coinbase’s and Robinhood’s losses came after October 14, once the hedge fund streak was over, and Friday alone took 10.6% off Coinbase and 7.2% off Robinhood.

The timing points to AI money for the miners, though it is no proof: Bitcoin’s own 8% slide and a weaker hashprice cut into their mining revenue too.

Discover: Oil Prices Climb Back Above $110 While Crypto Stocks Lose Up to 48% in a Month: Miners Are Falling Even Faster

IREN is the clearest test of the AI trade among crypto stocks, and it reports fiscal first-quarter results on Thursday, November 5. The stock closed Friday at $23.95, down 8.8% on the day, after touching $23.06, its lowest in a year.

The daily chart shows a stock that lost its floor. The July 29 low at $28.93 held through the summer, gave way on October 15, and turned into the ceiling: IREN’s bounce stalled at $28.88 on October 28 and fell the next two days.

May 12 to October 30, 2026: IREN 1D chart. Source: Yahoo Finance (Nasdaq).

Both averages are far above. The 50-day EMA (exponential moving average) sits at $35.64 and the 200-day at $40.82, and the 50-day crossed below the 200-day on September 30, just before the selling began.

For crypto stocks, Thursday is the first chance to see whether AI customers are still paying the miners, or whether October’s selling was right about the capital running out.

#5374. Reconciling the OCC’s Final Stablecoin Reserve Floors Against the Fed’s Proposal

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The OCC's final GENIUS Act rule sets a 5% cash floor and a 40% cap on any one counterparty. The Fed's open proposal uses neither figure, and its comment window runs until November 30.

Issuers now face two sets of reserve rules that share a redemption deadline and differ on almost everything else.

Ask a stablecoin issuer what its reserves must look like in 2027, and the honest answer is now: it depends which regulator you ask.

The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) gave its answer on October 21, the final rule implementing the GENIUS Act. Our October 19 piece on staggered agency filings expected that rule "before the end of October," and it came two days later. The rule sets specific numbers: at least 5% of reserves in demand deposits or similar instant-access funds, and no more than 40% of reserves with a single counterparty.

The Federal Reserve's answer is still a proposal. Its GENIUS Act rulemaking remains open for comment until November 30, and it contains neither of those numbers. Until the Fed finalizes its rule, any company planning to issue under both agencies' rules, or deciding which one to apply to, is working with one fixed set of numbers and one open-ended set of principles.

The OCC's final rule was published in the Federal Register on October 23 and takes effect on January 18, 2027, the same day as the GENIUS Act itself. Comptroller Jonathan V. Gould called it "a clear, practical framework for payment stablecoin innovation, with strong standards for reserve backing, redemption, and risk management."

The reserve rules are looser than the March proposal in several places:

The OCC also removed the rebuttable presumption that some affiliate yield arrangements break the GENIUS Act's ban on paying interest, though it kept its broader anti-evasion powers. The agency received about 328 comments.

For existing issuers, the timeline is short. Under OCC Bulletin 2026-51, firms already operating in the United States that file a "substantially complete" application by January 18 can generally expect a waiver of the prior-approval requirement.

The Fed released its two proposals on September 24. They were published in the Federal Register on September 29 under Docket No. R-1899, and comments are due November 30.

The main requirements proposal would require Board-supervised issuers to "fully back their stablecoins with certain permissible reserve assets". The reserves' fair value would have to equal or exceed the stablecoins' outstanding value at all times. Permissible assets include:

On diversification, however, the Fed sets no numbers. Reserves must be "sufficiently diverse" to keep one-to-one backing at all times, and issuers must manage concentration in uninsured deposits and repo counterparties. The Board says it generally expects reserves to be mostly Treasuries, but it sets no cash floor and no counterparty percentage.

Redemption is where the two agencies agree most closely. Both define timely redemption as no later than two business days after a request. The difference lies in what happens under stress.

The FDIC, in its own proposal, uses a third approach: issuers would report on their own when redemption requests exceed 10% of issuance within 24 hours.

The clearest conflict is not about how much cash an issuer must hold, but how each agency treats bank deposits.

Under the OCC rule, at least 5% of reserves must be held in demand deposits or similar balances. That is a direct requirement to hold bank money.

The Fed proposal has no deposit floor. Instead, it would charge 2% capital against reserves held as uninsured deposits at an insured bank, and the same charge applies to undercollateralized reverse repo. One agency requires a minimum amount in deposits, and the other makes issuers hold extra capital against the deposits they choose to keep.

Concentration works the same way. An issuer with 60% of its deposit reserves at one bank would breach the OCC's 40% cap, unless one of the custodian or government exemptions applies. Under the Fed's current text, that issuer would face only a judgment by its supervisor about whether it has managed concentration risk properly.

The rules for a reserve shortfall also differ:

The difference is largest on capital. The OCC sets an individualized capital requirement measured in GAAP tangible equity. It has a $5 million floor that now lasts for the issuer's whole life, plus an operational backstop equal to 12 months of total expenses, up to half of which can be funded with qualifying subordinated debt.

The Fed proposes a fixed formula. On top of the 2% charges on deposits and repo, it adds an operational-risk charge on outstanding issuance:

It also adds 25% of three-year average revenue from sources other than reserves, adjusted by a loss scalar.

For an issuer with $50 billion in circulation, the issuance charge alone works out to $850 million under the Fed's proposal, before the revenue add-on. The OCC rule has no comparable fixed figure. Its capital depends on the issuer's own risk profile, with the $5 million floor as the only set minimum.

For now, the OCC's figures are final and the Fed's are not. Issuers and banks that hold reserves can still argue for changes until the Fed's comment period closes on November 30, and the Fed has asked 277 questions.

The decisions that matter most are clear from the comparison above:

Both sets of rules apply from the same date, January 18, 2027. If the Fed's final rule keeps its current approach, the United States will begin regulating stablecoins with a common redemption deadline and two different reserve rulebooks, decided by which agency charters the issuer.

#5373. Ripple Moves $389 Million of XRP Amid Aid for Binance Hack

The San Francisco blockchain firm backing XRP, Ripple, has just pulled a mysterious XRP move that could barely go unnoticed considering the volume of the tokens involved.

According to the latest data provided by blockchain tracker Whale Alert, Ripple has been spotted moving hundreds of millions of XRP, a few hours after it announced support for Binance's attack.

Per the data, Ripple has conducted multiple transactions carrying a total of 310 million XRP worth over $389.08 million with an unidentified wallet address on Friday, October 30.

While the transfers were made in three separate transactions within just a few minutes, the data showed that they were conducted when XRP was trading at around $1.25.

The first transaction saw Ripple transfer 120 million XRP, worth about $150.57 million, to an unknown wallet. Meanwhile, the two other transactions saw 90,000,001 XRP worth $112.96 million and 99,999,999 XRP worth $125.56 million transferred to Ripple from wallets that could not be identified.

The timing and volume of such a transfer, especially from a renowned firm like Ripple, did not go unnoticed, and it has sparked concerns among market participants about the motive behind the transfers, as none has been stated yet.

Although speculations suggest that the move could have been attributed to Ripple selling XRP, especially at a volatile time like this, other commentators are raising a different concern.

Since the transfers arrived just hours after a Ripple executive confirmed that the company was assisting with efforts to address the recent exploit involving Binance, which led to the theft of some XRP, there are questions about whether the moves could be related.

Although Ripple had confirmed that it was actively freezing affected funds while coordinating with relevant parties, it remains uncertain if the XRP move is part of its aid in addressing the disturbing incident.

The annual growth of assets under management (AUM) on the Stellar network amounted to 360%, reaching the $4 billion mark. Retail investors, meanwhile, predominantly allocate funds within EVM-compatible L2 solutions.

Such single-day concentration should, however, be read with caution: one or two large institutional transfers can easily skew daily flow data, so the sustainability of Stellar’s lead will only become clear over weekly and monthly windows.

Tether Bitcoin holdings have reached 150,000 BTC, putting the company behind USDT among the world’s largest corporate Bitcoin holders.

CEO Paolo Ardoino revealed the figure during his keynote at the Plan ₿ Forum in Lugano, Switzerland, on November 3. The position is worth $11.5 billion at the current price.

🔥BIG: Tether holds about 150,000 BTC worth $11.5 BILLION, CEO Paolo Ardoino reveals.That tops every public company on BitcoinTreasuries’ list except Strategy, which holds 849,327 BTC, about 5.7 times as much.Privately held Tether sits outside the ranking.The figure is… pic.twitter.com/bDdTZ1G3DW

The disclosure places Tether behind only Strategy among major corporate Bitcoin treasury holders. It also highlights how the stablecoin giant is turning profits from its dollar-pegged business into a substantial Bitcoin position.

Tether has built its treasury through a strategy announced in May 2023. The company committed to allocating up to 15% of its net realized operating profits toward Bitcoin purchases.

Tether’s estimated 150,000 BTC position puts it well ahead of most companies pursuing Bitcoin treasury strategies. Strategy remains the clear leader, holding 849,327 BTC. Tether’s reported stack represents 18% of Strategy’s holdings, placing the stablecoin issuer among the industry’s largest corporate Bitcoin buyers.

The disclosure also puts Tether ahead of companies such as Metaplanet and Strive, whose Bitcoin treasuries remain below 50,000 BTC each.

Ardoino discussed the holdings while outlining Tether’s expanding role in the Bitcoin ecosystem. He also said the company serves more than 730 million users worldwide, adding 30 million wallets each quarter.

Tether’s Bitcoin strategy began in 2023, when the company announced plans to invest a portion of its operating profits into BTC. The policy allows Tether to accumulate Bitcoin using earnings from its business rather than relying entirely on external fundraising.

The company has also invested in gold, energy, Bitcoin mining infrastructure, and other technology projects. Bitcoin remains one of its most prominent long-term investment positions.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

Tether’s growing Bitcoin holdings are backed by a highly profitable stablecoin business. The company generated $4.5 billion in net operating profit during the first nine months of 2026, including $1.5 billion in the third quarter.

USDT issuance remained near $184 billion during the period, while Treasury bills and reverse repurchase agreements continued generating most of Tether’s income.

Tether’s third-quarter attestation showed $191.45 billion in reserve assets against $183.50 billion in liabilities. Its excess reserves climbed to $7.95 billion, nearly doubling from $4.1 billion at the end of June.

The company also reported $132.4 billion in direct and indirect US Treasury bill exposure, giving it a substantial source of recurring income.

This business model separates Tether from companies that raise capital specifically to buy Bitcoin. Strategy has relied heavily on stock sales and debt offerings to expand its treasury, while Tether can allocate a portion of its operating profits toward BTC.

Tether latest disclosure also puts its Bitcoin holdings above the amount listed in its third-quarter USDT reserve report. That report valued Bitcoin reserves at $8.37 billion on September 30, while Ardoino’s estimate puts the company’s total position near $11.5 billion.

Tether’s growing Bitcoin treasury shows how stablecoin profits can fund a major corporate crypto position. With USDT remaining one of the industry’s largest dollar-backed tokens, the company has a recurring earnings engine supporting its long-term Bitcoin strategy.

Strategy still holds a much larger stack, but Tether has emerged as a powerful corporate Bitcoin holder in its own right.

Dogecoin has just formed a death cross on its daily chart for the first time since 2026. The 50-day simple moving average (SMA) has crossed below the 200-day SMA, completing a death cross on the daily chart. The last time Dogecoin saw a death cross signal on its daily chart was in November 2025, which preceded months of downward price action.

The development comes only about three weeks after Dogecoin recorded a golden cross on its chart. On Oct. 5, Dogecoin's shorter-term moving average, the 50 DMA, moved above the 200 DMA in a bullish golden crossover.

Krisspax, a Dogecoin community member, highlighted this development in an X post: "We have a death cross on the Dogecoin chart when the 50-day SMA crosses below the 200-day SMA. It's only been about 3 weeks since we had a golden cross, the shortest crossover I've seen for DOGE of this type, stressing the volatility of Dogecoin trading."

The golden cross and death cross signals on Dogecoin's daily chart are unusually close to each other. There is about a 3-week gap between them, indicating a sudden change in momentum.

A golden cross is generally interpreted as a sign of improving medium-term momentum, while a death cross suggests that the shorter-term trend has weakened relative to the longer-term trend.

Dogecoin's price surprisingly rose ahead of the death cross signal, rising for three consecutive days to reach a high of $0.081 on October 29 before momentum slipped.

DOGE sharply fell to a low of $0.074 on Thursday, extending the drop on Friday to a low of $0.072, last seen in August 2026, as the market reacted to the news of Binance's $6.3 billion heist, deemed the largest in crypto history.

Total liquidations reached $1.68 billion in the last 24 hours, according to CoinGlass. Long positions, bets that prices would rise, accounted for the majority of the total at $1.43 billion.

Support is expected next at $0.069, while resistance stays near $0.086, around the daily moving averages.

#5367. Bitcoin Sellers Take a Week of Losses Below $80,000 as Strategy and Strive Keep Buying: Will $75,000 Hold?

All reviews, research, news and assessments of any kind on The Tokenist are compiled using a strict editorial review process by our editorial team. Neither our writers nor our editors receive direct compensation of any kind to publish information on tokenist.com. Our company, Tokenist Media LLC, is community supported and may receive a small commission when you purchase products or services through links on our website. Click here for a full list of our partners and an in-depth explanation on how we get paid.

Bitcoin (BTC) sellers booked their longest run of daily losses since mid-August last week, Glassnode said on Monday, November 2, as Strategy and Strive added 935 BTC between them, though Strategy spent three times as much buying back its own preferred stock.

Strategy bought 811 BTC for $65.5 million, at an average of $80,846, taking its stash to 849,327 BTC. The same filing shows $208.2 million going into STRC, the preferred stock Strategy sells to fund its purchases, which has been trading just under its $100 face value.

Strive bought 124 BTC for $10 million at $80,526 each, chief executive Matt Cole posted, bringing it to 43,124 BTC. For the first time, part of it was paid for by selling SATS, Strive’s own preferred stock.

Both companies bought above today’s price. Bitcoin trades at $77,948, below the $80,000 line where Glassnode says sellers have been accepting losses all week.

In August and September, the same kind of selling marked the bottom. So are sellers close to done again, or is the treasury buying too small to matter?

bitcoin:native sellers have been taking losses below $80k.Last week brought the longest run of daily net realized losses since mid-August.The August and September loss clusters both formed at the local lows. A hold above $75k would fit that pattern. pic.twitter.com/DCjbNfhoT7

A pattern that has twice marked a low. Glassnode tracks realized profit and loss, the gain or loss on each coin when it moves, against the price it last moved at. Since the October 29 Binance hack sent BTC under $80,000, the losses have outweighed the profits almost every day.

The firm’s chart, titled “Profit Taking Is Slowing Down,” marks the earlier loss clusters:

The logic is simple. Sellers who accept a loss are usually the ones who bought high and gave up, and once they are out, there are fewer coins left to dump.

“A hold above $75k would fit that pattern,” Glassnode wrote.

Two clusters in three months is a short record, though, and the August one came at a much lower price. The pattern only holds if buyers show up, which brings in the companies.

Its filings don’t say, but the price points to one reason. STRC is built to trade close to $100, and it closed Friday at $99.13. Strategy’s November 2 filing shows it bought back 2.09 million shares for $208.2 million, about $99.52 each.

That has become the bigger job. Over the last five weekly filings, Strategy spent $974.9 million on STRC and $137.8 million on BTC.

The board has topped up the buyback program by about $1 billion since mid-October, leaving $748.6 million to spend. Strategy now holds 849,327 BTC at an average cost of $75,451, about 3% below the current price.

Mostly with cash it already had. Strive’s 124 BTC came a week after it bought 6,182 BTC for $511.4 million, so the pace has dropped sharply.

The new part is SATS, Strive’s preferred stock. Its sales program was used for the first time, and all of the week’s program proceeds came from it rather than from ASST common shares, which fell 28% between October 21 and 30.

Cole also put Strive’s amplification ratio at 62.7%. That is its debt and preferred stock against the value of its BTC, so the lower the price, the higher it climbs. At Friday’s $76,764, Strive’s 43,124 BTC were worth $3.31 billion.

Discover: Bitcoin Rebound Faces a Test in Strategy’s STRC Funding

So far, it has held higher. BTC trades at $77,948 on Binance, down 0.5% on the day, and has stayed above its October 30 low of $76,326 for three days. That low sits right on the 200-day EMA (exponential moving average) at $76,510.

Both treasury companies bought above here, at $80,846 and $80,526, which is roughly where the 50-day EMA now caps the price at $80,287.

August 5 to November 2, 2026: BTCUSDT 1D chart. Source: Binance.

For Bitcoin, the test is the one Glassnode set: if $75,000 holds while the loss-takers finish, last week will look like August and September again.

#5366. Not Just Ledger: Karpeles Warns of Tampered Trezor Devices

The ex-CEO of the now-defunct Mt. Gox, Mark Karpeles, has flagged the potential compromise of Trezor hardware wallets sold by Southeast Asian reseller CryptoBilis, indicating that the recent supply chain attack on Ledger devices is not an isolated case.

"Ledger n'est pas la seule. @Trezor devices sold by CryptoBilis were also implanted," Karpeles said in an Oct. 30 post on X.

In his post, Karpeles advised customers who bought Trezor devices from CryptoBilis from March 2026 onwards to immediately transfer their cryptocurrency to new wallets with new recovery phrases.

He also offered to manually review potentially compromised devices, saying that he would be willing to cover the shipping fees if customers wished to get their wallets checked.

Karpeles's alert follows Trezor's confirmation that its security team was made aware of a credible report of a suspected hardware implant in a Trezor Safe 5 device.

As detailed in Trezor's Oct. 30 announcement, the device in question was acquired through the online marketplace Tokopedia in Indonesia in August 2026.

The report on the suspected device was received by Trezor on Oct. 28, and a video interview with the customer was conducted.

That said, Trezor said it hasn't checked the device in question in person to verify the report.

The report states that the suspected compromised device has an extra board between the main board and the screen.

The extra board has a cellular module and an antenna that can receive data from the device, such as the wallet's recovery phrase.

Afterwards, the data can be sent via a mobile network when the hardware wallet is plugged in.

This suspected modus operandi is similar to the highly advanced hardware implants previously found in Ledger devices sold by CryptoBilis.

In fact, Ledger's investigation into suspicious fund losses involving the reseller began on Oct. 9. Later, it was confirmed that some Ledger devices had been physically tampered with.

On the same day, Trezor decided to cut ties with CryptoBilis as an authorized reseller.

Four devices bought by CryptoBilis customers have been checked by Trezor, but no signs of tampering have been found so far.

According to Trezor, no CryptoBilis customers have reported losing funds in connection with the suspected Trezor implant.

Despite this, Trezor recommends that affected customers create a completely new wallet instead of just restoring their existing recovery phrases on other devices.
